title: Real Numbers: Divisibility, HCF & LCM
analogy: Think of every whole number as a LEGO model. Prime numbers are the single bricks that cannot be split any further, and every model (>1) is built from a unique set of bricks. HCF asks "which bricks do two models share?" and LCM asks "what is the smallest pile of bricks from which I could build either model?"
explain: ## Why primes matter

A **prime** is a number with exactly two factors, 1 and itself. Everything else >1 is **composite**, meaning it splits into smaller factors. If you keep splitting, you eventually run out of splits and are left with primes. The **Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic** says that this prime breakdown is **unique** (apart from order). 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5 and no other combination of primes multiplies to 360. All of divisibility, HCF, LCM and counting factors is just bookkeeping of these prime exponents.
## Divisors from exponents

Write N = p^a · q^b · r^c. A divisor of N picks an exponent for each prime independently: p can appear 0…a times (a + 1 choices), q 0…b times (b + 1 choices), and so on. By the multiplication principle the number of divisors is **(a+1)(b+1)(c+1)**. For 360: (3+1)(2+1)(1+1) = 24. A divisor count is odd only when every exponent is even, i.e. N is a perfect square — because divisors pair up as (d, N/d) and only √N pairs with itself.
## HCF and LCM from exponents

For each prime, the HCF takes the **smaller** exponent (what both numbers certainly contain) and the LCM takes the **larger** (what is needed to cover both). Because min + max = sum for any two numbers, HCF × LCM = a × b for **two** numbers (never for three). To find the largest tile that exactly fits a floor of 120×84, or the time at which two events next coincide, you are using HCF and LCM respectively: **"largest piece that divides all" → HCF; "first time all line up" → LCM**.
## Euclid's division lemma and the algorithm

For integers a > b > 0, we can always write a = bq + r with 0 ≤ r < b. Any common divisor of a and b also divides r (since r = a − bq) and any common divisor of b and r divides a. So HCF(a, b) = HCF(b, r). Repeating shrinks the numbers until the remainder is 0; the last non-zero remainder is the HCF. This is faster than factorising big numbers.
## Rational vs irrational and decimals

A **rational** number is p/q with q ≠ 0. Dividing p by q either terminates (remainders reach 0) or repeats (there are only q possible remainders so one must recur). Reduce p/q to lowest terms. It **terminates exactly when q has no prime factors other than 2 and 5**, because those are the primes dividing 10 (the base of our number system). Numbers like √2, √3, π have non-terminating non-repeating expansions and are **irrational**. A sum of a rational and an irrational is irrational; a product of a non-zero rational and an irrational is irrational; but √2 · √2 = 2 (surds can produce rationals).
formulae: a = bq + r, 0 ≤ r < b ⇒ HCF(a,b) = HCF(b,r)
digit sum divisible by 3 / 9;  alternating digit sum divisible by 11

s: Write a = ∏ p^α and b = ∏ p^β over the same primes (use exponent 0 if a prime is missing).
HCF has exponent min(α, β) and LCM has exponent max(α, β) for each prime p.
For any two numbers, min(α, β) + max(α, β) = α + β.
So HCF × LCM has exponent α + β for every prime, which is exactly the prime factorisation of a × b. ∎

derivation.t: Why the number of divisors is (a+1)(b+1)…
s: A divisor d of N = p^a q^b has the form p^i q^j with 0 ≤ i ≤ a and 0 ≤ j ≤ b (it cannot contain a prime that N does not).
There are a + 1 choices for i and b + 1 for j, independent of each other.
By the multiplication principle the total is (a + 1)(b + 1). ∎

derivation.t: Why the last non-zero remainder is the HCF
s: Let g = HCF(a, b). Then g divides a and b, hence g divides r = a − bq. So g is a common divisor of b and r.
Conversely any common divisor of b and r divides a = bq + r. So the pairs (a, b) and (b, r) have exactly the same common divisors, hence the same HCF.
The remainders strictly decrease and stay ≥ 0, so the process ends at a remainder 0, where HCF(x, 0) = x. ∎

solved.q: Find the number of divisors of 720 and how many of them are perfect squares.
s: A divisor is a perfect square only if all its exponents are even. Exponent of 2 ∈ {0,2,4} (3 choices), of 3 ∈ {0,2} (2 choices), of 5 ∈ {0} (1 choice).
Square divisors = 3 × 2 × 1 = 6.

solved.q: Two bells ring every 12 and 18 minutes. They ring together at 9:00 am. When next together, and how many times in the next 6 hours?
s: Next simultaneous ring after LCM(12, 18) = 36 minutes, so at 9:36 am.
In 360 minutes they ring together at 36, 72, …, 360 → 360/36 = 10 times (not counting 9:00 itself).

solved.q: Without dividing out, does 77/(2³ · 5² · 7) terminate?
s: The denominator has only the primes 2 and 5, so it terminates. The denominator 200 = 2³ · 5² → 11/200 = 0.055.

traps: HCF × LCM = product holds only for TWO numbers.
Always reduce a fraction to lowest terms before judging whether it terminates.
'Largest' (tiles, groups, rope lengths) → HCF. 'Smallest / first time again' → LCM.

title: Remainders, Cycles & Factorials
analogy: A clock. After 12 the hour hand wraps back to 1, so "15 o'clock" is just 3. Remainders are clock arithmetic with a clock that has n positions: you only care where the hand lands, never how many laps it made.
explain: ## What a remainder means

Dividing N by m gives N = mq + r with 0 ≤ r < m. We write N ≡ r (mod m). Two numbers are **congruent mod m** if they leave the same remainder, equivalently if m divides their difference. Because the laps (mq) disappear, **remainders can be added, subtracted and multiplied before reducing**: (a + b) mod m = ((a mod m) + (b mod m)) mod m, and likewise for products. This is why you can replace 2^100 with something manageable, step by step.
## Working with big powers

The trick is to find a power that is ≡ 1 or ≡ −1 and use it as a 'reset'. If 2⁵ = 32 ≡ 1 (mod 31), then 2¹⁰⁰ = (2⁵)²⁰ ≡ 1²⁰ = 1. For −1: 10 ≡ −1 (mod 11), so 10²⁰²⁵ ≡ (−1)²⁰²⁵ = −1 ≡ 10. Always look for the nearest multiple of the modulus to get a small positive or negative base.
## Cyclicity of the last digit

The last digit of aⁿ is aⁿ mod 10. Last digits of powers repeat in a cycle: for 2: 2, 4, 8, 6, 2, … (cycle length 4); for 3: 3, 9, 7, 1; for 7: 7, 9, 3, 1; for 4: 4, 6 (length 2); for 0, 1, 5, 6 the last digit never changes. To find the last digit of aⁿ, reduce the exponent n modulo the cycle length (using the cycle length itself when the remainder is 0).
## Fermat and Euler

If p is prime and p does not divide a, then **a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p)**. The reason: multiplying every number 1…p−1 by a just shuffles them mod p, so the product of both lists is the same, giving a^(p−1)·(p−1)! ≡ (p−1)!, and (p−1)! is invertible mod p. This gives the power-reset exponent p − 1.
## Factorials and trailing zeros

n! contains many 2s and 5s. Each (2 × 5) pair creates a trailing zero, and 5s are scarcer, so the number of trailing zeros equals the number of 5s in n!: ⌊n/5⌋ + ⌊n/25⌋ + ⌊n/125⌋ + … Also, n! is divisible by every number ≤ n, so for m ≤ n, n! ≡ 0 (mod m). Wilson's theorem: (p−1)! ≡ −1 (mod p) for prime p.
formulae: a ≡ b, c ≡ d (mod m) ⇒ a+c ≡ b+d, ac ≡ bd, aⁿ ≡ bⁿ
p prime, p ∤ a ⇒ a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p)
power of prime p in n!: ⌊n/p⌋ + ⌊n/p²⌋ + …
(a·b) mod m = ((a mod m)(b mod m)) mod m

derivation.t: Why a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p) — Fermat's little theorem
s: Take p prime and a not divisible by p. Consider the numbers a, 2a, 3a, …, (p−1)a.
No two of them are congruent mod p: if ia ≡ ja then p | (i − j)a, and since p ∤ a, p | (i − j), impossible for 1 ≤ i, j ≤ p−1 unless i = j.
So these p − 1 numbers leave the p − 1 distinct non-zero remainders, i.e. they are 1, 2, …, p−1 in some order.
Multiply them: a^(p−1) · (p−1)! ≡ (p−1)! (mod p).
(p−1)! has no factor p, so we can cancel it: a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p). ∎
A trailing zero is a factor of 10 = 2 × 5.
Among 1…n there are always more multiples of 2 than multiples of 5, so the 5s are the bottleneck.
Multiples of 5 contribute one 5 each (⌊n/5⌋); multiples of 25 contribute an extra one (⌊n/25⌋), multiples of 125 another (⌊n/125⌋), and so on. Add them. ∎

s: Powers of 2 mod 7: 2¹=2, 2²=4, 2³=8≡1. So the cycle length is 3 and 2³ ≡ 1.

solved.q: Find the last digit of 7²⁰²⁵ + 3¹⁰¹.
s: 7: cycle 7, 9, 3, 1 (length 4). 2025 = 4×506 + 1 → last digit 7.
3: cycle 3, 9, 7, 1 (length 4). 101 = 4×25 + 1 → last digit 3.
Sum of last digits 7 + 3 = 10 → last digit 0.

traps: When the exponent leaves remainder 0 modulo the cycle length, use the LAST item of the cycle (e.g. 3⁸ ends in 1, not 3).
Fermat needs p prime AND p not dividing a.
Negative remainders are fine as a tool, but the final answer must be reported in 0…m−1.

title: Percentages & Successive Change
analogy: A percentage is a price tag on a 100-slice pizza. 'Per cent' literally means 'per hundred', so 35% is 35 slices out of a pizza cut into 100. Every percentage problem is just: how many slices, out of which pizza?
explain: ## What it really is

x% means x/100. It is a fraction with the denominator fixed at 100 so different quantities can be compared on the same scale. 'x% of N' = (x/100) × N. The key skill is **identifying the base** — the quantity that represents 100%. 'A is 20% more than B' uses B as the base; 'B is how much % less than A' uses A as the base. The same absolute gap is a different percentage of each, which is the source of most mistakes.
## Multipliers make everything one step

Increase by r% ⇒ multiply by (1 + r/100). Decrease by r% ⇒ multiply by (1 − r/100). Successive changes just multiply their multipliers: +20% then −10% gives 1.2 × 0.9 = 1.08, a net +8%. You never add percentages across stages because each stage's base is different. The same idea gives population growth P(1 + r/100)ⁿ.
## Reversing a change

If a price rises by r%, it must fall by r/(100 + r) × 100 % to come back (e.g. +25% needs −20%). If it falls by r%, it must rise by r/(100 − r) × 100 %. The reason is the base changed: the original 100 became 125 and the 25 you need to remove is 25/125 = 20% of the new base.
## Fractions worth memorising

1/2 = 50%, 1/3 = 33⅓%, 1/4 = 25%, 1/5 = 20%, 1/6 = 16⅔%, 1/7 ≈ 14.28%, 1/8 = 12.5%, 1/9 = 11.11%, 1/11 = 9.09%, 1/12 = 8⅓%. Converting a percentage to such a fraction turns messy decimals into easy fractions. Also: x% of y = y% of x, which is often the shortcut to a hard-looking calculation (16% of 25 = 25% of 16 = 4).
## Percentage points vs percent
If an interest rate goes from 8% to 10%, it rose by **2 percentage points** but by **25 per cent** (2 is 25% of 8). Exam questions on shares and rates test this distinction.

derivation.t: Successive change formula a + b + ab/100
s: Start with 100. After an a% change it is 100(1 + a/100).
After a further b% change it is 100(1 + a/100)(1 + b/100) = 100 + a + b + ab/100.
The net change in percent is therefore (new − 100)/100 × 100 = a + b + ab/100 (use negative values for decreases). ∎
Take original = 100. After +r% it is 100 + r.
To return to 100 you must lose r out of 100 + r.
As a percentage of the new base: r/(100 + r) × 100 %. ∎

solved.q: A price is increased by 20% and then decreased by 20%. Find the net change.
s: Multiplier = 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96.
So the price ends at 96% of the original → net decrease of 4%.

solved.q: In an election with two candidates, the winner gets 62% of the votes and wins by 144 votes. How many votes were cast?
s: Loser gets 38%; margin = 62% − 38% = 24% of the total.

solved.q: The length of a rectangle is increased by 10% and its breadth is decreased by 10%. What happens to the area?
s: Area multiplier = 1.10 × 0.90 = 0.99.
Area decreases by 1%.

traps: The base of 'more than' / 'less than' is the quantity AFTER the word 'than'.
Never add percentages from different bases.
Percentage points ≠ percent.

title: Profit, Loss & Discount
analogy: A shopkeeper is a middleman: he buys at a wholesale price (CP), writes a bigger price tag (MP) to look generous, then 'gives a discount' to sell at SP. Profit and loss compare SP to CP; discount compares SP to MP. Two different gaps, two different bases.
explain: ## The three prices

**Cost price (CP)** is what the seller paid. **Selling price (SP)** is what the buyer actually pays. **Marked price (MP)** is the label price before any bargaining. Profit = SP − CP (if positive), loss = CP − SP. **Profit % and loss % always use CP as the base**: profit% = profit/CP × 100. **Discount** = MP − SP and **discount % always uses MP as the base**. Keeping the bases straight solves 80% of these problems.
## Multiplier method

Profit of r% ⇒ SP = CP × (1 + r/100). Loss of r% ⇒ SP = CP × (1 − r/100). Discount of d% ⇒ SP = MP × (1 − d/100). Chain them: if MP is x% above CP and the discount is d%, SP = CP × (1 + x/100)(1 − d/100). Successive discounts multiply too: two discounts of 10% and 20% are equal to a single discount of 1 − 0.9×0.8 = 28%, not 30%.
## Same price, two sales: always a loss

If you sell two articles at the same SP, one at x% profit and the other at x% loss, you always lose. Reason: the x% profit is earned on the cheaper article and the x% loss on the dearer, so the loss is bigger. The overall loss% is **x²/100 %**.
## Dishonest weights

A shopkeeper selling at cost but giving 900 g for a 'kg' earns a profit of (1000 − 900)/900 × 100 = 11.1%: he *sold* 1000 g worth but *delivered* 900 g, so the gain is measured against what he actually gave away (the cost of 900 g). General: gain% = (error)/(true weight − error) × 100.
## Using ratios

If CP : SP = 4 : 5 the profit is 1 on 4, i.e. 25%. When the same quantity is bought and sold in different sets (buy 12 for ₹100, sell 10 for ₹100) compare unit prices. Work with a convenient CP such as 100 or LCM-based values to avoid fractions.

derivation.t: Why selling two items at the same price with equal profit and loss % gives a loss of x²/100 %
s: Let both be sold at ₹S. The first is sold at x% profit: its cost c₁ = S/(1 + x/100). The second is sold at x% loss: cost c₂ = S/(1 − x/100).
Total cost = S[1/(1 + x/100) + 1/(1 − x/100)] = S · 2/(1 − x²/10⁴). Total revenue = 2S.
Loss = total cost − revenue = 2S[1/(1 − x²/10⁴) − 1] = 2S · (x²/10⁴)/(1 − x²/10⁴).
Loss % = loss/total cost × 100 = (x²/10⁴) × 100 = x²/100 %. ∎

solved.q: A trader marks goods 40% above cost and allows a 25% discount. Find his profit percent.
s: Profit = 5 on CP 100 → 5%.

solved.q: A man sells two articles at ₹1,200 each, one at 20% profit and the other at 20% loss. Find his overall gain or loss.
s: Equal SP with equal profit and loss % ⇒ loss of x²/100 = 400/100 = 4%.

solved.q: A dishonest dealer sells at cost price but uses a 960 g weight for a kg. What is his gain percent?
s: Reason: he is paid for 1000 g but gives goods costing 960 g.

traps: Profit/loss use CP as base; discount uses MP as base.
Two successive discounts of a% and b% are not (a+b)%.
False-weight gain uses the weight actually given, not the weight claimed.

title: Ratio, Proportion & Partnership
analogy: Mixing paint: a recipe of 3 parts red to 2 parts white gives the same shade whether you mix in a thimble or in a bucket. A ratio records the recipe, not the amount. Proportion says two recipes give the same shade.
explain: ## Ratio as a comparison by division

The ratio a : b compares two quantities **of the same kind** by division: a/b. Multiplying or dividing both terms by the same non-zero number does not change it, which is why 6 : 4 = 3 : 2. Ratios are unit-free, so quantities must first be converted to the same unit (₹ and paise, metres and cm).
## The 'parts' method

If a quantity T is split in the ratio a : b : c, then it has a + b + c equal parts and one part is T/(a+b+c). Everything follows from this: shares are a, b, c parts. If two ratios share a term, link them by making that term equal: given A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5, scale so B is the LCM 12: A : B : C = 8 : 12 : 15.
## Proportion and variation

a : b = c : d (a proportion) means ad = bc. **Direct variation** (y ∝ x): the ratio y/x is constant. **Inverse variation** (y ∝ 1/x): the product xy is constant. If 5 pumps empty a tank in 12 hours, 10 pumps take 6: more pumps (×2) but fewer hours (÷2). Joint variation combines: y ∝ x/z means y·z/x is constant.
## Componendo and dividendo
From a/b = c/d, we get (a + b)/(a − b) = (c + d)/(c − d), plus the simpler (a+b)/b = (c+d)/d. These give fast routes in equations of the form (x + y)/(x − y) = k.
## Partnership

Profit is divided in proportion to **investment × time**. If A invests ₹x for 12 months and B ₹y for 8 months, the profit ratio is 12x : 8y. Always compute 'capital-months' first. Working partners get the salary share before the remainder is split by capital-months.
## Changes in ratio

If a and b are increased by the same amount k the ratio moves toward 1:1, because the difference stays the same. Problems like 'the ratio of ages is 3 : 4 now and 4 : 5 in 6 years' are solved by writing 3x and 4x and using the second condition to form an equation.

a : b = c : d ⇔ ad = bc
y ∝ x ⇒ y/x = k;   y ∝ 1/x ⇒ xy = k
a : b = b : x ⇒ x = b²/a ;  a : b = c : x ⇒ x = bc/a

s: Let a/b = c/d = k, so a = kb and c = kd.
Similarly (c + d)/(c − d) = (kd + d)/(kd − d) = (k + 1)/(k − 1).
Both equal (k + 1)/(k − 1), so they are equal to each other. ∎

solved.q: A, B, C invest ₹20,000, ₹30,000 and ₹50,000. A is also a working partner for a salary of ₹5,000 from the profit. If the annual profit is ₹65,000, find B's share.
s: Pay the salary first: 65,000 − 5,000 = 60,000 remain.
Capital ratio = 2 : 3 : 5 (10 parts), one part = ₹6,000.

solved.q: The ages of two people are in the ratio 5 : 7. Eighteen years from now the ratio will be 8 : 10. Find their present ages.
s: Let ages be 5x and 7x. Then (5x + 18)/(7x + 18) = 8/10 = 4/5.
Ages: 30 and 42.

solved.q: If x/y = 3/4, find (2x + 3y)/(3x − y).
s: Put x = 3k, y = 4k. Numerator 6k + 12k = 18k; denominator 9k − 4k = 5k.
Ratio = 18/5.

traps: Convert to the same units before forming a ratio.
Partnership profit depends on capital × TIME, not capital alone.
Adding the same number to both terms changes the ratio; multiplying both terms does not.

title: Simple & Compound Interest
analogy: Rent for money. Simple interest is rent charged only on the sum you originally borrowed. Compound interest is rent that also charges rent on the previous rent: like a snowball picking up more snow the bigger it gets.
explain: ## Simple interest

If you borrow principal P at a rate of R% per year, the interest each year is the same fixed slice P × R/100. After T years the interest is SI = PRT/100 and the amount is A = P + SI. The growth is **linear**: equal interest every year, so the money grows along a straight line.
## Compound interest

With compounding, interest is added to the principal at the end of every period and then earns interest itself. Year 1 amount = P(1 + R/100). Year 2 interest is calculated on that new balance, so the amount becomes P(1 + R/100)². After n periods: **A = P(1 + R/100)ⁿ** and CI = A − P. The growth is **geometric (exponential)**: the amount multiplies by the same factor (1 + R/100) each period. If interest compounds half-yearly, use R/2 per period and 2n periods; quarterly: R/4 and 4n.
## SI vs CI in the first years

In year 1, CI = SI because compounding has not kicked in yet. In year 2 CI exceeds SI by the interest on the first year's interest: P(R/100)². For 2 years this difference gives a quick check: CI − SI = P(R/100)². For 3 years, CI − SI = P(R/100)²(3 + R/100).
## Growth, depreciation and doubling

The same formula describes populations (A = P(1 + r)ⁿ) and depreciation (A = P(1 − r)ⁿ). Under SI, money doubles in 100/R years. Under CI, the **Rule of 72** says it doubles in about 72/R years — an approximation that works for rates of 6–12%.
## Installments

Loans repaid in equal installments mix SI and CI: bring every payment to the same date using the interest rate, or discount each payment back to the start. Write the loan = present value of all installments.
formulae: A = P(1 + R/100)ⁿ;  CI = A − P
(1 + R/(100m))^m − 1 for m compoundings a year

s: SI for 2 years = 2PR/100.
Subtracting: CI − SI = P(R/100)². ∎ (It is exactly the interest earned on the first year's interest PR/100 at R%.)

derivation.t: Why compound interest is a geometric progression
s: End of year 1: A₁ = P + PR/100 = P(1 + R/100).
In year 2 the principal is A₁, so A₂ = A₁(1 + R/100) = P(1 + R/100)².
Each year multiplies the previous amount by the same factor r = 1 + R/100, so Aₙ = P·rⁿ. ∎

diagrams.cap: ₹100 at 12%: simple interest adds the same ₹12 each year (straight line). Compound interest adds 12% of an ever larger balance (curve). The curve starts level with the line but bends away.

solved.q: Find the compound interest on ₹10,000 for 2 years at 10% per annum compounded annually.
The difference between CI and SI on a sum for 2 years at 8% is ₹32. Find the sum.
A sum becomes 4 times itself in 20 years at simple interest. In how many years will it become 8 times?
s: Gain in 20 years = 3P ⇒ 3P/20 = 0.15P per year.
For 8 times we need a gain of 7P: 7P/(0.15P) = 46⅔ years.

traps: For half-yearly compounding halve the rate AND double the periods.
SI uses the original principal every year; CI uses the grown principal.
CI − SI = P(R/100)² only for exactly 2 years.

title: Averages & Weighted Means
analogy: A seesaw. The mean is the pivot point at which the bars on the left exactly balance the bars on the right. Move one value up and the pivot has to shift towards it.
explain: ## The mean as 'levelling out'

The **arithmetic mean** of n values is their sum divided by n. The right way to think about it: it is the single number that, if every item were replaced by it, would keep the **total** unchanged. So Mean × n = Total, and nearly every average problem reduces to working with totals. The deviations of values from the mean always add up to zero — that is the balance-point property.
## Changing the group

If a new member joins with value v, the new total is old total + v and the new mean is (old total + v)/(n + 1). The change in the mean equals (v − old mean)/(n + 1): the newcomer's 'excess' is shared among everyone. When one person is replaced, the mean changes by (difference)/n. This 'excess method' is faster than recomputing totals.
## Weighted average

If groups of sizes n₁, n₂ have means m₁, m₂, the combined mean is (n₁m₁ + n₂m₂)/(n₁ + n₂). It lies **between** m₁ and m₂, closer to the mean of the larger group. The weights matter. The same idea gives average speed for equal distances (harmonic mean 2ab/(a + b)) rather than the plain mean.
## Averages of arithmetic sequences

For consecutive integers, evenly spaced numbers, or any AP, the average equals the **middle** value (or the mean of the first and last). So the average of 1 to n is (n + 1)/2, and the average of the first n odd numbers is n.
## Other averages

The **median** is the middle value of the sorted data and the **mode** is the most frequent. For a roughly symmetric distribution mean ≈ median ≈ mode. The empirical relation for moderately skewed data: Mode ≈ 3·Median − 2·Mean. The mean is sensitive to extreme values; the median is not.

derivation.t: Why average speed over equal distances is 2ab/(a+b)
s: Distance d each way at speeds a and b. Times are d/a and d/b.
Total distance 2d, total time d(1/a + 1/b) = d(a + b)/(ab).
Average speed = total distance / total time = 2d · ab/(d(a + b)) = 2ab/(a + b). ∎

derivation.t: Mean always lies between the group means
s: Let m₁ ≤ m₂ and combined mean m = (n₁m₁ + n₂m₂)/(n₁ + n₂).
m − m₁ = n₂(m₂ − m₁)/(n₁ + n₂) ≥ 0 and m₂ − m = n₁(m₂ − m₁)/(n₁ + n₂) ≥ 0.
So m₁ ≤ m ≤ m₂, and it sits nearer the group with more people. ∎

solved.q: The average age of 30 students is 14. When the teacher's age is included the average rises to 15. Find the teacher's age.
s: Total of students = 30 × 14 = 420.
Total with teacher = 31 × 15 = 465.

solved.q: A car goes from A to B at 40 km/h and returns at 60 km/h. Find the average speed.
s: Equal distances → harmonic mean = 2·40·60/(40 + 60) = 4800/100 = 48 km/h.

solved.q: The mean of 5 numbers is 20. If one number is removed the mean becomes 18. Find the removed number.
s: Total = 100. Remaining total = 4 × 18 = 72.
Removed number = 100 − 72 = 28.

traps: Average speed over equal distances is NOT the arithmetic mean of speeds.
Use totals (mean × count) rather than guessing with means.
A weighted mean must weight by the group sizes.

title: Mixtures & Alligation
analogy: Blending two coffees. If a cheap and an expensive coffee are blended, the price of the blend must lie between them, and it sits closer to whichever there is more of. The seesaw again: the blend is the pivot, the amounts are the weights, and the distances from the pivot are inversely proportional to the amounts.
explain: ## What a mixture conserves

When two or more things are mixed, the **total quantity of the thing you care about** is conserved: litres of pure milk, kg of salt, rupees of cost, kilometres driven. So: (amount₁ × concentration₁) + (amount₂ × concentration₂) = (total amount) × (final concentration). This one balance equation covers every mixture, price blend or solution problem.
## Alligation — the shortcut for that equation

Rearranging the balance equation: q₁(c₁ − m) = q₂(m − c₂), so **q₁ : q₂ = (c₂ − m) : (m − c₁)**, where m is the mean (final) concentration and c₁ < m < c₂. In words: *the ratio of the quantities is the inverse ratio of the distances of each ingredient from the mean.* Draw the cross diagram: put the cheaper and dearer values on the left, the mean in the middle, and subtract diagonally.
## Repeated replacement

A vessel has V litres of pure liquid. You remove x litres and replace with water, and repeat n times. Each operation keeps a fraction (1 − x/V) of whatever was there. After n operations, the amount of the original liquid left is **V(1 − x/V)ⁿ**. The key insight: each time, you remove the same *fraction* of the current mixture, not the same amount of the original liquid.
## Selling at a profit or loss in a mixture
A mixture of two grades costing ₹a and ₹b per kg in the ratio q₁ : q₂ costs (aq₁ + bq₂)/(q₁ + q₂) per kg. Selling it at a certain profit then follows the profit & loss rules.
formulae: left after n steps = V(1 − x/V)ⁿ
x removed and replaced each time
water to add = V(c − m)/m for dilution from c% to m%

s: Let ingredient 1 have concentration c₁ and quantity q₁, ingredient 2 have c₂ and q₂. Mean concentration m = (q₁c₁ + q₂c₂)/(q₁ + q₂).
Cross multiply: m(q₁ + q₂) = q₁c₁ + q₂c₂ ⇒ q₁(m − c₁) = q₂(c₂ − m).
Therefore q₁/q₂ = (c₂ − m)/(m − c₁). ∎
Fraction of the original liquid in the vessel after one operation: (V − x)/V = 1 − x/V.
Removing x litres of the (now mixed) liquid always removes the same *fraction* x/V of what remains, so each repeat multiplies the original liquid by 1 − x/V.
After n operations: V(1 − x/V)ⁿ. ∎

diagrams.cap: Mixing a ₹20 and a ₹50 grade to get a ₹30 mix: subtract diagonally → 20 : 10, i.e. 2 : 1. Twice as much of the cheaper grade, because the mean sits twice as close to it.

solved.q: In what ratio must tea at ₹300/kg be mixed with tea at ₹400/kg so that the mix is worth ₹340/kg?
s: Mean 340: distances are 340 − 300 = 40 and 400 − 340 = 60.
q₁ : q₂ = 60 : 40 = 3 : 2 (more of the cheaper).

solved.q: A vessel contains 40 L of milk. 4 L is removed and replaced by water; this is done 2 times in total. How much milk is left?
s: Fraction retained per step = 1 − 4/40 = 0.9.
After 2 steps: 40 × 0.9² = 32.4 L.

solved.q: How many litres of water must be added to 30 L of a 40% acid solution to make it a 30% solution?
s: Acid = 40% of 30 = 12 L, which stays fixed.
Final volume V with 12/V = 0.3 ⇒ V = 40 L.
Water added = 40 − 30 = 10 L.

traps: Alligation subtracts diagonally: cheaper ratio uses the (dearer − mean) gap.
In replacement problems the removal is of the MIXTURE, so the fraction multiplies each time.
Track the substance that does not change when water is added (acid, salt).

title: Time & Work, Pipes & Cisterns
analogy: Filling a swimming pool with taps. Each tap has a rate, litres per hour. Add the rates when taps run together; subtract a rate when a drain is open. Work is the pool, time is how long it takes.
explain: ## Work, rate and time

The core equation is **Work = Rate × Time**, exactly like Distance = Speed × Time. Treat the whole job as 1 unit (or a convenient number such as the LCM of the individual times). If A finishes a job in 12 days, A's rate is 1/12 of the job per day. **Rates add** when people work together: A and B together do 1/12 + 1/6 = 3/12 = 1/4 of the job per day, so together they need 4 days. Never add the times.
## The LCM trick

Fractions get messy; instead assume total work = LCM of the times. If A takes 12 days and B takes 6 days, take 12 units of work: A does 1 unit/day, B does 2 units/day, together 3 units/day, so 12/3 = 4 days. Use this whenever times are whole numbers.
## Efficiency and wages
If A is twice as efficient as B, A takes half the time. Efficiency ∝ 1/time. When people are paid for a joint job, the pay is split in the ratio of **work done**, i.e. rate × days actually worked.
## Pipes and cisterns

An inlet pipe is a positive rate, an outlet is a negative rate. With a filling pipe of rate 1/6 and a leak of rate 1/10 the net rate is 1/6 − 1/10 = 1/15, so the tank fills in 15 hours. The leak is why the tank takes longer.
## Men × days × hours

If the work is proportional to M (men) × D (days) × H (hours per day) × E (efficiency), then M₁D₁H₁/W₁ = M₂D₂H₂/W₂. Doubling the men halves the days. Keep the effect of 'more of one → less of another' (inverse) straight, and 'more work → more time' (direct).
formulae: net rate = Σ inlets − Σ outlets

s: In one day A does 1/a of the work and B does 1/b.
Together: 1/a + 1/b = (a + b)/(ab) of the job per day.
Time for the whole job is the reciprocal: ab/(a + b). ∎

diagrams.cap: B is twice as fast as A (6 vs 12 days). Together the rates add: 1/12 + 1/6 = 1/4 per day, so the job takes 4 days, which is shorter than either person alone.

solved.q: A can do a piece of work in 10 days and B in 15 days. They work together for 4 days and then A leaves. How many more days does B take to finish?
s: Take total work 30 units: A = 3/day, B = 2/day.
Together in 4 days: 5 × 4 = 20 units. Remaining 10 units.
B alone: 10/2 = 5 days.

solved.q: A tank has an inlet that fills it in 6 hours and an outlet that empties it in 8 hours. If both are opened together, how long to fill?
s: Take capacity 24 units: inlet +4/h, outlet −3/h → net +1/h.
Time = 24 hours.

solved.q: 12 men can build a wall in 15 days. How many men would be needed to build it in 9 days?
s: Men needed = 180/9 = 20.

traps: Add RATES, never times.
An outlet or leak is a negative rate.
Pay is for work done, not simply days present.

title: Time, Speed & Distance
analogy: A speedometer integrated over a journey. Speed tells you how fast the distance counter on the dashboard grows. Distance, speed and time are three views of the same line on a graph.
explain: ## The only equation

**Distance = Speed × Time.** Everything else is a rearrangement. The pitfall is units: km/h × h = km, m/s × s = m. To convert km/h to m/s multiply by 5/18 (1000 m / 3600 s); to convert back multiply by 18/5.
## Proportionalities

At a fixed speed, distance ∝ time. For a fixed distance, speed ∝ 1/time. So if you increase the speed by one-third (×4/3), the time falls to ¾ of the old — a saving of ¼. If two people cover the same distance in times t₁ and t₂, their speeds are in the ratio t₂ : t₁.
## Average speed
Average speed = **total distance ÷ total time**, never the average of speeds. For equal distances at speeds a and b: 2ab/(a + b). For equal times: (a + b)/2.
## Relative speed

Two objects moving in the *same* direction approach/separate at the **difference** of their speeds. Moving in *opposite* directions they close at the **sum**. This turns two-body problems into one-body problems: a train passing a standing man of 20 m/s covers its own length at 20 m/s; passing another train moving the opposite way they cover the sum of lengths at the sum of speeds. The distance to cover when trains cross is the sum of their lengths (or just the train's length for a pole/person).
## Boats and streams
With a boat of still-water speed u in a current of speed v: downstream speed = u + v, upstream speed = u − v. Then u = (down + up)/2, v = (down − up)/2. Treat the stream as a head/tail wind.
## Circular tracks and races

On a circular track, two runners in the same direction meet when the faster has gained one full lap: time = track length ÷ (difference of speeds). In opposite directions: track ÷ (sum of speeds). For races: 'A beats B by 20 m in 100 m' means when A has run 100 m, B has run 80 m.
formulae: same direction: a − b;  opposite: a + b

derivation.t: Boat speeds from downstream and upstream speeds
s: Downstream: d = u + v. Upstream: s = u − v.
Adding: d + s = 2u ⇒ u = (d + s)/2. Subtracting: d − s = 2v ⇒ v = (d − s)/2. ∎

solved.q: A train 200 m long passes a platform 300 m long in 25 s. Find its speed in km/h.
s: Distance covered = train + platform = 500 m in 25 s → 20 m/s.

solved.q: A boat takes 3 hours to go 30 km downstream and 5 hours to come back. Find the speed of the stream.
s: Downstream = 30/3 = 10 km/h; upstream = 30/5 = 6 km/h.

solved.q: Two cities are 300 km apart. A leaves at 60 km/h towards B and B leaves at 40 km/h towards A at the same time. When do they meet?
s: Moving towards each other: relative speed 100 km/h.
Time = 300/100 = 3 hours.

traps: Don't average speeds to get average speed.
Trains: add LENGTHS when crossing another train/platform.
Convert units first, always.

title: Linear Equations & Inequalities
ncert: Class 10 · Ch 3 Pair of Linear Equations
analogy: A balance scale. An equation says both pans weigh the same. You may do anything to one pan as long as you do exactly the same to the other, and the scale stays balanced.
explain: ## Solving one equation

An equation like 3x + 5 = 20 is a statement that two expressions are equal. To find x, undo the operations in reverse order, applying every operation to **both sides** so equality is preserved: subtract 5, then divide by 3. The aim is to isolate the unknown. For equations with fractions, multiply every term by the LCM of denominators to clear them. Always check the solution by substituting back.
## Two unknowns need two facts

One equation in two unknowns (x + y = 10) has infinitely many solutions — it is a whole line of points. To pin the point down you need a second independent equation. Geometrically, each linear equation is a **line**, and the solution of the pair is the point where the two lines **meet**. This is why a pair can have exactly one solution (lines intersect), no solution (parallel lines) or infinitely many (the same line).
## Methods

**Substitution:** solve one equation for a variable and put it into the other. **Elimination:** multiply to make coefficients of one variable equal, then add/subtract to kill it. For a₁x + b₁y = c₁ and a₂x + b₂y = c₂, eliminating gives x = (c₁b₂ − c₂b₁)/(a₁b₂ − a₂b₁) and y = (a₁c₂ − a₂c₁)/(a₁b₂ − a₂b₁) (Cramer's rule). The denominator is the key: if it is 0, the lines are parallel or coincident.
## Consistency test
Compare ratios: a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂ ⇒ **unique solution**. a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂ ⇒ **no solution** (parallel, inconsistent). a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂ ⇒ **infinitely many** (coincident).
## Word problems

Translate in this order: (1) name the unknowns, (2) turn each sentence into an equation, (3) solve, (4) check against the story. Typical set-ups: ages (now / after / before), digit problems (10a + b), speed–time, fractions whose numerator/denominator change.
## Inequalities

Linear inequalities behave like equations with one exception: multiplying or dividing both sides by a **negative** number reverses the sign. The solution is an interval on the number line, and for two variables a half-plane bounded by the line.
formulae: x = (c₁b₂ − c₂b₁)/(a₁b₂ − a₂b₁),  y = (a₁c₂ − a₂c₁)/(a₁b₂ − a₂b₁)
multiply/divide by a negative ⇒ reverse the sign

s: Equations: a₁x + b₁y = c₁ … (1);  a₂x + b₂y = c₂ … (2).
Multiply (1) by b₂ and (2) by b₁: a₁b₂x + b₁b₂y = c₁b₂ and a₂b₁x + b₁b₂y = c₂b₁.
Subtract: (a₁b₂ − a₂b₁)x = c₁b₂ − c₂b₁, so x = (c₁b₂ − c₂b₁)/(a₁b₂ − a₂b₁).
Similarly eliminating x gives y = (a₁c₂ − a₂c₁)/(a₁b₂ − a₂b₁).
These exist only if a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ ≠ 0, i.e. a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂. ∎

diagrams.cap: Two non-parallel lines meet at exactly one point: the unique solution of x + 2y = 8, y = x − 1 (here x = 10/3, y = 7/3).
x + 2y = 8 and x + 2y = 12 have the same slope but different intercepts: parallel lines never meet, so there is no solution (a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂).

solved.q: Solve 2x + 3y = 12 and 3x − y = 7.
s: From the second equation y = 3x − 7.

solved.q: For what value of k does kx + 3y = 6 and 4x + 6y = 12 have infinitely many solutions?
The sum of the digits of a two-digit number is 9. If 27 is added, the digits reverse. Find the number.
s: Let the number be 10a + b with a + b = 9. Condition: 10a + b + 27 = 10b + a ⇒ 9b − 9a = 27 ⇒ b − a = 3.
Adding to a + b = 9: 2b = 12 ⇒ b = 6, a = 3. Number: 36 (check 36 + 27 = 63 ✓).

traps: Reverse the inequality when multiplying/dividing by a negative.
Check that your answer satisfies the original words, not just your equation.
'Infinite solutions' requires all three ratios equal.

title: Polynomials: Zeros & Remainder Theorem
analogy: A polynomial is a machine built only from adding, multiplying by constants, and raising x to whole-number powers. Its zeros are the inputs where the machine outputs zero: the places its graph touches the x-axis.
explain: ## Vocabulary

A **polynomial** in x is an expression a₀xⁿ + a₁xⁿ⁻¹ + … + aₙ with whole-number powers. Its **degree** is the highest power. A **zero** (root) is a value c such that p(c) = 0. Geometrically the zeros of p(x) are the x-coordinates where the graph of y = p(x) crosses or touches the x-axis. A polynomial of degree n has at most n real zeros (and exactly n complex zeros, counted with multiplicity).
## Remainder and factor theorems

When you divide p(x) by (x − c) you get p(x) = (x − c)q(x) + r, where the remainder r is a constant (its degree must be less than 1). Substitute x = c: the bracket vanishes and p(c) = r. So **the remainder on dividing by (x − c) is p(c)**. If p(c) = 0 the remainder is 0, so (x − c) is a factor — the **factor theorem**. For (ax − b) use p(b/a). This replaces long division with a single substitution.
## Relations between zeros and coefficients

If p(x) has zeros α, β, then p(x) = a(x − α)(x − β) = a[x² − (α + β)x + αβ], so comparing with ax² + bx + c: α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a. For a cubic ax³ + bx² + cx + d with zeros α, β, γ: Σα = −b/a, Σαβ = c/a, αβγ = −d/a. These let you find expressions in the roots (like α² + β² = (α+β)² − 2αβ) without ever finding the roots.
## Division algorithm

For polynomials, dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder with deg(remainder) < deg(divisor). If you know a quadratic divisor, the remainder is linear (px + q) and can be found by putting in both its roots.
## Identities

(a ± b)² = a² ± 2ab + b²; a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b); a³ ± b³ = (a ± b)(a² ∓ ab + b²); a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca), so if a + b + c = 0 then a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc. These make many 'evaluate' problems one-liners.
formulae: p = d·q + r, deg r < deg d

s: Divide p(x) by (x − c): p(x) = (x − c)q(x) + r where r has degree less than 1, so r is a constant.
Put x = c: p(c) = (c − c)q(c) + r = r.
Hence the remainder is p(c). ∎

derivation.t: Sum and product of zeros of a quadratic
s: If α and β are the zeros, then ax² + bx + c = a(x − α)(x − β) = a[x² − (α + β)x + αβ].
Compare coefficients: b = −a(α + β) and c = aαβ.
So α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a. ∎

diagrams.cap: p(x) = ½(x + 2)(x − 1)(x − 3): zeros −2, 1, 3 are exactly where the graph meets the x-axis. Up to the factor ½ it is x³ − 2x² − 5x + 6, so the relations check out: sum of zeros = 2 = −(−2)/1, product = −6 = −6/1.

solved.q: Find the remainder when x³ − 6x² + 11x − 5 is divided by (x − 2).
s: By the remainder theorem, remainder = p(2) = 8 − 24 + 22 − 5 = 1.

solved.q: If α, β are the zeros of x² − 5x + 3, find α² + β².
For what value of k is (x + 1) a factor of x³ + kx² − 4x − 4?
s: Factor theorem: p(−1) = 0 ⇒ −1 + k + 4 − 4 = 0 ⇒ k = 1.

traps: Remainder on dividing by (x + 2) is p(−2), not p(2).
A polynomial of degree n has at most n real roots — but exactly n complex roots.
Write x² − (sum)x + product, with the minus sign on the sum.

title: Quadratic Equations & Their Roots
ncert: Class 11 · Ch 4 Complex Numbers & Quadratic Equations
analogy: Throw a ball upward. Its height follows a parabola: it climbs, peaks at the vertex and falls. The roots are the two moments the ball is at ground level, and the discriminant tells you whether it ever reaches that level at all.
explain: ## The shape

A quadratic ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0) draws a parabola y = ax² + bx + c. The roots are where it cuts the x-axis. It opens upward if a > 0 and downward if a < 0. The axis of symmetry is x = −b/(2a), which is also the x-coordinate of the vertex.
## Completing the square — the source of the formula

Dividing by a and moving the constant: x² + (b/a)x = −c/a. Adding (b/2a)² to both sides makes the left side a perfect square: (x + b/2a)² = (b² − 4ac)/(4a²). Taking square roots gives x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)]/(2a). So the quadratic formula is just completing the square done once, for all quadratics.
## The discriminant

D = b² − 4ac is the thing under the square root. If D > 0: two distinct real roots (the parabola crosses the axis twice). If D = 0: one repeated root (it just touches the axis at the vertex). If D < 0: no real roots (the parabola floats entirely above or below the axis); the roots are a pair of complex conjugates. If a, b, c are rational and D is a perfect square, the roots are rational.
## Roots without solving

Sum α + β = −b/a, product αβ = c/a. Build a new quadratic with given roots: x² − (sum)x + product = 0. Symmetric expressions such as α² + β², 1/α + 1/β = (α + β)/(αβ) can all be computed from these two numbers.
## Maximum and minimum

By completing the square, ax² + bx + c = a(x + b/2a)² − D/(4a). If a > 0 the minimum value is −D/(4a) at x = −b/2a; if a < 0 it is the maximum value. This solves 'greatest area / least cost' problems without calculus.
## Equations reducible to quadratics

Substitute to reduce: x⁴ − 5x² + 4 = 0 with u = x²; x + 1/x = k with t = x + 1/x, using x² + 1/x² = t² − 2. Equations with radicals need squaring, so **always check roots** because squaring can add false roots.
formulae: D = b² − 4ac:  D>0 two real, D=0 equal, D<0 complex

derivation.t: Quadratic formula by completing the square
s: Start: ax² + bx + c = 0. Divide by a: x² + (b/a)x + c/a = 0.
Move the constant: x² + (b/a)x = −c/a.
Add (b/2a)² to both sides: (x + b/2a)² = b²/4a² − c/a = (b² − 4ac)/4a².
Square root: x + b/2a = ±√(b² − 4ac)/2a.
ax² + bx + c = a[(x + b/2a)² + (4ac − b²)/4a²] = a(x + b/2a)² − D/4a.
For a > 0 the squared term is ≥ 0, so the smallest value is −D/4a, at x = −b/2a. ∎

diagrams.cap: y = (x − 2)² − 3 = x² − 4x + 1. D = 12 > 0 so it cuts the x-axis twice, at 2 ± √3. The dashed line x = 2 is the axis of symmetry; the roots sit symmetrically about it, and the vertex gives the minimum −3.

solved.q: For what values of k does x² + kx + 9 = 0 have equal roots?
s: Equal roots ⇒ D = 0: k² − 36 = 0 ⇒ k = ±6.

solved.q: If α, β are roots of 2x² − 7x + 3 = 0, find 1/α + 1/β.
s: α + β = 7/2 and αβ = 3/2.

solved.q: A rectangle's perimeter is 40 m. Find the maximum possible area.
s: If length is x then breadth is 20 − x; area A = x(20 − x) = −x² + 20x.
Vertex at x = −b/2a = 10, A = 10 × 10 = 100 m².

traps: Check radical equations for extraneous roots.
Equal roots ⇔ D = 0, not D = 1.
In 'roots reciprocal of each other' c = a; in 'roots equal and opposite' b = 0.

title: Complex Numbers
ncert: Class 11 · Ch 4 Complex Numbers & Quadratic Equations
analogy: Extend the number line to a number PLANE. Real numbers sit on the horizontal axis; i is a step of one unit up. A complex number a + bi is a location: go a units across and b units up, like map coordinates, but with rules for adding and multiplying locations.
explain: ## Why invent i?

x² = −1 has no real solution because squares of real numbers are never negative. Rather than give up on equations like x² + 1 = 0, we **define** a new number i with i² = −1. Then every quadratic has roots. A complex number is z = a + bi where a is the **real part** and b the **imaginary part**. Arithmetic works as with polynomials in i, replacing i² by −1: (a + bi)(c + di) = (ac − bd) + (ad + bc)i.
## Powers of i repeat
i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1, then the pattern repeats every four. So iⁿ depends only on n mod 4. Any four consecutive powers add to 0 (i + (−1) + (−i) + 1 = 0), which makes long sums collapse.
## The plane picture

Plot a + bi as the point (a, b). The **modulus** |z| = √(a² + b²) is the distance from the origin. The **conjugate** z̄ = a − bi is the mirror image in the real axis, and z·z̄ = a² + b² = |z|² is always real and non-negative. Division uses this: (a + bi)/(c + di) = (a + bi)(c − di)/(c² + d²), which clears i from the denominator.
## Polar form and the argument

Let θ be the angle that the line from the origin to z makes with the positive real axis (the **argument**). Then z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) with r = |z|. **Multiplying complex numbers multiplies the moduli and adds the arguments** (this follows from the compound angle formulas), so multiplying by i rotates by 90°. De Moivre's theorem follows: (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ. The nth roots of unity are equally spaced points on the unit circle.
## Conjugate roots and cube roots of unity

If a quadratic with **real** coefficients has the root p + qi, then p − qi is also a root (D < 0 gives ± √D = ±i√|D|). The complex cube roots of 1 are 1, ω, ω² with ω = (−1 + i√3)/2. They satisfy 1 + ω + ω² = 0 and ω³ = 1, which collapse many expressions.
formulae: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), r = |z|
(cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ

s: Let z₁ = r₁(cos α + i sin α) and z₂ = r₂(cos β + i sin β).
z₁z₂ = r₁r₂[(cos α cos β − sin α sin β) + i(sin α cos β + cos α sin β)].
By the compound angle formulas, this is r₁r₂[cos(α + β) + i sin(α + β)]. ∎
ω is a root of x³ = 1 other than 1, so x³ − 1 = (x − 1)(x² + x + 1) = 0 and ω ≠ 1 forces ω² + ω + 1 = 0. ∎

diagrams.cap: z = 3 + 4i is the point (3, 4); |z| = 5 by Pythagoras, and the angle θ with the real axis is its argument. The conjugate z̄ = 3 − 4i is the reflection in the real axis, so z·z̄ = 25 = |z|².

solved.q: Evaluate i²⁰²⁵ + i²⁰²⁶ + i²⁰²⁷ + i²⁰²⁸.
s: Four consecutive powers of i sum to 0 (i, −1, −i, 1).
So the sum is 0.

solved.q: Write (3 + 2i)/(1 − i) in the form a + bi.
s: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate (1 + i): numerator (3 + 2i)(1 + i) = 3 + 3i + 2i + 2i² = 1 + 5i.
Denominator (1 − i)(1 + i) = 1 + 1 = 2.
Result: ½ + (5/2)i.

solved.q: Find the modulus and principal argument of z = −1 + i.
s: The point (−1, 1) is in the second quadrant on the line at 45° from the negative real axis, so arg z = π − π/4 = 3π/4.

traps: arg depends on the QUADRANT: tan⁻¹(b/a) alone can be off by π.
i² = −1, so (2i)² = −4, not 4.
Conjugate roots apply only when the coefficients are real.

title: Arithmetic & Geometric Progressions
analogy: Climbing a staircase vs. riding a rocket. In an arithmetic progression each step adds the same amount (a fixed-height stair). In a geometric progression each step multiplies by the same factor, so growth accelerates (or fades).
explain: ## Arithmetic progression (AP)

An AP has a constant **common difference** d: a, a + d, a + 2d, …. The nth term is Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d, because to reach the nth term you add d exactly n − 1 times. Any three consecutive terms satisfy b = (a + c)/2: the middle term is the average of its neighbours. The terms plotted against n lie on a straight line with slope d.
## Sum of an AP — Gauss's trick

Write the sum forwards and backwards and add: each pair (first + last, second + second-last, …) has the same sum, and there are n pairs, so 2S = n(a + l), giving S = n(a + l)/2 = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]. In words: **number of terms × average of first and last**.
## Geometric progression (GP)

A GP has a constant **common ratio** r: a, ar, ar², …. Tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹. Three consecutive terms satisfy b² = ac (the middle term is the geometric mean). The sum is Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) (r ≠ 1). If |r| < 1 the terms shrink to 0 and the infinite sum converges to **a/(1 − r)**; if |r| ≥ 1 it diverges.
## Means and inserting terms

The arithmetic mean of a, b is (a + b)/2; the geometric mean is √(ab); and for positive numbers AM ≥ GM, with equality only when a = b. The harmonic mean 2ab/(a + b) completes the family: AM ≥ GM ≥ HM. In an HP (harmonic progression) the reciprocals form an AP.
## Spotting the type

Differences constant → AP. Ratios constant → GP. Reciprocals form an AP → HP. For problems with 3 terms in AP, assume a − d, a, a + d (sum = 3a); for GP assume a/r, a, ar (product = a³). These symmetric choices cancel unknowns.

s: Write backwards: S = l + (l − d) + … + (a + d) + a.
Add the two: 2S = (a + l) + (a + l) + … (n times) = n(a + l).
S = a + ar + ar² + … + arⁿ⁻¹. Multiply by r: rS = ar + ar² + … + arⁿ.
Subtract: S − rS = a − arⁿ, so S(1 − r) = a(1 − rⁿ).

diagrams.cap: AP 5, 10, 15, …: the points lie on a straight line (constant gap). GP 3, 6, 12, …: the gaps keep doubling, so the points curve upward.

solved.q: Find the sum of the first 20 terms of the AP 3, 7, 11, …
Find the sum of the infinite GP 8, 4, 2, 1, …
Three numbers in AP have sum 15 and product 105. Find them.
s: Let them be a − d, a, a + d. Sum 3a = 15 ⇒ a = 5.
Numbers: 3, 5, 7.

traps: n − 1, not n, differences are added to reach Tₙ.
S∞ exists only for |r| < 1.
If Sₙ is given, Tₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁ (and T₁ = S₁).

title: Series, Telescoping & Means
analogy: Stacking oranges. 1 + 2 + 3 + … + n is a triangular pile; squares of numbers pile up as square-based pyramids. Each formula says how many oranges are in the pile, and the proofs are about rearranging the pile into a shape whose count is obvious.
explain: ## Key sums

Σk = n(n + 1)/2 (triangular numbers), Σk² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 (square pyramidal), Σk³ = [n(n + 1)/2]² (the sum of cubes is the square of the sum). With these three you can sum any polynomial series by splitting it up: Σ(3k² + 2k) = 3Σk² + 2Σk.
## Method of differences

If a term can be written as f(k + 1) − f(k), the sum **telescopes**: everything in the middle cancels, leaving f(n + 1) − f(1). Example: 1/(k(k + 1)) = 1/k − 1/(k + 1), so Σ = 1 − 1/(n + 1) = n/(n + 1). Look for partial fractions in denominators like k(k+1), k(k+1)(k+2) or √(k+1) − √k forms (after rationalising).
## Arithmetico-geometric and special series

A series like 1·2 + 2·4 + 3·8 + … has terms (arithmetic) × (geometric). Trick: multiply S by r and subtract, which turns it into a GP. For the series with terms k(k + 1), write it as k² + k and use the standard sums. Digit-based series (9 + 99 + 999 + …) are written as 10ᵏ − 1.
## Sums to estimate
For large n the sum Σk² ≈ n³/3: a smooth area-under-curve intuition. This connects to definite integration, where sums become integrals.

s: Write the sum twice: 1 + 2 + … + n and n + (n−1) + … + 1.
Add column-wise: each column sums to n + 1, and there are n columns, so 2Σk = n(n + 1). ∎
Use (k + 1)³ − k³ = 3k² + 3k + 1 and sum k = 1 … n.
Left side telescopes to (n + 1)³ − 1.
So (n + 1)³ − 1 = 3Σk² + 3Σk + n = 3Σk² + 3n(n + 1)/2 + n.

diagrams.cap: A staircase with rows of 1, 2, 3, 4 blocks. Two copies fit together into a 4 × 5 rectangle of 20 blocks, so one staircase has 10 = n(n + 1)/2 — the same idea as Gauss's pairing.

solved.q: Evaluate 1² + 2² + … + 10².

traps: Σk³ is the SQUARE of Σk.
In telescoping, check which terms survive at BOTH ends.
Σ of a constant c over n terms is nc, not c.

title: Binomial Theorem
analogy: Expanding (a + b)ⁿ is choosing, from each of n brackets, either the a or the b. The coefficient of aⁿ⁻ᵏbᵏ counts the number of ways to pick b from exactly k of the n brackets — that is 'n choose k'.
explain: ## Where the coefficients come from

(a + b)² = (a + b)(a + b). Expanding, each term takes either a or b from each bracket. The terms with one b come from choosing which bracket supplies b: 2 ways, so 2ab. For (a + b)ⁿ the coefficient of aⁿ⁻ᵏbᵏ equals the number of ways to choose which k of the n brackets give b: **C(n, k) = n!/(k!(n − k)!)**. That is the Binomial Theorem: (a + b)ⁿ = Σ C(n, k) aⁿ⁻ᵏ bᵏ.
## Pascal's triangle

The coefficients form Pascal's triangle, where each entry is the sum of the two above: C(n, k) = C(n − 1, k − 1) + C(n − 1, k). (Pick a special bracket: either it gives b — C(n−1, k−1) ways — or it gives a — C(n−1, k) ways.) The triangle is symmetric: C(n, k) = C(n, n − k).
## General term

The (r + 1)th term is Tᵣ₊₁ = C(n, r) aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ. To find a particular term, match the power of x: for (x² + 1/x)¹⁰ the general term is C(10, r)(x²)¹⁰⁻ʳ(1/x)ʳ = C(10, r)x²⁰⁻³ʳ, so a constant term needs 20 − 3r = 0 (no integer r ⇒ no constant term).
## Useful consequences

Put a = b = 1: ΣC(n, k) = 2ⁿ (total number of subsets). Put a = 1, b = −1: alternating sum = 0, so the sum of even-indexed coefficients equals the sum of odd-indexed ones, each 2ⁿ⁻¹. The sum of all coefficients of a polynomial in x is its value at x = 1.
## Middle and greatest term

The coefficients rise to the middle and then fall: for even n the middle term is the (n/2 + 1)th; for odd n two middle terms. The greatest *term* in (1 + x)ⁿ depends on x; compare consecutive terms with Tᵣ₊₁/Tᵣ = (n − r + 1)x/r.
## Approximations and remainders
For small x, (1 + x)ⁿ ≈ 1 + nx. Binomial expansion also gives remainder results: 7ⁿ = (8 − 1)ⁿ has a neat remainder mod 8.

derivation.t: Why the coefficient of aⁿ⁻ᵏbᵏ is C(n, k)
s: (a + b)ⁿ = (a + b)(a + b)…(a + b), n factors.
Multiplying out, each term of the expansion comes from picking a or b from every bracket.
A term aⁿ⁻ᵏbᵏ arises exactly when b is picked from k of the brackets and a from the remaining n − k.
The number of ways to choose those k brackets is C(n, k). ∎
In (1 + 1)ⁿ = ΣC(n,k)·1ⁿ⁻ᵏ·1ᵏ the left side is 2ⁿ and the right side is ΣC(n,k). ∎

solved.q: Find the coefficient of x³ in (1 + 2x)⁶.
s: General term: C(6, r)(2x)ʳ. For x³: r = 3 → C(6,3)·2³ = 20 × 8 = 160.

solved.q: Find the constant term in (x + 1/x)⁸.
s: General term: C(8, r)x⁸⁻ʳ · x⁻ʳ = C(8, r)x⁸⁻²ʳ.

solved.q: Find the remainder when 7¹⁰⁰ is divided by 8.
s: 7¹⁰⁰ = (8 − 1)¹⁰⁰. Every term except the last has a factor 8; the last is (−1)¹⁰⁰ = 1.
Remainder = 1.

traps: The (r+1)th term uses C(n, r), not C(n, r+1).
Constant term: set the TOTAL power of x to zero.
Don't forget numerical coefficients (2x)ʳ → 2ʳxʳ.

title: Exponents & Logarithms
ncert: Class 9 · Ch 1 Number Systems (laws of exponents)
analogy: Exponent and logarithm are an action and its undo button. 2³ = 8 asks 'what do I get if I double three times?'; log₂ 8 = 3 asks 'how many doublings does it take to reach 8?'. A logarithm is the exponent in disguise.
explain: ## Laws of exponents

aᵐ means a multiplied m times, so aᵐ·aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ (count the multiplications) and (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ. Dividing: aᵐ/aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ, which forces a⁰ = 1 and a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ so the rules stay true for all integers. Fractions: a^(1/n) is the nth root, because (a^(1/n))ⁿ = a¹. Most equations in exponents are solved by writing both sides with the same base and equating exponents.
## The logarithm

By definition **log_a N = x ⇔ aˣ = N** (a > 0, a ≠ 1, N > 0). So log₂ 32 = 5, log₁₀ 1000 = 3. It answers 'to what power must I raise the base to get N?'. Two immediate consequences: log_a 1 = 0 and log_a a = 1.
## Laws of logarithms

Because logs are exponents, the exponent laws translate directly. aᵐ·aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ becomes **log(MN) = log M + log N**; division gives log(M/N) = log M − log N; and (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ becomes log(Mᵖ) = p log M. Changing the base: log_a N = log_b N / log_b a. In particular log_a b · log_b a = 1.
## The graph

y = aˣ and y = log_a x are mirror images in the line y = x because they undo each other. The log curve passes through (1, 0), exists only for x > 0, and rises slowly (for a > 1). It also shows why a log of a negative number or zero is undefined.
## Digits and magnitude

The number of digits in N is ⌊log₁₀ N⌋ + 1. The characteristic ⌊log₁₀ N⌋ gives the order of magnitude. For leading-digit questions you need the fractional part of log₁₀ N. Other typical uses: solving aˣ = b via x = log b/log a, compound interest, and comparing huge numbers by comparing their logs.
## Inequalities with logs
For base > 1, log is increasing so log M > log N ⇔ M > N. For 0 < base < 1 the log is decreasing and the inequality flips. Always check the domain (arguments must be positive) at the end.
formulae: log MN = log M + log N;  log(M/N) = log M − log N
log_a N = log_b N / log_b a;   log_a b = 1/log_b a
log_a 1 = 0, log_a a = 1, a^(log_a N) = N

s: Let log_a M = p and log_a N = q, so M = a^p and N = a^q.
Then MN = a^p · a^q = a^(p+q).
By definition, log_a(MN) = p + q = log_a M + log_a N. ∎
Let x = log_a N, so aˣ = N.
Take log to base b of both sides: x log_b a = log_b N.
So x = log_b N / log_b a. ∎

diagrams.cap: y = 2ˣ and y = log₂x are reflections in the dashed line y = x. The exponential grows fast; the log grows slowly and is defined only for x > 0.

solved.q: If log₁₀ 2 = 0.3010, find the number of digits in 2⁶⁴.
Solve log₂(x + 3) + log₂(x − 3) = 4.

Check the domain after solving — reject roots that make an argument ≤ 0.

title: Modulus (Absolute Value)
analogy: |x| is distance from home, ignoring direction. |a − b| is the distance between two houses on a street: it does not matter who you start from, and it can never be negative.
explain: ## Definition as distance

|x| = x if x ≥ 0 and −x if x < 0. It is the distance of x from 0 on the number line, always non-negative. More generally **|x − a| is the distance between x and a**. This single idea solves most modulus problems without algebra: |x − 2| = 5 means 'x is 5 units from 2', so x = 7 or −3.
## Equations and inequalities

|x − a| = k (k > 0) ⇒ x = a ± k. |x − a| < k ⇒ **a − k < x < a + k** (within k of a, a bounded interval). |x − a| > k ⇒ x < a − k or x > a + k (further than k from a, two outer rays). If k < 0, |x − a| = k has no solution and |x − a| > k is true for every x.
## Several moduli — critical points

For an equation such as |x − 1| + |x − 4| = 7 split the number line at the critical points x = 1 and x = 4. On each piece, remove the modulus signs with the right sign, solve, and keep only answers inside that piece. Geometrically, |x − 1| + |x − 4| is the total distance from x to the two points 1 and 4: it equals 3 (the minimum) anywhere between them and grows once you go outside.
## Properties

|ab| = |a||b|; |a/b| = |a|/|b|; |a|² = a²; √(a²) = |a| (this is why square roots return the positive root); and the triangle inequality |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|, with equality when a and b have the same sign.
## Graphs
The graph of y = |f(x)| is the graph of y = f(x) with the parts below the x-axis reflected upward. The graph of y = |x − a| is a V with its vertex at (a, 0).
formulae: |a − b| = distance between a and b
x < a − k or x > a + k

derivation.t: |x − a| < k ⇔ a − k < x < a + k
s: |x − a| < k says the distance between x and a is less than k.
Numbers closer than k to a are exactly those between a − k and a + k.
Algebraically: if x ≥ a then x − a < k; if x < a then a − x < k, i.e. x > a − k. Together a − k < x < a + k. ∎
We have −|a| ≤ a ≤ |a| and −|b| ≤ b ≤ |b|.
Adding: −(|a| + |b|) ≤ a + b ≤ |a| + |b|.
That says |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|. ∎

diagrams.cap: y = |x − 1| is a V with vertex at x = 1. The line y = 3 cuts it where |x − 1| = 3, i.e. x = −2 and x = 4, which are 3 units either side of 1. The region below the line (|x − 1| < 3) is −2 < x < 4.

solved.q: Solve |2x − 3| ≤ 5.

s: Critical points 2 and 5.

solved.q: Find the minimum value of |x − 3| + |x + 2|.
s: It is the total distance from x to 3 and −2; minimum occurs when x is between them: distance 3 − (−2) = 5.

traps: |x| < k gives ONE interval; |x| > k gives TWO rays.
Check each piece's answer lies inside its piece.
√(x²) = |x|, not x.

title: Sets, Venn Diagrams & Counting
analogy: A set is a club; membership is yes/no. Union is merging two clubs' rosters, intersection is the people in both clubs, and complement is everyone in the school who is not in the club.
explain: ## Basics

A **set** is a well-defined collection of distinct objects. A is a **subset** of B (A ⊆ B) if every element of A is in B. The **universal set** U contains everything under discussion. The **empty set** ∅ has no elements and is a subset of every set. A set with n elements has **2ⁿ subsets** (each element is either in or out), of which 2ⁿ − 1 are non-empty and 2ⁿ − 2 are proper non-empty.
## Operations

**Union** A ∪ B: in A or B (or both). **Intersection** A ∩ B: in both. **Difference** A − B: in A but not B. **Complement** A′: in U but not A. **De Morgan's laws:** (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′. In words: 'not (A or B)' means 'not A and not B'.
## Counting with Venn diagrams

n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). If you simply add n(A) + n(B), the people in both have been counted twice, so you subtract the overlap once. For three sets: n(A∪B∪C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A∩B) − n(B∩C) − n(A∩C) + n(A∩B∩C). The inclusion–exclusion principle alternates between adding and subtracting overlaps. For word problems start from the innermost region (all three) and work outwards.
## Number sets and intervals
ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ. Intervals: (a, b) excludes the endpoints, [a, b] includes them. Set operations on intervals are best done on a number line: draw both and read off the overlap or merge.
## Relations between sets

Two sets are **disjoint** when A ∩ B = ∅ (no common elements). The **power set** P(A) is the set of all subsets of A, with 2ⁿ elements. Sets can be defined by listing (roster form) or by a property (set-builder form): {x : x is an even prime} = {2}.
formulae: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)

s: A ∪ B splits into three disjoint parts: A only, A ∩ B, and B only.
n(A) = n(A only) + n(A ∩ B) and n(B) = n(B only) + n(A ∩ B).
Adding: n(A) + n(B) = n(A only) + n(B only) + 2n(A ∩ B).
But n(A ∪ B) = n(A only) + n(B only) + n(A ∩ B). Subtract the two: n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∪ B) = n(A ∩ B). ∎
x ∈ (A ∪ B)′ ⇔ x ∉ A ∪ B ⇔ (x ∉ A and x ∉ B) ⇔ x ∈ A′ ∩ B′. ∎

solved.q: In a class of 60, 35 play cricket, 25 play football and 10 play both. How many play neither?
s: Neither = 60 − 50 = 10.

solved.q: A set has 5 elements. How many subsets have at least 2 elements?
s: Total subsets 2⁵ = 32. Remove the empty set (1) and the 5 single-element subsets.

solved.q: In a survey of 100: 60 like tea, 50 like coffee, 30 like both. How many like exactly one?
s: Tea only = 60 − 30 = 30; coffee only = 50 − 30 = 20.
Exactly one = 30 + 20 = 50.

traps: Subtract the overlap once for two sets; add the triple overlap back for three.
'Exactly one' ≠ 'at least one'.
∅ is a subset of every set and counts in 2ⁿ.

title: Relations & Functions
analogy: A vending machine. You press one button (input) and get exactly one snack (output). A function is a rule that gives each allowed input exactly one output; it is allowed to give the same snack for different buttons, but a single button can never give two snacks.
explain: ## Relations

A **relation** from set A to set B is any set of ordered pairs (a, b) with a ∈ A, b ∈ B — a rule that connects some elements of A to elements of B. Relations can have properties: **reflexive** (every a is related to itself), **symmetric** (a R b ⇒ b R a), **transitive** (a R b and b R c ⇒ a R c). A relation with all three is an **equivalence relation**; it splits the set into classes of 'equivalent' elements (for example, 'has the same remainder mod 5').
## Functions

A **function** f: A → B is a relation in which **every element of A has exactly one image in B**. A is the **domain**, B the **codomain**, and the set of actual outputs is the **range** (a subset of the codomain). The vertical line test checks this on a graph: a vertical line must cross the graph at most once, otherwise one input has two outputs.
## One-one, onto, bijective

**One-one (injective):** different inputs give different outputs (f(a) = f(b) ⇒ a = b). On a graph, a horizontal line meets it at most once. **Onto (surjective):** every element of the codomain is hit (range = codomain). **Bijective:** both. Only bijective functions have inverses. y = x² is not one-one on ℝ (both 2 and −2 give 4) and not onto ℝ (it never gives negatives), but restricted to [0, ∞) in both domain and codomain it is bijective.
## Counting functions

If |A| = m and |B| = n: total functions = nᵐ (each of m inputs chooses an output); one-one functions = n!/(n − m)! (the nP m number, if m ≤ n); onto functions need m ≥ n and are counted with inclusion–exclusion; bijections = n! when m = n.
## Composition and inverse

(g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)): apply f first, then g. It is not commutative in general. The inverse f⁻¹ undoes f: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x. To find it, write y = f(x), solve for x, then swap x and y. The graphs of f and f⁻¹ are mirror images in the line y = x.
## Domain and range tips

Domain restrictions come from: denominators ≠ 0, even roots need non-negative arguments, logs need positive arguments. For the range, think about the extreme values of the expression (complete the square, or solve y = f(x) for x and find which y allow a real x).
formulae: f(f⁻¹(x)) = x;  graphs mirror in y = x

derivation.t: Why there are nᵐ functions from an m-set to an n-set
s: Each of the m inputs must be given an image, chosen independently from the n elements of B.
By the multiplication principle: n × n × … × n (m times) = nᵐ. ∎
Collect x: x(y − 2) = 3y + 1, so x = (3y + 1)/(y − 2).
Swap names: f⁻¹(x) = (3x + 1)/(x − 2). ∎

If f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x², find g(f(2)) and f(g(2)).
s: g(2) = 4, so f(g(2)) = 11. They differ: composition is not commutative.

s: Need x − 1 ≥ 0 ⇒ x ≥ 1, and x ≠ 5.
Domain: [1, ∞) except 5.

A function must be defined for every element of the domain with ONE image.
Range ≠ codomain unless the function is onto.

title: Distance, Section Formula & Area
analogy: A city grid. Any address is two numbers: how far east and how far north. Once every point has an address, geometry becomes arithmetic: distances become Pythagoras, midpoints become averages.
explain: ## Locating a point

Draw two perpendicular number lines, the **x-axis** (horizontal) and **y-axis** (vertical), meeting at the **origin**. A point P(a, b) is found by going a units along x and b units along y. The axes split the plane into four quadrants: I (+,+), II (−,+), III (−,−), IV (+,−). Points on the x-axis have y = 0; on the y-axis have x = 0.
## Distance formula = Pythagoras

For A(x₁, y₁), B(x₂, y₂) draw a horizontal and a vertical line to form a right triangle with legs |x₂ − x₁| and |y₂ − y₁|. The distance AB is the hypotenuse: **d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²)**. The square makes the order of subtraction irrelevant. To prove a triangle is right-angled, check the Pythagoras relation among the squared sides; for a rhombus/parallelogram compare sides and diagonals.
## Section formula

A point P dividing AB **internally** in the ratio m : n is a weighted average of A and B, the weights being the *opposite* parts: x = (m x₂ + n x₁)/(m + n), y = (m y₂ + n y₁)/(m + n). The point is closer to the end with the larger weight. Midpoint: m = n = 1. For external division use (m x₂ − n x₁)/(m − n). To find the ratio in which an axis cuts a segment, let the ratio be k : 1 and put the relevant coordinate equal to zero.
## Centroid and area

The **centroid** of a triangle (intersection of medians) is the average of the three vertices; it divides each median 2 : 1. The **area** of a triangle with vertices (x₁,y₁), (x₂,y₂), (x₃,y₃) is ½|x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)| (shoelace). If this is zero the three points are **collinear**: the 'triangle' has collapsed to a line.
## Locus

A **locus** is the set of all points satisfying a geometric condition. 'Equidistant from A and B' gives the perpendicular bisector of AB; to find its equation, set PA² = PB² and simplify (the squares of x and y cancel, leaving a line).
formulae: area = 0, or slope AB = slope BC

s: Let P divide AB internally in the ratio m : n, so AP/PB = m/n. Drop perpendiculars to the x-axis; by similar triangles the horizontal gaps are in the same ratio: (x − x₁)/(x₂ − x) = m/n.
Cross-multiply: n(x − x₁) = m(x₂ − x) ⇒ nx + mx = mx₂ + nx₁.
So x = (mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n). The same argument gives y. ∎

derivation.t: Area of a triangle from coordinates
s: The area of a triangle ABC is half the area of the parallelogram on AB and AC, which is |AB × AC| (the 2-D cross product).
AB = (x₂ − x₁, y₂ − y₁), AC = (x₃ − x₁, y₃ − y₁). The cross product is (x₂ − x₁)(y₃ − y₁) − (x₃ − x₁)(y₂ − y₁).
Expanding and collecting terms gives x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂). So Area = ½|x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|. ∎

6k − 3 = 0 ⇒ k = 1/2. So the ratio is 1 : 2.

title: Straight Lines
analogy: A ski slope. The slope tells you how steeply it falls or rises; the intercept tells you where on the mountain you start. Two slopes decide whether pistes run parallel, cross, or meet at right angles.
explain: ## Slope

The **slope** (gradient) m of a line is rise over run: m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) = tan θ, where θ is the angle the line makes with the positive x-axis. Positive slope: rising; negative: falling; zero: horizontal; undefined: vertical. The ratio is the same between any two points on a line (similar triangles), which is what makes a line a line.
## Equations of a line

**Slope–intercept:** y = mx + c. **Point–slope:** y − y₁ = m(x − x₁). **Two-point:** (y − y₁)/(y₂ − y₁) = (x − x₁)/(x₂ − x₁). **Intercept form:** x/a + y/b = 1 (cuts axes at a and b). **General form:** Ax + By + C = 0, with slope −A/B. All say the same thing: every point on the line has the same slope to a fixed point of the line.
## Parallel and perpendicular

Parallel lines have equal slopes (m₁ = m₂). Perpendicular lines satisfy m₁m₂ = −1 (the slope of one is the negative reciprocal of the other). The angle θ between lines with slopes m₁, m₂ is given by tan θ = |(m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)|.
## Distance from a point to a line

The shortest distance from (x₁, y₁) to Ax + By + C = 0 is the length of the perpendicular: |Ax₁ + By₁ + C|/√(A² + B²). Distance between parallel lines Ax + By + C₁ = 0 and Ax + By + C₂ = 0 is |C₁ − C₂|/√(A² + B²). The numerator is simply the 'value of the equation at the point' — zero if the point is on the line.
## Family of lines

Lines through the intersection of L₁ = 0 and L₂ = 0 can be written L₁ + λL₂ = 0. Choose λ to satisfy an extra condition (passing through a point, having a certain slope). This avoids solving for the intersection first.

derivation.t: Distance from a point to a line
s: Let L: Ax + By + C = 0 and P(x₁, y₁). Let Q(x, y) be the foot of the perpendicular. PQ is parallel to the normal vector (A, B), so (x₁ − x, y₁ − y) = t(A, B) for some t.
Substitute Q = (x₁ − tA, y₁ − tB) into the line: A(x₁ − tA) + B(y₁ − tB) + C = 0 ⇒ t = (Ax₁ + By₁ + C)/(A² + B²).
Distance PQ = |t|√(A² + B²) = |Ax₁ + By₁ + C|/√(A² + B²). ∎
A line of slope m has direction vector (1, m). Perpendicular lines have perpendicular direction vectors: (1, m₁)·(1, m₂) = 0.
1 + m₁m₂ = 0 ⇒ m₁m₂ = −1. ∎

diagrams.cap: y = ½x + 1 and y = −2x + 6 have slopes ½ and −2, whose product is −1, so they meet at a right angle at (2, 2).

solved.q: Find the equation of the line through (2, 3) perpendicular to 3x − 2y + 5 = 0.
s: Given line slope = 3/2. Perpendicular slope = −2/3.

solved.q: Find the distance from (1, 2) to the line 3x + 4y − 5 = 0.
Find the angle between y = x and y = √3 x.
s: tan 15° = 2 − √3, so θ = 15°. (Check: the lines are at 45° and 60°.)

traps: Perpendicular needs m₁m₂ = −1, not m₁ = −m₂.
A vertical line has no slope: use x = a.
Make the line's right side 0 before using the distance formula.

title: Circles in the Plane
analogy: A circle is a compass drawing: fix the pointed end at the centre, keep the pencil at a constant distance (the radius), and every point the pencil visits is on the circle. The equation is that sentence written with the distance formula.
explain: ## Standard equation

A point P(x, y) lies on the circle with centre C(h, k) and radius r exactly when PC = r. Squaring the distance formula: **(x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²**. For a circle centred at the origin: x² + y² = r². A point is inside, on, or outside the circle according to whether (x − h)² + (y − k)² is <, =, or > r².
## General form

Expand: x² + y² − 2hx − 2ky + (h² + k² − r²) = 0. So any equation x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 is a circle with **centre (−g, −f)** and **radius √(g² + f² − c)**, provided g² + f² − c > 0. Recognise it by: equal coefficients of x² and y², no xy term. To convert, complete the square in x and y.
## Tangent and power of a point

The **length of a tangent** from an external point P(x₁, y₁) to the circle is √(S₁) where S₁ = x₁² + y₁² + 2gx₁ + 2fy₁ + c. (It is the Pythagoras triangle with legs: tangent length and r, hypotenuse: distance from P to the centre; S₁ is also called the **power** of the point.) A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. A line y = mx + c touches x² + y² = r² iff c² = r²(1 + m²) (distance from the centre equals r).
## Line and circle

To find how a line meets a circle, substitute the line into the circle's equation to get a quadratic: D > 0 (two points, a **secant**), D = 0 (**tangent**), D < 0 (miss). Equivalently compare the perpendicular distance from the centre with r. The chord intercepted has length 2√(r² − d²), where d is the distance from the centre to the line.
## Two circles

Circles with centres distance d apart and radii r₁, r₂: d > r₁ + r₂ — separate; d = r₁ + r₂ — externally tangent; |r₁ − r₂| < d < r₁ + r₂ — intersect at two points; d = |r₁ − r₂| — internally tangent; d < |r₁ − r₂| — one inside the other.
formulae: y = mx + c touches x²+y²=r² ⇔ c² = r²(1+m²)
d vs r₁ + r₂ and |r₁ − r₂|

derivation.t: Centre and radius from the general form
s: x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 ⇒ (x² + 2gx + g²) + (y² + 2fy + f²) = g² + f² − c.
So (x + g)² + (y + f)² = g² + f² − c, i.e. centre (−g, −f) and r² = g² + f² − c. ∎
Let T be the point of contact and C the centre. CT ⟂ PT, so PT² = PC² − r².
PC² = (x₁ + g)² + (y₁ + f)² and r² = g² + f² − c.
PT² = x₁² + 2gx₁ + g² + y₁² + 2fy₁ + f² − g² − f² + c = x₁² + y₁² + 2gx₁ + 2fy₁ + c. ∎
