title: Parabola, Ellipse & Hyperbola
analogy: Shine a torch on a wall. The beam is a cone of light; tilt the wall and the lit shape changes: circle, ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola. They are all slices of one cone, and all described by one rule about distances.
explain: ## One definition for all

Fix a point F (the **focus**) and a line (the **directrix**). A conic is the set of points P for which **PF = e × (distance of P from the directrix)**, where e is the **eccentricity**. e = 1: parabola. 0 < e < 1: ellipse. e > 1: hyperbola. (e = 0 is the circle.) Eccentricity measures how stretched or open the curve is.
## Parabola

For y² = 4ax: focus (a, 0), directrix x = −a, vertex at the origin, axis the x-axis. The **latus rectum** is the chord through the focus perpendicular to the axis, length 4a. Every point is equidistant from the focus and directrix; a point at coordinate x is at focal distance x + a. Reflecting property: rays parallel to the axis reflect to the focus — the principle of a satellite dish.
## Ellipse

x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 (a > b): the set of points whose **sum** of distances to two fixed foci F₁, F₂ is a constant 2a. Foci at (±c, 0) with c² = a² − b²; eccentricity e = c/a < 1; major axis 2a, minor axis 2b; latus rectum 2b²/a. The more elongated, the larger e. A circle is an ellipse with c = 0.
## Hyperbola

x²/a² − y²/b² = 1: the set of points whose **difference** of distances to the foci is the constant 2a. Foci (±c, 0) with **c² = a² + b²** (plus, unlike the ellipse), e = c/a > 1, asymptotes y = ±(b/a)x, which the branches approach but never touch. Latus rectum 2b²/a. A rectangular hyperbola has a = b (asymptotes perpendicular).
## Identifying a conic

Look at the equation: squared terms of the same sign and equal coefficients → circle; same sign unequal → ellipse; one squared term only → parabola; opposite signs → hyperbola. To find the parameters, rewrite in standard form by completing squares.
formulae: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1;  c² = a² − b²;  e = c/a;  LR = 2b²/a
x²/a² − y²/b² = 1;  c² = a² + b²;  e = c/a;  asymptotes y = ±(b/a)x

derivation.t: Parabola equation from focus and directrix
s: Focus F(a, 0), directrix x = −a. A point P(x, y) is on the parabola iff PF = distance to the directrix.
√((x − a)² + y²) = x + a. Square both sides: (x − a)² + y² = (x + a)².
x² − 2ax + a² + y² = x² + 2ax + a² ⇒ y² = 4ax. ∎

derivation.t: Ellipse equation from the focal-sum property
s: Foci (±c, 0), constant sum 2a: √((x − c)² + y²) + √((x + c)² + y²) = 2a.
Isolate one root, square, and simplify twice to get (a² − c²)x² + a²y² = a²(a² − c²).
Put b² = a² − c² and divide by a²b²: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1. ∎

diagrams.cap: Ellipse x²/16 + y²/9 = 1: a = 4, b = 3, c = √7, e = √7/4. For any point P on it, PF₁ + PF₂ = 2a = 8.
Parabola y² = 4x (a = 1): every point P is as far from the focus F as from the directrix x = −1 (PF = PM).

solved.q: Find the eccentricity and the foci of x²/25 + y²/9 = 1.
Find the latus rectum of y² = 12x.
s: 4a = 12 ⇒ a = 3. Latus rectum = 4a = 12.

solved.q: For the hyperbola x²/9 − y²/16 = 1 find the eccentricity.

traps: Ellipse: c² = a² − b². Hyperbola: c² = a² + b².
In an ellipse a is the SEMI-major axis (larger denominator).
The parabola's latus rectum is 4a (not 2a).

title: Vectors & 3-D Geometry
analogy: An arrow on a map: it has a length and a direction. Walking 3 km east then 4 km north is an arrow of length 5 km pointing north-east of east. A vector is the arrow itself, independent of where it starts; coordinates are the recipe: so much in each direction.
explain: ## Vectors

A **vector** has magnitude and direction; a scalar has magnitude only. In components, a = a₁î + a₂ĵ + a₃k̂ = (a₁, a₂, a₃), where î, ĵ, k̂ are the unit vectors along the x, y, z axes. The magnitude is |a| = √(a₁² + a₂² + a₃²), and the unit vector in the direction of a is a/|a|. Vectors add head-to-tail (the triangle/parallelogram law) and subtract component-wise; the vector from A to B is B − A (position vector of the head minus the tail).
## Dot product — 'how much do they agree?'

a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ = |a||b| cos θ. It is a **scalar** measuring how much of one vector lies along the other. If a · b = 0 the vectors are **perpendicular**; if cos θ = 1 they are parallel. The scalar projection of a on b is (a · b)/|b|. The angle between vectors: cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|).
## Cross product — 'the area and the normal'

a × b is a **vector** perpendicular to both a and b with magnitude |a||b| sin θ, which equals the **area of the parallelogram** on a and b (half of it is the triangle's area). It is computed as the determinant of rows (î ĵ k̂ / a₁ a₂ a₃ / b₁ b₂ b₃). a × b = 0 means parallel. Order matters: b × a = −(a × b).
## Triple product
[a b c] = a · (b × c) = determinant of the three vectors; its modulus is the **volume of the parallelepiped** on them. If it is zero, the three vectors are coplanar.
## Three dimensions

A point is (x, y, z). Distance: √(Δx² + Δy² + Δz²). The section and midpoint formulae simply gain a z-term. **Direction cosines** (l, m, n) are the cosines of the angles with the axes; l² + m² + n² = 1. A line through a point with direction (a, b, c) has symmetric form (x − x₁)/a = (y − y₁)/b = (z − z₁)/c. A plane with normal (A, B, C) is Ax + By + Cz = D; the distance of a point from it is |Ax₁ + By₁ + Cz₁ − D|/√(A² + B² + C²).
## Angles
Between two lines: angle between direction vectors. Between line and plane: sin φ = |d · n|/(|d||n|). Between two planes: angle between normals.

derivation.t: a · b = |a||b| cos θ ⇔ component form
s: Consider triangle with sides a, b and a − b. By the cosine rule |a − b|² = |a|² + |b|² − 2|a||b| cos θ.
Expanding in components: |a − b|² = Σ(aᵢ − bᵢ)² = |a|² + |b|² − 2Σaᵢbᵢ.
Equate: Σaᵢbᵢ = |a||b| cos θ. ∎

derivation.t: |a × b| is the area of the parallelogram
s: A parallelogram with sides a and b has base |a| and height |b| sin θ.
Area = |a||b| sin θ = |a × b|. ∎

title: Triangles & Similarity
analogy: A photocopier with a zoom control. Zooming changes the size but not the shape, so all angles stay the same and every length scales by the same factor. Similar triangles are the maths of zoom, and almost every geometry trick comes from it.
explain: ## Congruence

Two triangles are **congruent** (same size and shape) if they satisfy any of: SSS, SAS, ASA/AAS, or RHS (right angle, hypotenuse, one side). 'SSA' does not work in general. Congruent triangles give equal corresponding parts (CPCT), which is how we prove sides or angles equal.
## Similarity

Two triangles are **similar** if their corresponding angles are equal, or equivalently their corresponding sides are in the same ratio k. AA (two equal angles) is enough, since the third angle follows from the 180° sum. SAS-similarity and SSS-similarity also exist. For similar figures: lengths scale by k, **areas by k²**, volumes by k³ — the reason area ratios are the *squares* of side ratios.
## Basic proportionality theorem

A line drawn parallel to one side of a triangle, cutting the other two sides, divides them in the same ratio: AD/DB = AE/EC. This follows because ΔADE ~ ΔABC. Its converse lets you prove lines are parallel. The **angle bisector theorem**: the bisector of an angle divides the opposite side in the ratio of the adjacent sides.
## Pythagoras

In a right triangle the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of squares on the other sides: **c² = a² + b²**. The converse says if c² = a² + b² the triangle is right-angled. Common triples: (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (8,15,17), (7,24,25). In general, if c² > a² + b² the angle is obtuse and if c² < a² + b² it is acute.
## Special centres

Medians meet at the **centroid** (divides each 2 : 1). Angle bisectors meet at the **incentre** (centre of the inscribed circle, r = Area/s). Perpendicular bisectors of sides meet at the **circumcentre** (centre of the circumscribed circle, R = abc/4Δ). Altitudes meet at the **orthocentre**.
## Area formulas
Δ = ½ × base × height = ½ab sin C = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)) (Heron) where s is the semi-perimeter. For an equilateral triangle of side a: Δ = (√3/4)a², height = (√3/2)a.

s: In right triangle ABC (right angle at C) drop the altitude CD to the hypotenuse AB = c.
Triangles ACD, CBD and ABC are all similar (they share an acute angle and have a right angle).
From ΔACD ~ ΔABC: AC/AB = AD/AC ⇒ b² = c·AD. From ΔCBD ~ ΔABC: a² = c·DB.
Add: a² + b² = c(AD + DB) = c·c = c². ∎

derivation.t: Areas of similar triangles are in the ratio of the squares of sides
s: Let ΔABC ~ ΔPQR with ratio k = PQ/AB. Corresponding altitudes also scale by k.
Area(PQR)/Area(ABC) = (½·PQ·h′)/(½·AB·h) = k·k = k². ∎

solved.q: Two similar triangles have areas 16 cm² and 49 cm². If a side of the smaller is 8 cm, find the corresponding side of the larger.
s: Area ratio = k² = 49/16 ⇒ k = 7/4.

traps: Areas scale by k², not k.
SSA is not a congruence test.
Match corresponding vertices when writing similarity (ΔABC ~ ΔPQR order matters).

title: Polygons & Quadrilaterals
analogy: Walk around the edge of any polygon and turn at each corner. By the time you are back where you started you have turned exactly once all the way round, 360° in total. That one fact explains all the angle formulas.
explain: ## Angle sums

Any polygon with n sides can be cut into (n − 2) triangles by drawing diagonals from one vertex. Each triangle has angle sum 180°, so the **interior angle sum is (n − 2) × 180°**. At each vertex, interior + exterior angle = 180°, and walking around the polygon the exterior angles add to **360°** (a full turn), for any convex polygon.
## Regular polygons

All sides and all angles equal. Each exterior angle = 360°/n; each interior angle = 180° − 360°/n = (n − 2)·180°/n. Hexagon: 120°; octagon: 135°; if the interior angle is given, n = 360°/(180° − interior).
## Diagonals
Number of diagonals = n(n − 3)/2: each of n vertices connects to n − 3 non-adjacent vertices, and each diagonal is counted twice.
## Quadrilaterals

Parallelogram: opposite sides equal and parallel; diagonals bisect each other. Rectangle: parallelogram with equal diagonals. Rhombus: all sides equal; diagonals bisect at right angles. Square: both. Trapezium: one pair of parallel sides. Kite: two pairs of adjacent equal sides. Areas: parallelogram = base × height; rhombus = ½ d₁d₂; trapezium = ½(a + b)h. A quadrilateral is **cyclic** if opposite angles add to 180°.
## Area of a regular polygon
A regular n-gon of side a splits into n isosceles triangles from the centre: Area = (n a²/4)·cot(π/n). For a regular hexagon: (3√3/2)a² (six equilateral triangles).

s: Choose one vertex and draw diagonals to every non-adjacent vertex: this makes n − 2 triangles that exactly tile the polygon.
The angles of the triangles together make up the interior angles of the polygon.
So the sum is (n − 2) × 180°. ∎
From each vertex, lines can be drawn to n − 1 other vertices, but 2 of those are adjacent (sides), leaving n − 3 diagonals per vertex.
n vertices give n(n − 3), but each diagonal has two endpoints and is counted twice.
So the number is n(n − 3)/2. ∎

solved.q: Each interior angle of a regular polygon is 150°. How many sides does it have?
How many diagonals does a decagon have?
The diagonals of a rhombus are 16 cm and 12 cm. Find its side and area.
s: Diagonals bisect at right angles: half-diagonals 8 and 6, so side = √(64 + 36) = 10 cm.
Area = ½ × 16 × 12 = 96 cm².

traps: Exterior angles of ANY convex polygon sum to 360°.
Remember to divide by 2 for diagonals.
A rectangle's diagonals are equal but do not cross at right angles unless it's a square.

title: Circles: Chords, Tangents & Angles
analogy: A circle is perfectly symmetric about its centre, so anything that happens at the circumference is tied to what happens at the centre. The theorems are different ways of saying: the centre sees the same thing from twice as close.
explain: ## Chords and the centre

The perpendicular from the centre to a chord **bisects** the chord, and conversely the line from the centre to a chord's midpoint is perpendicular to it. Equal chords are equidistant from the centre. If r is the radius and d the distance from the centre, the chord length is 2√(r² − d²) (Pythagoras on the half-chord).
## Angles in a circle

The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is **twice** the angle it subtends at any point on the remaining circumference. Angles in the same segment are equal. The angle in a **semicircle is 90°** (centre angle 180°, half of it). In a cyclic quadrilateral, opposite angles add to 180°, and an exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle.
## Tangents

A tangent touches the circle at exactly one point and is **perpendicular to the radius** at that point. Tangents drawn from an external point are **equal in length**. **Alternate segment theorem:** the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.
## Power of a point

For two chords AB and CD through P inside the circle: PA × PB = PC × PD. For an external point with a secant PAB and tangent PT: PT² = PA × PB. These products are constant for a given point and circle, and are the basis of many length-finding problems.
## Arcs, sectors, segments
A sector of angle θ has arc length (θ/360°)·2πr and area (θ/360°)·πr². The area of a segment is the sector minus the triangle. The incircle of a right triangle has radius r = (a + b − c)/2.
formulae: angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference
tangent ⟂ radius;  tangents from a point are equal

derivation.t: Angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference
s: Let arc AB subtend ∠AOB at centre O and ∠APB at P on the circle. Draw PO and extend to Q.
OA = OP, so ∠OAP = ∠OPA; the exterior angle ∠AOQ = ∠OAP + ∠OPA = 2∠OPA. Likewise ∠BOQ = 2∠OPB.
Adding, ∠AOB = 2(∠OPA + ∠OPB) = 2∠APB. ∎

derivation.t: Tangents from an external point are equal
s: Let PA and PB touch the circle at A and B, with centre O. OA ⟂ PA and OB ⟂ PB.
Triangles OAP and OBP: OA = OB (radii), OP common, right angles at A and B ⇒ congruent (RHS).
Hence PA = PB. ∎

solved.q: A chord of length 16 cm is 6 cm from the centre of a circle. Find the radius.
s: Half-chord = 8. r² = 8² + 6² = 100 ⇒ r = 10 cm.

solved.q: From a point 13 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm, find the length of the tangent.
s: Tangent ⟂ radius: length² = 13² − 5² = 144 ⇒ 12 cm.

solved.q: Two chords AB and CD intersect at P inside the circle. PA = 6, PB = 4, PC = 3. Find PD.
s: PA·PB = PC·PD ⇒ 24 = 3·PD ⇒ PD = 8.

title: Areas & Volumes of Solids
ncert: Class 10 · Ch 11 Areas Related to Circles
analogy: Area is how much paint covers a wall; volume is how much water fills a tank; surface area is how much wrapping paper covers a gift. Each formula is just counting unit squares or unit cubes in a smart way.
explain: ## 2-D areas

Rectangle lw; triangle ½bh; parallelogram bh; trapezium ½(a + b)h; circle πr²; sector (θ/360)πr². Perimeters add up the sides; the circumference of a circle is 2πr. The key unit principle: area is in square units, volume in cubic units; when lengths scale by k, areas by k² and volumes by k³.
## 3-D solids

**Cuboid** (l, b, h): volume lbh, total surface area 2(lb + bh + hl), diagonal √(l² + b² + h²). **Cube** side a: volume a³, TSA 6a². **Cylinder** (r, h): volume πr²h, curved surface 2πrh, total 2πr(r + h) — the curved surface is a rectangle 2πr × h when unrolled. **Cone**: volume ⅓πr²h, slant height l = √(r² + h²), curved surface πrl (an unrolled sector), total πr(l + r). **Sphere**: volume ⁴⁄₃πr³, surface 4πr². **Hemisphere**: volume ⅔πr³, curved surface 2πr², total 3πr².
## Why the cone is one-third of the cylinder

A cone and a cylinder with the same base and height: the cone holds exactly one-third of the cylinder's volume. This is a calculus fact — add up thin discs whose radius shrinks linearly — and it is also demonstrable by pouring water: three coneful of water fill a cylinder.
## Combinations and conversions

Many problems join solids (a cone on a hemisphere, a cylinder with a conical top) — compute each part separately, adding volumes but counting only the **exposed** surfaces for surface area. When a solid is melted and recast, **volume is conserved**: n small spheres of radius r from one big sphere of radius R satisfy n r³ = R³. Frustum of a cone: volume ⅓πh(R² + Rr + r²), curved surface π(R + r)l.
## Flow problems
Water flowing through a pipe forms a cylinder: volume per unit time = cross-sectional area × speed. Convert everything to the same unit before multiplying (cm vs m).
formulae: V = ⅓πr²h;  CSA = πrl;  l² = r² + h²
V = ⅓πh(R² + Rr + r²);  CSA = π(R+r)l
length × k ⇒ area × k², volume × k³

derivation.t: Curved surface of a cone = πrl
s: Cut the cone along a slant line and unroll it: you get a sector of a circle of radius l (the slant height) and arc length 2πr (the base circumference).
The sector is the fraction (2πr)/(2πl) = r/l of the full circle of radius l, so its area is (r/l)·πl² = πrl. ∎

At height y above the centre a slice of a sphere of radius R is a disc of area π(R² − y²). A cylinder of radius R and height 2R with two cones removed has, at the same height, a slice (ring) of area πR² − πy² — identical.
So the sphere has the same volume as cylinder minus two cones: 2πR³ − 2·(⅓πR³) = ⁴⁄₃πR³. ∎

solved.q: A solid is a cone of height 12 cm and radius 5 cm surmounted on a hemisphere of radius 5 cm. Find its total volume in terms of π.
s: Cone: ⅓π·25·12 = 100π. Hemisphere: ⅔π·125 = 250π/3.

solved.q: A metallic sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and recast into spheres of radius 2 cm. How many spheres?
Find the slant height and curved surface area of a cone of radius 7 cm and height 24 cm (π = 22/7).

traps: Cone volume has the ⅓; the cylinder does not.
Slant height ≠ height.
In combined solids, join faces are not part of the surface.

title: Trigonometric Ratios & Identities
analogy: A trig ratio is a scale-free description of a slope. A ramp that rises 1 m for every 2 m of horizontal run has the same steepness no matter how long it is. sin, cos and tan give that steepness a name for each angle.
explain: ## Where the ratios come from

All right triangles with the same acute angle θ are similar, so the ratios of their sides depend only on θ. Define, for the angle θ: **sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite/adjacent**. The reciprocals are cosec θ = 1/sin θ, sec θ = 1/cos θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ. Also tan θ = sin θ/cos θ.
## The Pythagorean identities

Pythagoras gives opp² + adj² = hyp². Divide by hyp²: **sin²θ + cos²θ = 1**. Divide by adj²: 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ. Divide by opp²: 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ. If you know one ratio you can find all the others by drawing the triangle and using Pythagoras.
## Standard angle values

From an equilateral triangle (cut in half) and an isosceles right triangle: sin 30° = ½, sin 45° = √2/2, sin 60° = √3/2, and cos goes in the reverse order: cos 30° = √3/2, cos 45° = √2/2, cos 60° = ½. tan 30° = 1/√3, tan 45° = 1, tan 60° = √3. sin 0 = 0, sin 90° = 1, cos 0 = 1, cos 90° = 0.
## Complementary angles

Since the other acute angle is 90° − θ, the opposite side for θ is the adjacent side for 90° − θ: **sin(90° − θ) = cos θ**, tan(90° − θ) = cot θ, sec(90° − θ) = cosec θ. This explains the 'co' in cosine (complement's sine).
## Evaluating and simplifying

To prove identities, convert everything to sin and cos, then use sin² + cos² = 1. Typical forms: (1 − cos θ)(1 + cos θ) = sin²θ; (sin θ + cos θ)² = 1 + 2 sin θ cos θ; (sec θ − tan θ)(sec θ + tan θ) = 1.
formulae: sin = opp/hyp,  cos = adj/hyp,  tan = opp/adj
sin²θ + cos²θ = 1;  1 + tan²θ = sec²θ;  1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ
sin(90°−θ) = cos θ,  tan(90°−θ) = cot θ
−1 ≤ sin θ, cos θ ≤ 1;  sec, cosec ≥ 1 in magnitude

s: In a right triangle with hypotenuse h, opposite o and adjacent a: o² + a² = h² (Pythagoras).
Divide every term by h²: (o/h)² + (a/h)² = 1.
That is sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. ∎
Take an equilateral triangle of side 2 and draw the altitude: it splits the triangle into two right triangles with angles 30°, 60°, 90° and sides 1, √3, 2.
sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √3/2, tan 30° = 1/√3; and for 60° swap sin and cos: sin 60° = √3/2, cos 60° = 1/2, tan 60° = √3. ∎

diagrams.cap: The angle θ at the left. 'Opposite' is across from θ, 'adjacent' is next to it (not the hypotenuse). The side names switch when you look from the other acute angle.

solved.q: If sin θ = 5/13 and θ is acute, find cos θ and tan θ.
s: Opposite 5, hypotenuse 13 ⇒ adjacent = √(169 − 25) = 12.

solved.q: Evaluate sin 30° cos 60° + cos 30° sin 60°.
Prove (1 + tan²θ)cos²θ = 1.
s: 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ, and sec²θ·cos²θ = 1. ∎

traps: tan θ = sin θ / cos θ, not sin θ · cos θ.
sin(A + B) ≠ sin A + sin B.
Opposite/adjacent depend on which acute angle you look from.

title: Heights & Distances
ncert: Class 10 · Ch 9 Some Applications of Trigonometry
analogy: Measuring a tree without climbing it: stand some distance away, measure the angle your eyes tilt up to the top, and let the tan ratio do the rest. It's surveying — right triangles hiding in the real world.
explain: ## The setting

The **line of sight** is the straight line from the observer's eye to the object. The **angle of elevation** is measured *upward* from the horizontal to the line of sight (looking up at a bird); the **angle of depression** is measured *downward* from the horizontal (looking down from a cliff). Since the horizontal lines are parallel, the angle of depression from the top equals the angle of elevation from the bottom (alternate angles).
## The method

1) Draw a clear figure with the vertical object, the horizontal ground, and the line of sight, marking known angles and lengths. 2) Locate the right triangle(s). 3) Pick the ratio that connects what you know to what you want: opposite and adjacent → tan; opposite and hypotenuse → sin; adjacent and hypotenuse → cos. For the common angles 30°, 45°, 60° the values are exact: tan 45° = 1, tan 30° = 1/√3, tan 60° = √3.
## Two observations

Many problems give two angles at two positions. Let the unknown height be h and unknown distance d. Write h = d tan α from one observation and h = (d ± s) tan β from the other (s is the distance moved). Equate and solve for d, then h. When two vertical objects are involved, the *same horizontal distance* is shared by both right triangles.
## Typical shapes

Ladder problems (hypotenuse and angle to the ground), tower–flagstaff (two angles from one point, subtract heights), observer on a building looking at the top and bottom of another building, boat approaching a lighthouse. The 'cot' form is often neat: distance moved = h(cot β − cot α).
formulae: height = L sin θ;  foot distance = L cos θ
angle of depression from top = angle of elevation from bottom

s: From the first point (distance x₁ from the foot) the elevation is α, and from a nearer point (distance x₂, with x₁ − x₂ = s) it is β (> α).
h = x₁ tan α = x₂ tan β ⇒ x₁ = h cot α and x₂ = h cot β.
The distance moved is s = x₁ − x₂ = h(cot α − cot β), so h = s/(cot α − cot β). ∎

diagrams.cap: The observer sees the top at angle of elevation θ. The right triangle has horizontal side d, vertical side h and the line of sight as hypotenuse; tan θ = h/d.

solved.q: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point 30 m from its foot is 60°. Find the height.
From the top of a 60 m building the angle of depression of a car is 30°. How far is the car from the building's foot?
s: Angle of elevation from the car = 30°. tan 30° = 60/d ⇒ d = 60/tan 30° = 60√3 m.

solved.q: A tower's elevation from a point is 30°. After walking 100 m towards it the elevation is 60°. Find the height.

traps: Angle of depression is measured from the horizontal DOWN, not from the vertical.
Draw the diagram first — most errors are wrong triangles.
Eye height of the observer matters if the problem states it.

title: Trigonometric Functions & Formulae
analogy: A Ferris wheel. As the wheel turns at a constant rate, a rider's height above the centre traces a smooth wave (sine) and the horizontal position traces the same wave shifted a quarter turn (cosine). Trigonometric functions are about rotation, and the wave is that rotation viewed from the side.
explain: ## Radians — the natural angle unit

One **radian** is the angle at the centre of a circle subtended by an arc equal in length to the radius. Because the full circle has circumference 2πr, the full turn is 2π radians: **π rad = 180°**. With radians, arc length is simply l = rθ and sector area is ½r²θ, with no extra constants. To convert: degrees × π/180 = radians.
## The unit circle

On a circle of radius 1 centred at the origin, the point at angle θ (measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis) has coordinates **(cos θ, sin θ)**. This extends the right-triangle definition to **all** angles, including those beyond 90° and negative angles. Signs follow the quadrants (ASTC: All, Sin, Tan, Cos positive in I, II, III, IV). sin² + cos² = 1 is the equation of the unit circle.
## Graphs and periodicity

sin and cos are periodic with period 2π (one full turn): sin(θ + 2π) = sin θ. Their values oscillate between −1 and 1 (amplitude 1). tan has period π with vertical asymptotes where cos = 0. For y = A sin(Bθ + C) + D: amplitude |A|, period 2π/|B|, phase shift −C/B, midline D. Reduction: sin(π − θ) = sin θ, cos(π − θ) = −cos θ, sin(π + θ) = −sin θ, sin(90° + θ) = cos θ, sin(−θ) = −sin θ, cos(−θ) = cos θ.
## Compound angle formulae

sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B; cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B; tan(A ± B) = (tan A ± tan B)/(1 ∓ tan A tan B). Everything else follows: double angles sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A; cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A; tan 2A = 2tan A/(1 − tan²A). Product-to-sum: 2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A − B), and sum-to-product reverses it.
## Maxima and minima
a sin θ + b cos θ = R sin(θ + φ) where R = √(a² + b²), so its range is [−R, R]. Complete the square for expressions like sin²θ + sin θ.
## Trigonometric equations
sin x = sin α ⇒ x = nπ + (−1)ⁿα. cos x = cos α ⇒ x = 2nπ ± α. tan x = tan α ⇒ x = nπ + α. To count solutions in an interval, sketch the graph and count intersections with the horizontal line.
formulae: π rad = 180°;  l = rθ;  A = ½r²θ
sin(A±B) = sinAcosB ± cosAsinB;  cos(A±B) = cosAcosB ∓ sinAsinB
a sinθ + b cosθ = R sin(θ+φ),  R = √(a²+b²)
sin x = sin α: x = nπ + (−1)ⁿα;  cos x = cos α: x = 2nπ ± α;  tan x = tan α: x = nπ + α

derivation.t: cos(A − B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B
s: On the unit circle take P = (cos A, sin A) and Q = (cos B, sin B). The angle between OP and OQ is A − B.
Distance PQ² by the distance formula = (cos A − cos B)² + (sin A − sin B)² = 2 − 2(cos A cos B + sin A sin B).
By the cosine rule in triangle OPQ: PQ² = 1 + 1 − 2 cos(A − B) = 2 − 2cos(A − B).
Equate: cos(A − B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B. Other compound formulae follow by substitution (B → −B, A → 90° − A). ∎
Put B = A in the compound formulae: sin 2A = sin A cos A + cos A sin A = 2 sin A cos A.
cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A. Using sin² = 1 − cos² gives 2cos²A − 1; using cos² = 1 − sin² gives 1 − 2sin²A. ∎

diagrams.cap: A point on the unit circle at angle θ has coordinates (cos θ, sin θ). The right triangle has hypotenuse 1, so its legs ARE cos θ and sin θ.
Over one period 0 to 2π, sin starts at 0 and rises; cos starts at 1: the same wave shifted by π/2 (cos θ = sin(θ + π/2)).

solved.q: Find the maximum value of 3 sin x + 4 cos x.
s: R = √(9 + 16) = 5. Range [−5, 5], so maximum = 5.

solved.q: If sin A = 3/5 and cos B = 5/13 (A, B acute), find sin(A + B).
s: cos A = 4/5, sin B = 12/13.

solved.q: How many solutions does sin 2x = 1/2 have in [0, 2π]?
s: sin 2x completes 2 full waves in [0, 2π]; each wave meets y = ½ twice. Total 4.

traps: Work in radians for calculus and arc-length formulas.
sin(A + B) ≠ sin A + sin B.
General solutions need the (−1)ⁿ for sine.

title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
analogy: Reading a ramp backwards. The ordinary sine says: 'given the angle, how high am I?'. The inverse sine says: 'given the height, what angle did I climb at?'. Because many angles give the same height, we must agree on one agreed range of angles, the principal values, so the answer is unique.
explain: ## Why restrict the range

A function has an inverse only if it is one-one. sin x is not (sin 30° = sin 150°), so we **restrict** it to a stretch where it is one-one and onto [−1, 1]: x ∈ [−π/2, π/2]. On that stretch sin is strictly increasing, so for each y in [−1, 1] there is exactly one x with sin x = y; that x is **sin⁻¹ y**. This agreed answer is the **principal value**.
## Principal value ranges

sin⁻¹ : [−1, 1] → [−π/2, π/2]. cos⁻¹ : [−1, 1] → [0, π]. tan⁻¹ : ℝ → (−π/2, π/2). cot⁻¹ : ℝ → (0, π). sec⁻¹ and cosec⁻¹ are defined for |x| ≥ 1. The cosine uses [0, π] because cos is decreasing there and covers all values once. Remember that the domain of sin⁻¹ and cos⁻¹ is [−1, 1] because a sine or cosine can never exceed 1.
## Inverse of a function vs. its inverse trig

The graph of sin⁻¹ is the mirror image of the restricted sine graph in the line y = x. The inversion only 'works back' in one direction automatically: **sin(sin⁻¹ x) = x** for x ∈ [−1, 1], but **sin⁻¹(sin x) = x only if x is in [−π/2, π/2]**. For other x you must first find the angle in the principal range with the same sine: sin⁻¹(sin 5π/6) = sin⁻¹(1/2) = π/6, not 5π/6.
## Identities

sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 (for x ∈ [−1,1]), tan⁻¹x + cot⁻¹x = π/2, sin⁻¹(−x) = −sin⁻¹x, cos⁻¹(−x) = π − cos⁻¹x. **Addition:** tan⁻¹a + tan⁻¹b = tan⁻¹((a + b)/(1 − ab)) if ab < 1; add π when ab > 1 and a, b > 0. Also 2tan⁻¹x = sin⁻¹(2x/(1 + x²)) = cos⁻¹((1 − x²)/(1 + x²)) = tan⁻¹(2x/(1 − x²)) in the right ranges.
## Problem types

Evaluate a principal value; simplify an expression such as sin(cos⁻¹ x) by drawing the right triangle (if cos⁻¹x = θ then adjacent = x, hypotenuse 1, opposite = √(1 − x²), so sin θ = √(1 − x²)); solve equations; find the domain.
formulae: sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2;  tan⁻¹x + cot⁻¹x = π/2
sin(sin⁻¹x) = x;  sin⁻¹(sin x) = x only for x ∈ [−π/2, π/2]

s: Let θ = sin⁻¹x so sin θ = x and θ ∈ [−π/2, π/2].
Then cos(π/2 − θ) = sin θ = x, and π/2 − θ ∈ [0, π] which is the principal range of cos⁻¹.
So cos⁻¹x = π/2 − θ, i.e. sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2. ∎
Let α = tan⁻¹a, β = tan⁻¹b so tan α = a, tan β = b.
tan(α + β) = (a + b)/(1 − ab).
If ab < 1 then α + β ∈ (−π/2, π/2), so α + β = tan⁻¹((a+b)/(1−ab)). ∎

diagrams.cap: sin⁻¹x rises from −π/2 to π/2 on [−1, 1]; cos⁻¹x falls from π to 0. The two curves are mirror images in the dashed line y = π/4, which is the identity sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 drawn.

solved.q: Find the principal value of sin⁻¹(sin(2π/3)).
s: sin(2π/3) = √3/2. The principal angle with that sine is π/3. So the value is π/3 (not 2π/3).

solved.q: Evaluate tan⁻¹(1/2) + tan⁻¹(1/3).
s: tan⁻¹1 = π/4.

solved.q: Find sin(cos⁻¹(3/5)).
s: Let θ = cos⁻¹(3/5): adjacent 3, hypotenuse 5, opposite 4. sin θ = 4/5.

traps: sin⁻¹(sin x) = x only on [−π/2, π/2].
sin⁻¹x is NOT 1/sin x.
The tan⁻¹ addition formula needs ab < 1; otherwise adjust by π.

title: Limits
analogy: Walking toward a door in the dark. You can't touch the door (maybe it isn't there at all), but if every step brings you closer to one specific spot, that spot is where you are headed. The limit is the place the function is heading, not necessarily where it ends up.
explain: ## The idea

The **limit** of f(x) as x → a, written lim f(x) = L, means: f(x) can be made as close to L as we like by taking x close enough to a (but x ≠ a). The value of f at a itself is irrelevant. Example: f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) is undefined at x = 2, but for every other x it equals x + 2, so as x → 2 the limit is 4. A limit describes the **trend**, not the value at the point.
## Left and right

The limit exists only if the **left-hand limit** (x → a⁻, approaching from below) and **right-hand limit** (x → a⁺) both exist and are equal. For |x|/x the left limit is −1 and the right limit is +1, so the limit at 0 does not exist.
## Techniques

1) **Direct substitution** if the function is continuous at a. 2) If you get 0/0, **factorise and cancel**, or **rationalise** (multiply by the conjugate when square roots are present). 3) For x → ∞, divide every term by the highest power of x: rational functions go to the ratio of leading coefficients if degrees match, to 0 if the denominator is of higher degree, and to ±∞ if the numerator is. 4) Use the standard limits below.
## Standard limits

lim sin x/x = 1 (x → 0, x in radians) because for small angles sin x ≈ x. lim (1 − cos x)/x² = ½. lim tan x/x = 1. lim (eˣ − 1)/x = 1, lim ln(1 + x)/x = 1, lim (aˣ − 1)/x = ln a. lim (1 + 1/x)ˣ = e as x → ∞. lim (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = naⁿ⁻¹ — this one is really the definition of the derivative of xⁿ.
## L'Hôpital's rule

If lim f/g gives 0/0 or ∞/∞, then lim f/g = lim f′/g′ provided the latter exists. It is a shortcut once you have derivatives, but standard limits and algebra are often faster and safer on tests. Indeterminate forms: 0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞ − ∞, 1^∞, 0⁰, ∞⁰.
formulae: lim (eˣ − 1)/x = 1;  lim ln(1+x)/x = 1;  lim (aˣ − 1)/x = ln a

s: Take 0 < x < π/2 on the unit circle. Compare areas: triangle OAP (½ sin x) < sector OAP (½x) < triangle OAT (½ tan x).
Divide by ½ sin x: 1 < x/sin x < 1/cos x, or cos x < sin x/x < 1.
As x → 0, cos x → 1, so sin x/x is squeezed to 1 (squeeze theorem). ∎
xⁿ − aⁿ = (x − a)(xⁿ⁻¹ + xⁿ⁻² a + … + aⁿ⁻¹).
Cancel (x − a) (allowed since x ≠ a): the limit is xⁿ⁻¹ + … + aⁿ⁻¹ at x = a, which has n terms each equal to aⁿ⁻¹, giving n aⁿ⁻¹. ∎

diagrams.cap: f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) = x + 2 (x ≠ 2): the graph is the line y = x + 2 with a hole at x = 2. The limit is 4 even though f(2) is undefined.

solved.q: Evaluate lim_{x→3} (x² − 9)/(x − 3).
Evaluate lim_{x→0} sin 5x / (3x).
Evaluate lim_{x→∞} (3x² + 2x)/(5x² − 1).
s: Divide by x²: (3 + 2/x)/(5 − 1/x²) → 3/5.

traps: Never cancel a factor and forget it was zero: the limit is about nearby values.
sin x / x → 1 only in RADIANS.
Check both one-sided limits at piecewise points.

title: Continuity & Differentiability
analogy: Drawing a graph without lifting your pen. A function is continuous at a point if you can draw through it smoothly with no gap, no jump and no vertical leap. Differentiability is stricter: no sharp corner either, because a corner has no single tangent.
explain: ## Definition

f is **continuous at x = a** if all three hold: (1) f(a) is defined; (2) lim_{x→a} f(x) exists; (3) the limit equals f(a). In short **LHL = RHL = f(a)**. A function is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every point. Polynomials, sin, cos, eˣ are continuous everywhere; rational functions are continuous except where the denominator is zero; |x| is continuous everywhere.
## Types of discontinuity

**Removable:** the limit exists but differs from f(a) or f(a) is undefined (a single hole). **Jump:** LHL and RHL exist but are different. **Infinite:** the function blows up (vertical asymptote, as in 1/x at 0). For problems with a parameter k in a piecewise function, set LHL = RHL = f(a) and solve for k.
## Continuity of combinations

Sums, differences, products of continuous functions are continuous; so is a quotient where the denominator ≠ 0; and a composition g(f(x)) is continuous if f is continuous at a and g is continuous at f(a). That is why you can evaluate most limits by direct substitution.
## Differentiability

f is differentiable at a if lim_{h→0} [f(a + h) − f(a)]/h exists (the left and right derivatives agree). **Differentiable ⇒ continuous**, but not the converse: |x| is continuous at 0 but has a corner there (slope −1 on the left, +1 on the right), so it is not differentiable at 0. A vertical tangent (like x^(1/3) at 0) also fails.
## Intermediate value theorem

If f is continuous on [a, b] and N lies between f(a) and f(b), then f takes the value N somewhere in the interval. In particular, if f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs there is a root between — the basis of locating roots by sign changes.
formulae: f continuous on [a,b], N between f(a), f(b) ⇒ ∃c: f(c) = N

s: Suppose f′(a) exists. For h ≠ 0: f(a + h) − f(a) = [ (f(a + h) − f(a))/h ] · h.
As h → 0 the bracket → f′(a) and h → 0, so the product → f′(a) × 0 = 0.
So f(a + h) → f(a): f is continuous at a. ∎

diagrams.cap: Left of x = 2 the function follows y = x (approaching 2), right of 2 it follows y = x + 1.5 (starting at 3.5). The one-sided limits disagree, so there is a jump discontinuity.

solved.q: Find k so that f(x) = kx + 1 (x ≤ 3), 2x − 5 (x > 3) is continuous at x = 3.
Is f(x) = |x − 2| differentiable at x = 2?
s: Slope to the left is −1, to the right is +1; the two one-sided derivatives differ, so f is not differentiable at 2 (it is continuous there).

solved.q: At which points is f(x) = (x + 1)/(x² − 4) discontinuous?
s: Denominator zero at x = ±2: infinite discontinuities there.

traps: Continuity needs the limit to EQUAL f(a), not just exist.
A corner is continuous but not differentiable.
Compare one-sided limits for piecewise definitions.

title: Derivatives & Rules of Differentiation
analogy: A speedometer. Average speed over a journey is distance divided by time — that is the slope of a secant. The speedometer reading at one instant is what that average becomes as the time interval shrinks toward zero: the slope of the tangent, the derivative.
explain: ## The derivative as a limit of slopes

Pick two points P(x, f(x)) and Q(x + h, f(x + h)) on a curve. The slope of the secant PQ is [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h. As h → 0, Q slides toward P and the secant turns into the tangent. The **derivative** is f′(x) = lim_{h→0} [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h: the instantaneous rate of change of f, the slope of the tangent.
## Differentiation rules

Constant: 0. Power: (xⁿ)′ = nxⁿ⁻¹. Sum: (f + g)′ = f′ + g′. **Product rule:** (fg)′ = f′g + fg′ (change in f times g, plus f times change in g). **Quotient rule:** (f/g)′ = (f′g − fg′)/g². **Chain rule:** (f(g(x)))′ = f′(g(x))·g′(x): differentiate the outside, then multiply by the derivative of the inside. The chain rule is what lets you differentiate compositions like sin(x²) or (3x + 1)⁵.
## Standard derivatives

(sin x)′ = cos x, (cos x)′ = −sin x, (tan x)′ = sec²x, (eˣ)′ = eˣ, (aˣ)′ = aˣ ln a, (ln x)′ = 1/x, (sin⁻¹x)′ = 1/√(1 − x²), (tan⁻¹x)′ = 1/(1 + x²). These are worth memorising; most others come from the rules.
## Implicit, parametric and logarithmic

**Implicit:** differentiate both sides of F(x, y) = 0 with respect to x, remembering d/dx(yⁿ) = n yⁿ⁻¹ dy/dx, then solve for dy/dx. **Parametric:** x = x(t), y = y(t): dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). **Logarithmic:** for y = f(x)^g(x) or products/quotients of many factors, take ln of both sides first, then differentiate.
## Higher derivatives
f″ is the derivative of f′: the rate of change of the slope (curvature, acceleration). If f′ > 0 the function rises, if f″ > 0 the graph curves upward (concave up).

derivation.t: Power rule from first principles (for xⁿ)
s: f′(x) = lim [(x + h)ⁿ − xⁿ]/h. Expand with the binomial theorem: (x + h)ⁿ = xⁿ + nxⁿ⁻¹h + C(n,2)xⁿ⁻²h² + …
Subtract xⁿ and divide by h: nxⁿ⁻¹ + C(n,2)xⁿ⁻²h + …
As h → 0 all terms with h vanish, leaving nxⁿ⁻¹. ∎
[f(x+h)g(x+h) − f(x)g(x)]/h. Add and subtract f(x+h)g(x) in the numerator.
As h → 0 (f is continuous so f(x+h) → f(x)): → f(x)g′(x) + g(x)f′(x). ∎

derivation.t: Quotient rule from the product rule
s: Write f/g = f · g⁻¹ and use the product and chain rules: (f/g)′ = f′g⁻¹ + f(−g⁻²)g′.
Combine over g²: (f′g − fg′)/g². ∎

diagrams.cap: The dashed secant through P and Q has slope Δy/Δx. As Q slides toward P the secant rotates into the solid tangent; its slope is the derivative at P.

solved.q: Differentiate y = x²·sin x.
s: Product rule: y′ = 2x sin x + x² cos x.

solved.q: Differentiate y = (3x + 1)⁵.
s: Chain rule: y′ = 5(3x + 1)⁴·3 = 15(3x + 1)⁴.

solved.q: If x² + y² = 25, find dy/dx at (3, 4).
s: 2x + 2y dy/dx = 0 ⇒ dy/dx = −x/y = −3/4.

traps: Chain rule: don't forget to multiply by the derivative of the inside.
The product rule has a PLUS between two terms (not just f′g′).
d/dx(yⁿ) = n yⁿ⁻¹·dy/dx for implicit differentiation.

title: Applications of Derivatives
analogy: Hiking a trail. On the climb the slope is positive, on the descent negative; at the summit it is exactly zero for an instant. Finding that flat spot (f′ = 0) finds peaks and valleys. The second derivative tells you whether the ground is curving like a bowl (valley) or a dome (peak).
explain: ## Rate of change

dy/dx tells how fast y changes per unit change in x. For related rates, if two quantities both depend on time, differentiate their relationship with respect to t using the chain rule. E.g. a circle's area A = πr²: dA/dt = 2πr·dr/dt. Always plug in numbers *after* differentiating.
## Tangent and normal

At the point (x₀, y₀) the slope of the tangent is m = f′(x₀) and its equation is y − y₀ = m(x − x₀). The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so its slope is −1/m and its equation is y − y₀ = −(1/m)(x − x₀). If m = 0 the tangent is horizontal and the normal is vertical.
## Increasing and decreasing

If f′(x) > 0 on an interval the function is **increasing** there; if f′(x) < 0 it is **decreasing**. To find the intervals, solve f′ = 0, mark the critical points on a number line, and test the sign of f′ in each stretch.
## Maxima and minima

At a local extremum of a smooth function the tangent is horizontal, so f′(c) = 0 (a **critical point**). **First-derivative test:** f′ changes + → − at c ⇒ local max; − → + ⇒ local min. **Second-derivative test:** f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) < 0 ⇒ local max; f″(c) > 0 ⇒ local min; f″(c) = 0 is inconclusive. The absolute max/min on a closed interval [a, b] is found by comparing values at critical points and endpoints.
## Optimisation

Steps: (1) draw and name variables, (2) write the quantity to maximise or minimise, (3) use constraints to express it in ONE variable, (4) set the derivative to zero, (5) confirm max/min and check the domain, (6) answer the question asked. Classic results: for a fixed perimeter, the rectangle with the largest area is a square; for a given volume, the cylinder with minimum surface has h = 2r.

derivation.t: Why f′ = 0 at a local maximum
s: Suppose f has a local max at c and is differentiable there. For small h > 0, f(c + h) ≤ f(c), so [f(c + h) − f(c)]/h ≤ 0: the right-hand derivative is ≤ 0.
For small h < 0, dividing by a negative number reverses the sign: the left-hand derivative is ≥ 0.
Since the derivative exists, left = right, so f′(c) ≤ 0 and f′(c) ≥ 0 ⇒ f′(c) = 0. ∎

derivation.t: Rectangle of fixed perimeter has maximum area when it is a square
s: Perimeter 2P: sides x and P − x. Area A = x(P − x) = Px − x².
A′ = P − 2x = 0 ⇒ x = P/2, A″ = −2 < 0 so it is a maximum.
Then both sides equal P/2: a square. ∎

diagrams.cap: f(x) = x³/3 − 2x² + 3x + 1: f′ = (x − 1)(x − 3). At x = 1 the slope changes from + to − (a peak); at x = 3 it changes from − to + (a valley).

solved.q: Find the equation of the tangent to y = x² + 3x at x = 1.
The radius of a spherical balloon increases at 2 cm/s. How fast is the volume increasing when r = 5 cm?
s: V = ⁴⁄₃πr³ ⇒ dV/dt = 4πr²·dr/dt = 4π(25)(2) = 200π cm³/s.

solved.q: Find the local maximum value of f(x) = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x.

traps: f′ = 0 is necessary but not sufficient: check the sign change or f″.
For absolute extrema, test the endpoints too.
In related rates, substitute numbers after differentiating.

title: Indefinite Integration
analogy: Rewinding a film. Differentiation takes a position and tells you the speed; integration takes the speed and recovers the position. But a speed doesn't say where you started, so you always get a family of answers differing by a constant (the + C).
explain: ## Antiderivatives

An **antiderivative** of f is a function F with F′ = f. If F is one, so is F + C for every constant C, because constants vanish on differentiation. We write ∫f(x) dx = F(x) + C and call it the **indefinite integral**. Geometrically, F + C is a family of curves, each a vertical shift of the others, all having the same slope f(x) at each x.
## Basic integrals

Reverse the derivative table: ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C (n ≠ −1), ∫1/x dx = ln|x| + C, ∫eˣ dx = eˣ + C, ∫aˣ dx = aˣ/ln a + C, ∫sin x dx = −cos x + C, ∫cos x dx = sin x + C, ∫sec²x dx = tan x + C, ∫1/√(1 − x²) dx = sin⁻¹x + C, ∫1/(1 + x²) dx = tan⁻¹x + C. Integration is linear: ∫(af + bg) = a∫f + b∫g.
## Substitution — the chain rule backwards

If the integrand has the form f(g(x))·g′(x), put u = g(x) so that du = g′(x) dx; the integral becomes ∫f(u) du. Example: ∫2x cos(x²) dx with u = x² gives ∫cos u du = sin(x²) + C. The tell-tale sign: you see a function and (up to a constant) its derivative sitting next to it.
## Integration by parts — the product rule backwards

From (uv)′ = u′v + uv′ we get ∫u v′ dx = uv − ∫u′v dx. Choose u to be the part that gets *simpler* when differentiated (follow ILATE: Inverse trig, Log, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential — earlier in the list is chosen as u). Example: ∫x eˣ dx: u = x, v′ = eˣ ⇒ x eˣ − ∫eˣ dx = (x − 1)eˣ + C. The special formula ∫eˣ[f(x) + f′(x)] dx = eˣ f(x) + C is a common shortcut.
## Partial fractions and special forms

A rational function P(x)/Q(x) with factorable Q is split into simpler fractions, e.g. 1/((x − 1)(x − 2)) = 1/(x − 2) − 1/(x − 1), each of which integrates to a log. Quadratics under roots or in denominators are handled by completing the square and using the sin⁻¹ / tan⁻¹ forms.
formulae: ∫eˣ dx = eˣ + C;  ∫aˣ dx = aˣ/ln a + C
∫eˣ[f + f′]dx = eˣ f(x) + C;  ∫f′/f dx = ln|f| + C

derivation.t: Integration by parts from the product rule
s: (uv)′ = u′v + uv′.
Integrate both sides: uv = ∫u′v dx + ∫uv′ dx.
Rearranging, ∫uv′ dx = uv − ∫u′v dx. ∎
d/dx [xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1)] = (n + 1)xⁿ/(n + 1) = xⁿ, so xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) is an antiderivative. This fails for n = −1 (division by zero), where d/dx ln|x| = 1/x takes over. ∎

diagrams.cap: Three antiderivatives of f(x) = x are x²/2 + C for different C. Each tiny tangent segment on any vertical line has the same slope: shifting a curve vertically does not change its slope.

solved.q: Evaluate ∫(3x² + 2x + 1) dx.
s: = x³ + x² + x + C.

solved.q: Evaluate ∫2x·cos(x²) dx.
s: u = x², du = 2x dx ⇒ ∫cos u du = sin u + C = sin(x²) + C.

solved.q: Evaluate ∫x eˣ dx.
s: u = x, v′ = eˣ: x eˣ − ∫eˣ dx = x eˣ − eˣ + C = (x − 1)eˣ + C.

traps: Never forget + C for indefinite integrals.
∫1/x dx = ln|x|, not x⁰/0.
In by-parts, pick u so that u′ is simpler.

title: Definite Integrals & Their Properties
analogy: Counting the water that flows through a river in a day: add up the flow rate times tiny time slices. The definite integral is exactly that — a limit of sums of 'rate × tiny width'. The Fundamental Theorem shows that this huge sum can be found in one step by simply subtracting an antiderivative at the ends.
explain: ## Area as a limit of sums

Cut the interval [a, b] into n thin strips of width Δx = (b − a)/n. Approximating the area under y = f(x) on each strip by a rectangle of height f(xᵢ) gives Σ f(xᵢ)Δx. As n → ∞ the rectangles fit the curve ever more closely, and the sum approaches the **definite integral** ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx. Areas below the x-axis count as negative, so the integral is a *signed* area.
## Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

Differentiation and integration are inverse processes. If F′ = f then **∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a)**. This turns an infinite sum into two evaluations. The other half: the area function A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt satisfies A′(x) = f(x).
## Properties

∫ₐᵃ f = 0; ∫ₐᵇ f = −∫_b^a f; ∫ₐᵇ f = ∫ₐᶜ f + ∫cᵇ f; ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(a + b − x)dx (King's property — reflect the interval); for an **even** function ∫₋ₐᵃ f = 2∫₀ᵃ f; for an **odd** function ∫₋ₐᵃ f = 0 (the positive and negative areas cancel). The substitution rule works with the limits changed to match the new variable.
## Useful tricks

Use symmetry first. For ∫₀^{π/2} sin x/(sin x + cos x) dx, the King's property gives the same integral with cos in the numerator, so adding the two gives ∫₀^{π/2} 1 dx = π/2 and the original is π/4. Periodic functions: ∫₀^{nT} f = n∫₀^T f.
## Estimating
Since f ≥ g on [a, b] implies ∫f ≥ ∫g, and m ≤ f ≤ M implies m(b − a) ≤ ∫f ≤ M(b − a), you can bound integrals you cannot evaluate. The average value of f on [a, b] is (1/(b − a))∫ₐᵇ f.
formulae: ∫ₐᵇ f dx = F(b) − F(a),  F′ = f

s: Let A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt. Then A(x + h) − A(x) = ∫ₓˣ⁺ʰ f(t) dt ≈ f(x)·h for small h (a thin strip).
So [A(x + h) − A(x)]/h → f(x): A′ = f.
If F is any antiderivative of f then F = A + C, so F(b) − F(a) = A(b) − A(a) = ∫ₐᵇ f. ∎
Substitute u = a + b − x, so du = −dx, and x = a ↦ u = b, x = b ↦ u = a.
∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫_b^a f(a + b − u)(−du) = ∫ₐᵇ f(a + b − u) du. ∎

diagrams.cap: Six rectangles under y = 0.4x² + 0.5 between a and b. Using more, thinner rectangles makes the stair-step sum approach the exact area ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx.

solved.q: Evaluate ∫₀² (3x² + 1) dx.
s: Antiderivative F = x³ + x. F(2) − F(0) = 8 + 2 − 0 = 10.

solved.q: Evaluate ∫₋₂² x³ dx.
s: x³ is odd and the interval is symmetric, so the integral is 0.

solved.q: Evaluate ∫₀^{π/2} sin x/(sin x + cos x) dx.
s: Let I be the integral. King's property gives I = ∫ cos x/(cos x + sin x) dx.
Adding: 2I = ∫₀^{π/2} 1 dx = π/2 ⇒ I = π/4.

traps: Change the limits when you substitute (or revert to x).
Area below the axis is negative in ∫: take absolute values for geometric area.
Check for odd/even symmetry before computing.

title: Area Using Integrals
analogy: Cutting a shape out of a sheet. The area between two curves is 'the top curve's area under it' minus 'the bottom curve's area under it', slice by slice. Each thin vertical slice has height (top − bottom) and width dx; adding up the slices is integration.
explain: ## Area under a curve

For f(x) ≥ 0 on [a, b], the area between the curve and the x-axis is ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx. If f dips below the axis, the integral counts that portion negatively, so for the true geometric area you must **split at the zeros** of f and add absolute values. Example: sin x between 0 and 2π has integral 0, but its area is 4.
## Area between two curves

If f(x) ≥ g(x) on [a, b], the area between them is **∫ₐᵇ [f(x) − g(x)] dx**: each vertical strip has height f − g. The limits a and b are the x-coordinates where the curves **meet** (solve f = g). Sketching first tells you which curve is on top and prevents sign errors.
## Horizontal strips
Sometimes it is easier to slice horizontally: for x as a function of y, area = ∫ (right curve − left curve) dy. Parabolas like y² = 4ax are naturally handled this way.
## Standard results

Area under one arch of sin x (0 to π) = 2. Area of a circle of radius r = πr² (from ∫√(r² − x²)). Area bounded by y² = 4ax and x² = 4ay = 16a²/3. Area of the ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 is πab. Use symmetry to halve or quarter the work.
## Steps that always work

1) Sketch. 2) Find intersection points. 3) Decide the slicing direction. 4) Write the integrand (upper − lower). 5) Integrate and substitute the limits. 6) Check that the answer is positive and plausible.

derivation.t: Area between y = x² and y = 2x
s: Intersections: x² = 2x ⇒ x = 0 or 2. On (0, 2) the line is above the parabola.

derivation.t: Area of a circle by integration
s: The upper half is y = √(r² − x²). Area = 2∫₋ᵣʳ √(r² − x²) dx = 4∫₀ʳ √(r² − x²) dx.
With x = r sin θ: 4∫₀^{π/2} r² cos²θ dθ = 4r²·(π/4) = πr². ∎

diagrams.cap: Between y = x² and y = 2x from x = 0 to 2, the strip height is 2x − x². Integrating gives the shaded area 4/3.

solved.q: Find the area bounded by y = x², the x-axis, and x = 1 and x = 3.
Find the area enclosed between y = x² and y = 4.
s: Intersection x = ±2. A = ∫₋₂² (4 − x²) dx = 2[4x − x³/3]₀² = 2(8 − 8/3) = 32/3.

solved.q: Find the area enclosed by y = sin x and the x-axis from 0 to 2π.
s: The two half-waves have equal areas: 2 + 2 = 4 (the integral alone would give 0).

traps: Sketch to decide which curve is on top.
When the curve crosses the axis, split the integral.
The area is always positive.

title: Differential Equations
analogy: A recipe for change. Instead of saying where something is, a differential equation says how it changes right now ('it grows at a rate proportional to its size'). Solving the equation means finding the whole story (the function) that obeys this rule of change.
explain: ## What is a differential equation?

An equation involving an unknown function y(x) and its derivatives, e.g. dy/dx = 2x or d²y/dx² + y = 0. The **order** is the highest derivative that appears; the **degree** is the power of that highest derivative (after clearing fractions and radicals; defined only if the equation is polynomial in the derivatives). The solution is a *function*, not a number.
## General vs particular solutions

A solution containing arbitrary constants is the **general solution**: a first-order equation has one constant, a second-order equation two (order = number of independent arbitrary constants). Fixing the constants using given conditions (initial values like y(0) = 3) gives a **particular solution**. Forming a differential equation from a family of curves is the reverse: differentiate to eliminate the constants.
## Variables separable

If dy/dx = f(x)g(y), separate: dy/g(y) = f(x) dx and integrate both sides. Example: dy/dx = ky ⇒ ∫dy/y = ∫k dx ⇒ ln|y| = kx + C ⇒ y = Aeᵏˣ — exponential growth/decay. Population growth, radioactive decay, Newton's law of cooling are all of this form.
## Homogeneous equations
If dy/dx = F(y/x), substitute y = vx so dy/dx = v + x dv/dx. This turns the equation into a separable one in v and x.
## Linear first-order equations

Standard form dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x). Multiply by the **integrating factor** IF = e^(∫P dx). Then the left side becomes d/dx(y · IF), and integrating gives y·IF = ∫Q·IF dx + C. The factor is designed so that the product rule runs backward.
## Interpretation

A slope field draws a little tangent segment at many points showing the slope dy/dx there; solution curves follow these slopes like a river current. For dy/dx = −x/y the segments are tangent to circles about the origin.
formulae: dy/dx + Py = Q;  IF = e^(∫P dx);  y·IF = ∫Q·IF dx + C
number of arbitrary constants in the general solution
power of the highest derivative (polynomial form)

derivation.t: Solution of the linear equation by integrating factor
s: Multiply dy/dx + Py = Q by IF = e^(∫P dx). Since d(IF)/dx = P·IF, we get (IF)dy/dx + P(IF)y = Q·IF.
The left side is exactly d/dx(y·IF) by the product rule.
Integrate both sides: y·IF = ∫Q·IF dx + C. ∎
dy/dx = ky ⇒ dy/y = k dx.
Integrate: ln|y| = kx + C₁ ⇒ |y| = e^(C₁) eᵏˣ.
Write A = ±e^(C₁): y = Aeᵏˣ, and y(0) = A is the initial value. ∎

diagrams.cap: Slope field of dy/dx = −x/y. The tiny segments are tangent to concentric circles around the origin; each circle x² + y² = C is a solution curve.

solved.q: Solve dy/dx = 2xy with y(0) = 1.
s: dy/y = 2x dx ⇒ ln y = x² + C. y(0) = 1 ⇒ C = 0. So y = e^(x²).

solved.q: Find the order and degree of (d²y/dx²)³ + (dy/dx)² = 0.
s: Highest derivative: second ⇒ order 2; its power is 3 ⇒ degree 3.

solved.q: Solve dy/dx + y = e^(−x) with y(0) = 0 using an integrating factor.
s: IF = e^(∫1 dx) = eˣ. d/dx(y eˣ) = e^(−x)·eˣ = 1 ⇒ y eˣ = x + C.

traps: Degree is defined only after the equation is polynomial in derivatives.
Don't lose the +C before applying initial conditions.
For linear equations make the coefficient of dy/dx equal to 1 first.

title: Matrices
analogy: A spreadsheet that knows how to act. A matrix is a rectangular table of numbers, but its real life is as a machine: feed it a point and it moves it (rotates, stretches, shears). Multiplying matrices means doing one machine's action after another's.
explain: ## What a matrix is

A **matrix** is a rectangular array of numbers with m rows and n columns (an m × n matrix). Special types: square (m = n), row/column matrix, zero matrix, identity I (1s on the diagonal), diagonal, symmetric (Aᵀ = A), skew-symmetric (Aᵀ = −A). Two matrices are equal if they have the same order and equal entries. The **transpose** Aᵀ swaps rows and columns.
## Addition and scalar multiplication
Matrices of the **same order** add entry by entry; multiplying by a scalar multiplies every entry. These follow the usual algebra rules (commutative and associative for addition).
## Multiplication — why it looks odd

The product AB exists only if the number of **columns of A = rows of B**. The (i, j) entry of AB is the **dot product of row i of A with column j of B**. This definition is chosen so that matrix products represent composition of linear transformations: (AB)x = A(Bx). Consequences: AB ≠ BA in general (doing rotation-then-stretch differs from stretch-then-rotation), AB = 0 does not force A = 0 or B = 0, and (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ.
## Matrix as transformation

A 2 × 2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]] sends the unit vectors î = (1, 0) to (a, c) and ĵ = (0, 1) to (b, d) — its columns are where the basis vectors land. The unit square becomes a parallelogram; its area gets multiplied by |det A|. Rotation by θ is [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]].
## Powers and polynomials

Powers Aⁿ are repeated products. Diagonal matrices power entry-wise. A matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation (Cayley–Hamilton): for a 2 × 2 matrix, A² − (trace)A + (det)I = 0. This lets you reduce high powers.
## Inverse

A⁻¹ satisfies AA⁻¹ = A⁻¹A = I. It exists only if det A ≠ 0 (covered in determinants). For a 2 × 2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]], A⁻¹ = (1/(ad − bc))[[d, −b], [−c, a]]. (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹ (shoes and socks: reverse the order).

s: The (i, j) entry of (AB)ᵀ is the (j, i) entry of AB: Σₖ Aⱼₖ Bₖᵢ.
The (i, j) entry of BᵀAᵀ is Σₖ (Bᵀ)ᵢₖ (Aᵀ)ₖⱼ = Σₖ Bₖᵢ Aⱼₖ — the same sum. ∎
Divide by ad − bc: the second matrix over (ad − bc) is the inverse. ∎

diagrams.cap: The matrix [[2, 1], [0, 1]] sends î to (2, 0) and ĵ to (1, 1). The unit square becomes a parallelogram whose area is 2 = det of the matrix.

solved.q: Find the inverse of [[2, 1], [5, 3]].
Express A = [[1, 2], [4, 3]] as the sum of a symmetric and a skew-symmetric matrix.
s: A = P + Q.

traps: Matrix multiplication is NOT commutative.
The product exists only if columns of A = rows of B.
A⁻¹ exists only when det A ≠ 0.

title: Determinants & Linear Systems
analogy: The area-scaling factor of a transformation. If a matrix stretches the plane, its determinant tells you by what factor every area gets multiplied (and whether the plane is flipped, if negative). If the determinant is 0 the plane is squashed flat onto a line — information is lost, which is why such a matrix can't be undone (no inverse).
explain: ## Definition for 2 × 2 and 3 × 3

For [[a, b], [c, d]], det = ad − bc. For a 3 × 3, **expand along a row (or column)**: each entry times its cofactor, alternating signs +, −, + (checkerboard). The **minor** Mᵢⱼ is the determinant left after deleting row i and column j; the **cofactor** is Cᵢⱼ = (−1)^(i+j) Mᵢⱼ. Expanding along the row or column with the most zeros saves work.
## Geometric meaning

|ad − bc| is the **area of the parallelogram** formed by the column vectors (a, c) and (b, d); for 3 × 3 it is the volume of the parallelepiped. The sign records orientation. The determinant is zero exactly when the vectors are parallel (area collapses), which for three points means collinear, and for 3 vectors means coplanar.
## Properties that save time

Swapping two rows changes the sign. A row of zeros or two identical (or proportional) rows gives 0. Multiplying a row by k multiplies det by k. Adding a multiple of one row to another changes nothing — the standard way to create zeros. det(AB) = det A · det B; det Aᵀ = det A; det(kA) = kⁿ det A for n × n. For triangular matrices det = product of the diagonal.
## Adjoint and inverse
The **adjoint** adj A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix. Then A·adj A = (det A)I, so **A⁻¹ = adj A / det A** (when det ≠ 0). Also det(adj A) = (det A)ⁿ⁻¹.
## Solving linear systems

For AX = B: if det A ≠ 0 the system has a unique solution X = A⁻¹B (Cramer's rule: xᵢ = Dᵢ/D). If det A = 0 the system is either inconsistent or has infinitely many solutions — check (adj A)B: if it is the zero matrix there are infinitely many solutions, otherwise none. A homogeneous system AX = 0 has non-trivial solutions iff det A = 0.
formulae: det A = Σⱼ aᵢⱼ Cᵢⱼ,  Cᵢⱼ = (−1)^(i+j) Mᵢⱼ
A·adj A = (det A)I;  det(adj A) = (det A)ⁿ⁻¹

s: The (i, i) entry of A·adj A is Σⱼ aᵢⱼ Cᵢⱼ = det A (cofactor expansion along row i).
For i ≠ j, Σₖ aᵢₖ Cⱼₖ is the expansion of a determinant with two identical rows (row i copied into row j), so it equals 0.
Hence A·adj A = (det A)I. ∎
For a₁x + b₁y = c₁, a₂x + b₂y = c₂, eliminate y: (a₁b₂ − a₂b₁)x = c₁b₂ − c₂b₁.
So x = D₁/D where D = a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ and D₁ = c₁b₂ − c₂b₁ (D with the x-column replaced by the constants). Similarly y = D₂/D. ∎

s: D = 1·k − 2·1 = k − 2 = 0 ⇒ k = 2. (Then 2x + 2y = 4 vs 5: inconsistent.)

title: Linear Programming
analogy: Planning a factory shift with limited machine time and materials. Each limit is a fence (a line); the allowed plans are inside the fenced region. Because profit rises in a straight line as you move in a direction, the best plan will always be in a corner of the fenced-off field.
explain: ## The ingredients

A linear programming problem has (1) an **objective function** Z = ax + by to be maximised or minimised (profit, cost), (2) **constraints** that are linear inequalities (limits on time, material, demand), and (3) non-negativity x, y ≥ 0. Any (x, y) satisfying all constraints is **feasible**; the set of all feasible points is the **feasible region**.
## Graphing the region

Each inequality ax + by ≤ c describes a half-plane: draw the line ax + by = c, and shade the side containing the origin if c > 0 (test (0, 0)). The feasible region is the **intersection** of all the half-planes. It is a convex polygon (any segment between two feasible points stays inside). It may be bounded (a closed polygon) or unbounded.
## The corner point theorem

For a bounded feasible region, the maximum and minimum of Z occur at **corner points** (vertices). Reason: Z = ax + by is a linear function, so on any line segment it is monotonic and the extreme values land at the ends; applying this repeatedly, the extreme values sit at the vertices. So: (1) find all vertices (solve pairs of boundary lines), (2) evaluate Z at each, (3) pick the largest/smallest.
## Unbounded regions

If the region is unbounded a maximum or minimum may not exist. For a minimum: draw the half-plane Z < M (M = value at the best vertex); if it has no point in common with the feasible region, M is the minimum. Similarly for maximum.
## Typical problems

Product mix (maximise profit with machine-hour limits), diet problems (minimise cost meeting nutrient minimums), transportation. Translate carefully: define x, y as quantities; write each limit as an inequality; avoid forgetting x, y ≥ 0.
formulae: optimum of Z (if it exists) is at a vertex of the feasible region
solve two boundary equations at a time; verify it satisfies all constraints
if Z = M at two vertices, Z = M along the whole edge

derivation.t: Why the optimum is at a corner
s: Along a line segment from P to Q, write a point as (1 − t)P + tQ, 0 ≤ t ≤ 1. Then Z = (1 − t)Z(P) + tZ(Q), which is a straight-line function of t.
So its maximum on the segment is at one of the ends (P or Q), whichever has the larger Z.
Any feasible point of a bounded convex polygon lies on a segment joining two boundary points, and so on; repeating shows the extreme values occur at vertices. ∎

diagrams.cap: Constraints x + y ≤ 6, x + 2y ≤ 8, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 give the shaded quadrilateral. Evaluate the objective at its four corners — the answer is among them.

solved.q: Maximise Z = 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≤ 6, x + 2y ≤ 8, x, y ≥ 0.
s: Corners: (0,0), (6,0), (0,4), and intersection of x + y = 6 with x + 2y = 8: y = 2, x = 4 ⇒ (4,2).

solved.q: A factory makes tables (₹30 profit each) and chairs (₹20 profit). A table needs 2 hours of carpentry and a chair 1 hour; 40 hours are available. Maximum 25 pieces. Set up the problem.
s: Let x tables, y chairs. Maximise Z = 30x + 20y.
Constraints: 2x + y ≤ 40, x + y ≤ 25, x, y ≥ 0.

solved.q: Minimise Z = 2x + 3y subject to 4 ≤ x + y ≤ 8, x, y ≥ 0.
s: Minimum 8 at (4, 0).

traps: Test each vertex against ALL constraints.
Don't forget x, y ≥ 0.
For unbounded regions the optimum might not exist.

title: Statistics: Mean, Median, Mode, Variance
analogy: A class photo from far away. You can't see every face, but you can say the typical height (the mean or median) and how spread out the class is (the standard deviation). Statistics squeezes a crowd of numbers into a few summary numbers while telling you how much detail was lost.
explain: ## Measures of centre

The **mean** is the sum divided by the count; it balances all values. The **median** is the middle value of the sorted data (for even n, the average of the two middle values) and is unaffected by extreme values. The **mode** is the most frequent value. For grouped data, assume values in a class are at its **mid-point** to estimate the mean: x̄ = Σfx/Σf.
## Grouped data: median and mode

For a frequency table with classes of width h: the **median class** is the one containing the (N/2)th observation (find it from the cumulative frequency column). Median = l + [(N/2 − cf)/f] × h, where l is the lower boundary of that class, cf the cumulative frequency before it, f its frequency. This is linear interpolation inside the class. **Mode** = l + [(f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × h where f₁ is the modal class frequency and f₀, f₂ the neighbours' frequencies. Empirical relation: Mode ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean.
## Measures of spread

The **range** (max − min) is crude. The **variance** σ² is the mean of the squared deviations from the mean: σ² = Σ(x − x̄)²/n = Σx²/n − x̄². The **standard deviation** σ = √variance, in the same units as the data. Squaring stops positive and negative deviations from cancelling. Small σ means the data hug the mean; large σ means they are scattered.
## Effect of changing the data

Adding a constant c to every value shifts the mean by c but leaves the variance and SD unchanged (spread is about *differences*). Multiplying every value by k multiplies the mean and SD by |k| and the variance by k². Combining groups needs combined means (weighted) and a combined variance formula.
## Coefficient of variation
To compare the consistency of two data sets with different units or means, use CV = (σ/x̄) × 100 %. The smaller CV is the more consistent set.
## Graphs

A **histogram** draws bars whose area is proportional to the class frequency; a cumulative frequency curve (ogive) gives the median graphically; pie charts show proportions as angles (360° × fraction).
formulae: mean → a·mean + b;  σ → |a|σ;  σ² → a²σ²

s: σ² = (1/n)Σ(x − x̄)² = (1/n)Σ(x² − 2x̄x + x̄²).
= (1/n)Σx² − 2x̄·(Σx/n) + x̄² = (1/n)Σx² − 2x̄² + x̄² = Σx²/n − x̄². ∎

derivation.t: Why scaling by a multiplies the SD by |a|
s: If yᵢ = axᵢ + b then ȳ = ax̄ + b and yᵢ − ȳ = a(xᵢ − x̄).
So Σ(yᵢ − ȳ)²/n = a²Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²/n = a²σₓ², and σ_y = |a|σₓ. The shift b cancels. ∎

title: Probability: Events & Rules
analogy: Betting odds without the money. If you could repeat an experiment thousands of times, probability is the fraction of times an outcome would show up. Counting the favourable cases and dividing by all cases is simply how you predict that fraction ahead of time.
explain: ## Sample space and events

A random experiment has a set of possible outcomes, the **sample space** S. An **event** is a subset of S. If all outcomes are **equally likely**, P(E) = (number of outcomes in E)/(number of outcomes in S). For a fair die, P(even) = 3/6 = ½. The probability is always between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain), and P(E) + P(not E) = 1.
## Addition rule

P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B): adding both double-counts the overlap, so subtract it once (the same inclusion–exclusion as for sets). If A and B are **mutually exclusive** (cannot occur together), P(A ∩ B) = 0 and the probabilities simply add.
## Independent events and the multiplication rule

Events are **independent** if the occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other, and then P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B). Independence is a statement about the situation, not about 'being different': tossing two coins, drawing with replacement. Without replacement, outcomes depend on each other.
## Complement trick
'At least one' is almost always easier as 1 − P(none). P(at least one head in 5 tosses) = 1 − (½)⁵ = 31/32. Likewise for 'at least one six in 4 rolls'.
## Counting-based probabilities

Combine with permutations and combinations: P(drawing 2 red from 5 red + 3 blue) = C(5,2)/C(8,2) = 10/28. Because selection order doesn't matter, use combinations for numerator and denominator consistently.
## Common spaces

Two dice: 36 outcomes (sum 7: 6 ways → 1/6). Three coins: 8 outcomes. Cards: 52 (13 of each suit, 4 of each rank, 12 face cards, 26 red). Birthdays, committees, digit arrangements: use C(n, r) and n!.

s: A ∪ B is made of three disjoint parts: A only, A ∩ B, B only.
P(A) = P(A only) + P(A ∩ B); P(B) = P(B only) + P(A ∩ B).
Adding P(A) and P(B) counts P(A ∩ B) twice, so P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). ∎
E and E′ are mutually exclusive and together cover the whole sample space, so P(E) + P(E′) = P(S) = 1. ∎

diagrams.cap: The 36 outcomes of two dice. The six highlighted cells give a sum of 7, so P(sum 7) = 6/36 = 1/6 — a picture of 'favourable ÷ total'.

solved.q: Two cards are drawn without replacement from a standard deck. Find P(both are aces).
A bag has 4 red and 6 blue balls. Two are drawn at once. Find P(at least one red).
s: P(at least one red) = 1 − 1/3 = 2/3.

solved.q: If P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.7, find P(A ∩ B) and check independence.
s: P(A)P(B) = 0.2 = P(A ∩ B) ⇒ independent.

traps: Equally likely outcomes are required for favourable/total.
'Mutually exclusive' ≠ 'independent'.
For 'at least one', use the complement.

title: Conditional Probability & Bayes
analogy: Updating your guess after a clue. If a friend says 'the number is even', the probability of getting a 6 jumps from 1/6 to 1/3 because the clue shrank the world of possibilities. Conditional probability measures chance inside the new, smaller world.
explain: ## The definition

P(A | B) is the probability of A **given that B has happened**: restrict the sample space to B, then ask how much of B is also A. P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B), for P(B) > 0. Example: roll a die; B = 'even' (3 outcomes), A = '6'. A ∩ B = {6}. P(A | B) = (1/6)/(3/6) = 1/3.
## Multiplication rule

Rearranging the definition: P(A ∩ B) = P(B)P(A | B) = P(A)P(B | A). This is how tree diagrams work: multiply along the branches. If A and B are independent then P(A | B) = P(A), which is the formal reason independent events multiply.
## Total probability

If E₁, E₂, … partition the sample space (disjoint and exhaustive), the probability of any event A is P(A) = ΣP(Eᵢ)P(A | Eᵢ): the weighted average of the probability of A in each 'world'. In the tree: add the products along all the branches that end in A.
## Bayes' theorem — reverse the condition

Knowing that A has occurred, how likely was each cause Eᵢ? P(Eⱼ | A) = P(Eⱼ)P(A | Eⱼ)/ΣP(Eᵢ)P(A | Eᵢ). Numerator: the path through Eⱼ that ended in A; denominator: all paths ending in A. It updates the 'prior' P(Eⱼ) to the 'posterior' P(Eⱼ | A) using the evidence. Typical set-ups: faulty items from machines, medical tests, which urn was picked.
## Common errors

P(A | B) ≠ P(B | A). A test being 99% accurate does not mean a positive result is 99% likely to be correct — that depends on how rare the condition is (the base rate). Bayes' theorem corrects that intuition.

s: By the multiplication rule, P(Eⱼ ∩ A) = P(Eⱼ)P(A | Eⱼ) = P(A)P(Eⱼ | A).
So P(Eⱼ | A) = P(Eⱼ)P(A | Eⱼ)/P(A).
Expand P(A) by total probability: P(A) = ΣP(Eᵢ)P(A | Eᵢ). ∎

title: Random Variables & Binomial Distribution
analogy: A game with a scoreboard. Instead of listing every outcome of the game, you track the single number that matters, say points scored. The random variable is that scoreboard; its distribution lists each possible score with its probability; the mean is the average score over many plays.
explain: ## Random variable and distribution

A **random variable** X assigns a number to each outcome of an experiment (number of heads, sum of two dice). Its **probability distribution** lists the possible values xᵢ and their probabilities pᵢ, with pᵢ ≥ 0 and Σpᵢ = 1. That sum rule is the quickest way to find a missing probability.
## Mean (expectation) and variance

**E(X) = Σ xᵢpᵢ**: the long-run average, the value on which a see-saw with weights pᵢ at positions xᵢ would balance. **Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]²** where E(X²) = Σxᵢ²pᵢ; the SD is √Var. For a fair game, E(winnings) = 0. For a linear change, E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b and Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X).
## Bernoulli and binomial

A **Bernoulli trial** has two outcomes, success (prob. p) and failure (q = 1 − p). Repeating n **independent** identical trials and counting successes gives the **binomial distribution** B(n, p): **P(X = k) = C(n, k) pᵏ qⁿ⁻ᵏ**. Reason: choose which k of the n trials succeed (C(n, k) ways), each such pattern has probability pᵏqⁿ⁻ᵏ. The mean is np and the variance is npq.
## Using the binomial

Typical questions: exactly k successes; at most/at least k (add terms, or use the complement); the most likely value (around np); the number of trials needed for a probability to exceed a level. Check the four conditions: fixed n, two outcomes, constant p, independent trials.
## Why np and npq

X is a sum of n independent Bernoulli variables Xᵢ (each is 1 with prob. p, else 0). Each has E(Xᵢ) = p, Var(Xᵢ) = pq. Means add, and for independent variables variances add, so E(X) = np, Var(X) = npq.

s: A particular sequence with k successes and n − k failures (e.g. SSF…) has probability pᵏqⁿ⁻ᵏ because trials are independent.
There are C(n, k) distinct sequences with exactly k successes.
These are mutually exclusive, so P(X = k) = C(n, k)pᵏqⁿ⁻ᵏ. ∎

derivation.t: Mean and variance of B(n, p)
s: Write X = X₁ + … + Xₙ with Xᵢ = 1 (success) or 0. E(Xᵢ) = p; E(Xᵢ²) = p so Var(Xᵢ) = p − p² = pq.
E(X) = np; independence ⇒ Var(X) = n·pq. ∎

title: Counting Principle & Permutations
analogy: Filling seats one at a time. The first seat can be taken by anyone in the room; once someone sits, there is one fewer person for the next seat. Multiply the number of choices for each seat. Permutations are about arrangements where order matters.
explain: ## The fundamental principle of counting

If one task can be done in m ways and a second independent task in n ways, doing **both** (one after the other) can be done in **m × n** ways (multiplication principle). If the tasks are **alternatives** (do one or the other) the total is **m + n** (addition principle). Almost every counting problem is a careful use of these two rules: 'and' means multiply, 'or' means add.
## Permutations

A **permutation** is an ordered arrangement. The number of ways to arrange r distinct objects chosen from n is nPr = n(n − 1)…(n − r + 1) = **n!/(n − r)!**, because the first position has n choices, the second n − 1, and so on for r positions. Arranging all n distinct objects: n!. By convention 0! = 1.
## Repeated objects

If some objects are identical, dividing removes the over-count: arrangements of n objects with p identical of one kind, q of another, … = n!/(p! q! …). MISSISSIPPI: 11!/(4! 4! 2!) = 34,650. Each distinct word is counted p! q!… times in n!, so divide.
## Restrictions

**Objects together:** glue them into one block, arrange the blocks, then arrange inside the block (multiply by that block's internal arrangements). **Objects never together:** total − together, or place the others first and slot the restricted ones into the gaps. **Fixed positions:** place those first. **Digits:** the leading digit cannot be 0; for even numbers choose the last digit first.
## Circular arrangements

In a circle there is no fixed 'first' seat, so rotations count as the same arrangement: n distinct people can be seated in (n − 1)! ways (fix one person, arrange the rest). If clockwise and anticlockwise are the same (necklaces, garlands), divide by 2: (n − 1)!/2.
## Rank of a word

To find the rank of a word in a dictionary order, count the arrangements that come before it letter by letter: for each position, count how many smaller unused letters could go there, times the arrangements of the remaining letters.

s: Filling r positions in order: n choices for the first, n − 1 for the second, …, n − r + 1 for the r-th.
Product = n(n − 1)…(n − r + 1). Multiply and divide by (n − r)! to get n!/(n − r)!. ∎
In a line there are n! arrangements. In a circle each arrangement can be rotated into n different line-arrangements that are really the same circular seating.
So circular arrangements = n!/n = (n − 1)!. ∎

title: Combinations & Selections
analogy: Picking a team, not a batting order. When you choose 3 people from 10 for a committee, who sits where doesn't matter. A combination is a permutation with the ordering thrown away, so you divide out the number of ways the same group could have been ordered.
explain: ## From permutations to combinations

A **combination** is a selection where **order does not matter**. If you pick r objects from n, each group of r can be arranged in r! orders. The permutations nPr count each group r! times, so **nCr = nPr/r! = n!/(r!(n − r)!)**. Test: swapping two chosen items gives the same selection? → combination. A different result? → permutation.
## Properties

nC0 = nCn = 1; nCr = nC(n−r) (choosing r to include is the same as choosing n − r to leave out); nCr + nC(r−1) = (n+1)Cr (Pascal's rule); n·(n−1)C(r−1) = r·nCr. The sum of all nCr is 2ⁿ (each item is in or out). Also, nCr is largest at r = n/2.
## Selections with conditions

'Both A and B are in': choose the remaining from n − 2. 'Neither A nor B': choose from n − 2 without them. 'At least one of a type': total − none of the type. 'Exactly k from group 1 and m from group 2': C(n₁,k)·C(n₂,m). For committees with more than one group, multiply across groups.
## Distributing objects

Dividing 2n people into two equal groups: (2n)!/(n! n! 2!) when the groups are unlabelled. Distributing n identical items among r people (any can get 0): C(n + r − 1, r − 1) — the 'stars and bars' formula. The number of non-negative integer solutions to x₁ + … + xᵣ = n is the same.
## Geometry counts

Number of lines through n points (no three collinear) = nC2. Number of diagonals of an n-gon = nC2 − n. Number of triangles from n points = nC3 (minus collinear triples). Number of rectangles in an n × n grid of squares = (n+1 choose 2)².
formulae: C(n + r − 1, r − 1) solutions to x₁+…+xᵣ = n, xᵢ ≥ 0

s: Each set of r chosen objects can be arranged in r! ways.
Counting ordered selections gives nPr = (number of sets) × r!, so number of sets = nPr/r! = n!/(r!(n − r)!). ∎
Represent n identical items as n stars and the divisions between r people as r − 1 bars. Any arrangement of the n stars and r − 1 bars corresponds to one distribution.
Number of arrangements = choose positions of the bars among n + r − 1 symbols = C(n + r − 1, r − 1). ∎
