solved.q: A committee of 4 is to be chosen from 6 men and 4 women, with at least 2 women. In how many ways?
In how many ways can 10 identical sweets be distributed among 3 children if each gets at least 1?
s: Give each 1 first; 7 remain to distribute freely: C(7 + 3 − 1, 2) = C(9, 2) = 36.

solved.q: How many diagonals does a hexagon have?

traps: Choose first, arrange later (if arrangement matters).
'At least' → add cases or use complement.
Identical vs distinct objects change the method.

title: Data Interpretation: Tables & Charts
analogy: Reading a map before a trip. The graph or table already contains the answer; the skill is knowing which part to look at, what the units are, and which calculation (percentage, ratio, change) the question actually wants.
explain: ## Step 1: read the frame before the numbers

Before touching a question note: the **title**, **units** (₹ crore, thousands, %), the **axes labels**, the **legend** (which series is which), and the **scale** (does the y-axis start at zero?). Half the errors in DI are a unit slip or a mis-read legend.
## Step 2: know the calculations

Almost every DI question is one of: **percentage of total** (part/whole × 100), **percentage change** ((new − old)/old × 100), **ratio** of two quantities, **average**, **difference**, or a **ranking**. Percentage points vs percent is again tested: a rise from 20% to 25% is 5 percentage points but a 25% relative increase.
## Chart types

**Table:** exact values; use row/column totals. **Bar graph:** compare categories; the height is the value. **Line graph:** trend over time; slope shows growth rate, a steeper segment means faster change. **Pie chart:** shares of a whole; the angle = percentage × 3.6° (or fraction × 360°). Questions often combine: the pie gives percentages, a table gives the total, and you need the value of a slice.
## Approximation strategies

You rarely need exact values: round sensibly and compare. To compare two percentages like 37/52 vs 45/61 use cross-multiplication or compare each to a reference (e.g. both vs 0.7). For growth over several years, check whether the question wants average of yearly percentage rates or overall percentage — they differ.
## Missing data and caselets

Caselet DI gives information in sentences; convert it into a table first, then use totals to fill gaps. Always check whether numbers are **in** or **out of** some stated total; whether percentages are of the row or column; and whether data is cumulative.
## Working under time pressure

Skim the whole set to see what's shared, answer the easiest questions first, avoid long multiplications by using fractions (e.g. 12.5% = 1/8, 16.67% = 1/6), and flag questions whose data is incomplete. Practise estimating: close options usually need precise calculation, far-apart options allow rounding.

s: A full circle is 360° and represents 100%.
So 1% corresponds to 3.6°, and a share of x% has angle 3.6x°. ∎

derivation.t: Why percentage change uses the OLD value as base
s: The change is measured relative to where you started: (new − old) is the absolute change, and dividing by old tells how big that change is compared with the starting level.
That is why going 50 → 75 is +50%, but 75 → 50 is −33.3%. ∎

diagrams.svg: <svg class="fig" viewBox="0 0 360 200" role="img" aria-label="bar graph of sales" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line class="ax" x1="28" y1="172" x2="338" y2="172"/><line class="ax" x1="28" y1="22" x2="28" y2="172"/><rect class="fa a" x="42.4" y="85.6" width="47.1" height="86.4"/><text class="t" x="66.0" y="80.6" text-anchor="middle">42</text><text class="tm" x="66.0" y="186" text-anchor="middle">2021</text><rect class="fa a" x="118.4" y="58.9" width="47.1" height="113.1"/><text class="t" x="142.0" y="53.9" text-anchor="middle">55</text><text class="tm" x="142.0" y="186" text-anchor="middle">2022</text><rect class="fa a" x="194.4" y="93.8" width="47.1" height="78.2"/><text class="t" x="218.0" y="88.8" text-anchor="middle">38</text><text class="tm" x="218.0" y="186" text-anchor="middle">2023</text><rect class="fa a" x="270.4" y="44.5" width="47.1" height="127.5"/><text class="t" x="294.0" y="39.5" text-anchor="middle">62</text><text class="tm" x="294.0" y="186" text-anchor="middle">2024</text></svg>
diagrams.cap: Sales (₹ crore): 42, 55, 38, 62. Growth 2021→2022: (55 − 42)/42 ≈ 31%. 2022→2023: (38 − 55)/55 ≈ −31% . Note how the same bar-height difference gives different percentages.

solved.q: Sales were 40, 50, 45 (₹ crore) in 3 years. Find the percentage growth from year 1 to year 2 and from year 2 to year 3.
A pie chart shows a company's expenses: salaries 36°, rent 54°, others the rest. Total expense ₹4,000. Find the rent amount.
A table shows exports of 120, 150, 180 in 3 years. In which year was the percentage increase highest?
s: Year 2: 30/120 = 25%. Year 3: 30/150 = 20%. Year 2 has the higher percentage increase though both rose by 30.

traps: Read the units and the legend first.
Percentage change uses the old value as base.
Pie chart gives shares, not values, unless a total is given.

title: Syllogisms
analogy: Nested boxes. If every pug is a dog and every dog is a mammal, the 'pug' box sits inside the 'dog' box which sits inside the 'mammal' box — so every pug must be a mammal. A syllogism is a drawing exercise: place the boxes, and read off what must be true in every possible drawing.
explain: ## The four statement types

**All A are B** (A ⊆ B): the A circle is wholly inside B (or equal to it). **No A is B**: the circles are separate. **Some A are B**: the circles overlap (at least one A is B). **Some A are not B**: part of A lies outside B. 'Some' means **at least one** (possibly all). 'Some A are B' also tells us 'Some B are A' (the overlap is shared), but 'All A are B' does **not** give 'All B are A'.
## Conclusions must be true in EVERY diagram

A conclusion 'follows' only if it is true in every way of drawing the premises — not merely in the diagram you happened to draw. From 'All A are B' and 'All B are C' you get 'All A are C' always. From 'Some A are B' and 'Some B are C' you get nothing about A and C: the overlaps could be in different places. Always try to draw a diagram that **breaks** the conclusion; if you can, it doesn't follow.
## Method

1) Draw the circles for the premises as loosely as allowed (A inside B, but B might also equal A). 2) For each conclusion, check if it must hold in all drawings. 3) Check complementary pairs ('Some P are Q' / 'No P is Q'): when exactly one of a complementary pair must be true but you can't tell which, the answer is 'either … or …'.
## Quick rules

All + All → All (A→B→C gives All A are C). All + Some → Some (All A are B, Some B are C gives nothing definite; All A are B, some A are C gives Some B are C). All + No → No. Some + All → Some. Some + No → Some…not. No + All → Some…not (the 'No' premise gives 'some not' for the middle).
## Possibility statements
'Possibility' conclusions ('Some A may be B') are true if there is any diagram that allows them, which makes them easy marks when premises do not rule them out.
formulae: All A→B, All B→C ⇒ All A→C

derivation.t: Why 'All A are B, All B are C' ⇒ 'All A are C'
s: Take any element a of A. Since all A are B, a ∈ B.
Since all B are C, a ∈ C.
So every element of A is in C. ∎

derivation.t: Why 'Some A are B, Some B are C' gives nothing
s: Draw A and B overlapping, and B and C overlapping — but with the A∩B region and the B∩C region in different parts of B.
Then A and C need not meet. A diagram where they don't overlap shows 'Some A are C' is not forced. ∎

diagrams.cap: Pugs ⊂ Dogs ⊂ Mammals. Because the smallest circle is inside the middle, which is inside the largest, 'All pugs are mammals' is forced.

solved.q: Statements: All books are pens. Some pens are pencils. Conclusions: I. Some books are pencils. II. Some pencils are pens.
s: Books ⊆ Pens; Pens and Pencils overlap somewhere.
II: 'Some pens are pencils' converts to 'Some pencils are pens' ✓ follows.
I: the overlap of pens and pencils could lie outside the books region, so it does NOT follow.

solved.q: Statements: No cat is a dog. All dogs are animals. Conclusion: Some animals are not cats.
s: Dogs are inside Animals and disjoint from Cats. So the dogs are animals that are not cats.
'Some animals are not cats' follows.

solved.q: Statements: Some A are B. All B are C. Conclusion: Some A are C.
s: The A that are B are also C (B inside C). So some A are C ✓.

traps: 'Some' includes 'all', but never assume 'all'.
Test every possible diagram, not just your first.
'Some A are not B' has no converse.

title: Seating Arrangements
analogy: A stage-manager's chart. You are given a handful of clues ('A sits next to B', 'C is second to the right of D') and must slot everyone into chairs. The skill is drawing the empty chairs first and then placing the most definite clue before the vague ones.
explain: ## Set up the frame

Draw the empty row or circle with the right number of seats and note **which way people face**. This is the biggest source of mistakes: in a row facing north, the left of a person is *west* (the left of the diagram if you face the same way you draw), but for people facing south left and right swap. In a circle facing the **centre**, a person's left is **clockwise**; facing **outward**, the left is anticlockwise. Write this rule at the top of your rough work.
## Clue types and how to use them

**Absolute clues** ('A sits at the extreme left', 'B sits third from the right') fix positions — place them first. **Relative clues** ('C sits to the immediate right of D', 'E is two seats away from F') link people; combine linked people into a block and try both orientations. **Negative clues** ('B is not next to C') rule out options — save them for last. **Counting clues** ('there are two people between A and B') define a spacing.
## Case-splitting

When a clue leaves two possibilities, draw both and carry on; wrong branches die when a later clue contradicts them. Keep branches small and labelled. After placing everything, verify that **every** clue holds.
## Circular specifics

In a circle of n people, 'opposite' means n/2 seats apart (for even n). 'Second to the left' means two places anticlockwise or clockwise depending on facing. Fix one person (the one mentioned most) at the top to eliminate rotation. Mixed facing (some inward, some outward) requires per-person left/right tracking.
## Double-row and square tables

For two rows facing each other, people in one row face one way and the other row the opposite way — so 'left' differs between rows. Make a table: Row 1: positions P1…Pn; Row 2: Q1…Qn, with Pᵢ opposite Qᵢ.
formulae: if k people are between A and B, they are k + 1 seats apart
left = west; facing south: left = east

diagrams.cap: Six people around a table facing the centre. Facing the centre, a person's LEFT neighbour is the next person CLOCKWISE (e.g. A's left is B).

solved.q: Five people A–E sit in a row facing north. B is at the extreme right. A is to the immediate left of B. C is not next to A. D is to the left of C. Who is at the centre?
s: Positions 1–5 (left→right). B = 5, A = 4. C is not next to A so C ≠ 3 → C ∈ {1, 2}.
D is to the left of C ⇒ D = 1, C = 2, leaving E = 3.
Row: D, C, E, A, B. The centre is E.

solved.q: Six friends sit around a circular table facing the centre: A is opposite D; B is to the immediate left of A; C sits between D and E. Who sits opposite B?
s: Place A at position 1 (top). D opposite at 4. Facing the centre, left = clockwise, so B is at 2.
C is between D and E: D at 4, so C at 5 and E at 6 or C at 3 and E at 2 – but 2 is B, so C = 5, E = 6, F = 3.
Opposite B (2) is position 5 = C.

solved.q: In a row of 20 people A is 7th from the left and B is 9th from the right. How many people are between them?
s: B's position from the left = 20 − 9 + 1 = 12. Between positions 7 and 12 there are 12 − 7 − 1 = 4 people.

traps: Fix the facing direction before reading 'left/right'.
Place absolute clues first, negative clues last.
Check ALL clues against the final arrangement.

title: Scheduling & Days
analogy: A weekly planner with sticky notes. Each clue tells you when something cannot or must happen. You build a grid (people × days), strike out impossibilities, and the schedule falls out.
explain: ## Build a grid

List the items (people, meetings, tasks) on one axis and the slots (days, times) on the other. Mark each clue directly in the grid with ✓ (confirmed) or ✗ (excluded). When a row or column has one cell left, that cell must be ✓ — this chain of eliminations drives the whole problem.
## Calendar logic

A week has 7 days; moving k days ahead is (k mod 7) days forward in the week. 'The day after tomorrow', 'three days before Sunday' are mod-7 shifts. For dates: 30-day months give an extra 2 days beyond 4 weeks, 31-day months give 3, February gives 0 or 1. So the same date next month falls 2 or 3 days later in the week.
## Odd days and the calendar

An ordinary year has 365 = 52 weeks + 1 **odd day**; a leap year has 2. Over 100 years there are 5 odd days (76 ordinary + 24 leap → 76 + 48 = 124 ≡ 5). Century odd days: 100 yrs = 5, 200 = 3, 300 = 1, 400 = 0. Use these to find the day of the week for any date: add odd days for completed centuries, years, months and the date, then reduce mod 7 (0 = Sunday, 1 = Monday …).
## Constraints with ordering

Typical statements: 'X is before Y but after Z', 'W is exactly two days after V', 'no two consecutive days'. Convert each to a chain (Z < X < Y) and merge chains. For circular timetables (e.g. weekly rotas) remember that after Sunday comes Monday.
## Verifying
Once a schedule is built, re-read every clue and tick it off. If the question changes a condition ('if Y moves to Monday'), rework locally rather than starting over.
formulae: total odd days mod 7: 0 Sun, 1 Mon, … 6 Sat
n days later → (n mod 7) days forward in the week

s: 100 years contain 24 leap years and 76 ordinary years (the century year itself is ordinary unless divisible by 400).

solved.q: If 5 March 2024 is a Tuesday, what day is 5 March 2025?
s: The period from 5 March 2024 to 5 March 2025 does not contain a 29 February (the 2024 leap day came before 5 March), so it is 365 days = 52 weeks + 1 odd day.
Tuesday + 1 = Wednesday.

solved.q: Five meetings P, Q, R, S, T are held Monday to Friday, one per day. Q is held before R, S is on Wednesday, T is the day after P, and R is not on Friday. Find a valid day for Q.
s: S = Wed. R is not Friday and Q is before R. T = P + 1.
Remaining days: Mon, Tue, Thu, Fri. P, T consecutive: (Mon, Tue) or (Thu, Fri). If P, T = Thu, Fri then Q, R = Mon, Tue ✓ (Q before R, R not Fri).
If P, T = Mon, Tue then Q, R = Thu, Fri but R can't be Fri ✗. So Q = Monday.

solved.q: What day of the week was 15 August 1947 if 1 January 1947 was a Wednesday?
s: Days from 1 Jan to 15 Aug: Jan 31 + Feb 28 + Mar 31 + Apr 30 + May 31 + Jun 30 + Jul 31 = 212, plus 14 more days = 226 days after 1 Jan.
226 mod 7 = 2 (226 = 32×7 + 2). Wednesday + 2 = Friday.

traps: Count odd days with the correct leap-year rule.
Build the grid, don't keep it in your head.
Re-check the solution against every clue.

title: Ranking & Ordering
analogy: People in a queue. If you know your place from the front and your place from the back, together they overlap you twice, so total = front + back − 1. Ranking problems are queue arithmetic with sets of people who might be counted twice.
explain: ## The core identity

If a person is the m-th from the left and the n-th from the right in a row of N people, then **N = m + n − 1** (they are counted in both numbers). So the position from the other end is N − m + 1. The number of people **between** two people at positions p < q is q − p − 1; the number of people from p to q inclusive is q − p + 1.
## Rank and comparison

When many people are compared (taller/older/heavier), write each statement as an inequality and chain them: 'A > B, B > C' gives A > B > C. Draw a number line or vertical list. If two statements give no link between two people, their relative order is **undetermined**. Check whether the question asks 'who is the tallest' (needs a definite maximum) or 'who can be'.
## Interchanging positions

If A and B swap places and now A is at position x, B takes A's old position. Use the two descriptions (before and after) to deduce the difference in positions and thus the total. For example, if A is 8th from the left and after swapping with B he is 15th from the left, B was 15th and the number of people between them is 15 − 8 − 1 = 6.
## Both ends and 'at least' problems

If some people rank above you in two different lists, add carefully: ranks in class A and class B combine as ranks in an overall merged list only if you know the relative order. 'At least' and 'at most' problems ask you to consider extreme arrangements — use the maximum overlap or the minimum overlap.
## Typical shortcuts

Total in the row = rank from top + rank from bottom − 1. If you are the k-th from the top among n students and p students are added who all score higher than you, your new rank = k + p. To find the number of students who passed with a given rank, convert to who is above who.
formulae: new rank = old rank + number added above

s: The person is counted among the m people from the left and among the n people from the right. Together the two groups cover everybody, and the person himself is in both.
So m + n = N + 1, i.e. N = m + n − 1. ∎

diagrams.svg: <svg class="fig" viewBox="0 0 360 110" role="img" aria-label="ranking line" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line class="ax" x1="21.9" y1="55.0" x2="338.1" y2="55.0"/><circle class="dot" cx="77.2" cy="55.0" r="3.6"/><text class="t" x="77.2" y="43.0" text-anchor="middle">A: 4th from left</text><circle class="dot" cx="219.5" cy="55.0" r="3.6"/><text class="t" x="219.5" y="43.0" text-anchor="middle">B: 9th from right</text><text class="tm" x="180.0" y="79.6" text-anchor="middle">total 20, so B is 12th from left</text><text class="tm" x="180.0" y="26.3" text-anchor="middle">people between = 12 − 4 − 1 = 7</text></svg>
diagrams.cap: 20 people in a row. A is 4th from the left; B is 9th from the right, i.e. 12th from the left. The people between them: 12 − 4 − 1 = 7.

solved.q: In a class of 40, Ravi is 12th from the top. What is his rank from the bottom?
A is taller than B. C is shorter than B but taller than D. E is shorter than D. Who is the second tallest?
s: A > B > C > D > E. The second tallest is B.

solved.q: Seema is 15th from the left in a row. After swapping places with Reena she is 22nd from the left. How many people are between them?
s: Positions 15 and 22: 22 − 15 − 1 = 6.

traps: Don't forget the −1 in N = m + n − 1.
Between p and q means q − p − 1, not q − p.
If no chain links two people, their order is undetermined.

title: Blood Relations
analogy: Drawing your own family tree. The trick is to start from the person asked about, move one link at a time, and keep the male/female and generation level of each person clear.
explain: ## Symbols and layout

Use a diagram: □ or + for male, ○ or − for female; a horizontal line = married couple (same generation), a vertical line = parent→child; a horizontal line with a slash or a dashed line = siblings. Draw **generations in rows**, grandparents at the top, so levels are obvious.
## Relation vocabulary

Father's/mother's father = grandfather; father's/mother's sister = aunt; father's/mother's brother = uncle (paternal if father's side, maternal if mother's); aunt's/uncle's children = cousins; your brother's/sister's children = nephew/niece; spouse's brother/sister = brother/sister-in-law; your son's wife = daughter-in-law. 'Mother's only brother' = maternal uncle. 'Father's father's only son' = your father (or uncle if more sons).
## Reading a statement

Translate chains from the end: 'A is the mother of the father of B' means A → mother of (father of B), so A is B's paternal grandmother. Process each relation left to right, writing what each link makes the person in terms of the first person. For 'pointing at a photograph' problems, say 'his' or 'her' refers to someone one level removed; the phrase 'the son of my father's only son' = your own son.
## Coded relations

Sometimes symbols define the relation: 'A + B' means A is the mother of B, 'A × B' means A is the brother of B, and so on. Treat the symbols as a lookup table and chain them. Draw the tree after each step.
## Gender and 'cannot be determined'

If gender is not given, the relation may be undetermined: 'X is the child of Y' doesn't say if X is a son or daughter. The answer 'cannot be determined' is legitimate when the gender or the exact link is missing.

diagrams.cap: A compact tree with generations in rows. Father's brother is your uncle; his child is your cousin; your father's father is your grandfather.

solved.q: Pointing to a man, Rita says, 'His mother is the only daughter of my mother.' How is the man related to Rita?
s: Only daughter of Rita's mother = Rita herself. So the man's mother is Rita; he is Rita's son.

solved.q: A is B's sister. C is B's mother. D is C's father. E is D's mother. How is A related to D?
s: C is B's mother, D is C's father so D is the grandfather of both A and B. A is D's granddaughter.

solved.q: If A + B means A is the mother of B, and A × B means A is the brother of B, what does P + Q × R mean?
s: P + Q: P is the mother of Q. Q × R: Q is the brother of R. So P is the mother of Q, and R is Q's sibling; P is R's mother.
solved.a: P is the mother of R

traps: Work from the person asked about, one link at a time.
'Only son/daughter' pins down a person — use it.
If gender isn't given, the answer may be 'cannot be determined'.

title: Direction Sense
analogy: Walking with a pocket compass and graph paper. Every move is a step on the grid; at the end you subtract coordinates to see how far you are and in which direction, using nothing more than Pythagoras.
explain: ## Coordinates for compass

Treat the start as the origin (0, 0), North as +y, East as +x. A move of 5 m North adds (0, 5); 3 m West adds (−3, 0). After all moves, the net displacement is (Σx, Σy). The **shortest distance** from the start is √(Σx² + Σy²) (Pythagoras), and the **direction** comes from the signs of Σx and Σy (e.g. +x, +y = north-east).
## Turns

A **right turn** rotates you 90° clockwise: facing North, a right turn takes you East; facing East, a right turn takes you South. A **left turn** is 90° anticlockwise: facing North, left → West. Track the *heading* separately from the *position*. A 'U-turn' is 180°. The 8 directions: N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW; between adjacent ones is 45°.
## Shadows

At sunrise the sun is in the East, so shadows point West; at sunset the sun is in the West, so shadows point East. At noon (in the northern hemisphere) shadows point North. If at sunrise a person's shadow falls to his right, he faces South (shadow West is to his right when facing South).
## Relative direction

For 'B is to the north-west of A' draw A, then B up-left. For multi-step problems with several people, put everybody on the same grid. When the final answer is a direction of one person from another, subtract coordinates (target − origin).
## Clock-based directions
Imagine standing at the centre of a clock facing 12 as North. The hour hand pointing at 3 is East, 6 is South, and 9 is West. Angles between directions: each hour mark is 30°; a quarter turn is 90°.
## Pitfalls
Do not confuse **distance travelled** (sum of all path lengths) with **displacement** (straight-line from start to end). Questions on 'how far from the starting point' ask for displacement.

diagrams.cap: Walk 4 N, 3 E, 3 S: the net displacement is (3, 1). The straight-line distance is √(3² + 1²) = √10, while the distance walked is 10.

solved.q: A man walks 5 km north, then 12 km east. How far is he from the start and in which direction?
s: Displacement = √(25 + 144) = 13 km, towards north-east (more east than north).

solved.q: Ram faces North and turns right, then right again, then left. Which direction is he facing?
s: North → right → East → right → South → left → East.

solved.q: At sunset Rohan's shadow falls to his left. Which way does he face?
s: At sunset shadow points East. Shadow on his left means East is his left, so he faces South.

traps: Distance walked ≠ displacement.
Track heading and position separately.
A right turn is always clockwise from the current heading.

title: Coding–Decoding
analogy: Breaking a simple cipher the way a child decodes a secret message: find the rule by comparing the original and coded forms, check it on a second example, then apply it.
explain: ## Strategy

Compare the original with its code **position by position**. Ask: is every letter shifted by a constant? Is there a reversal, a swap of positions, or a substitution of letters by numbers? Test your hypothesis on a second word; if it holds, apply it. If not, try another rule.
## Letter coding

Learn the alphabet positions: A = 1 … Z = 26. Opposite letters satisfy position + opposite position = 27 (A↔Z, B↔Y, …). Typical rules: shift every letter by +k (CAT → DBU for +1), alternating shifts (+1, −1, +1…), reversal of the word, swapping first and last letters, converting each letter to the next consonant or vowel.
## Number coding and sums

Replace letters by numbers (A = 1…) and compute something: sum of positions, product, or place values. For substitution tables ('sky' = 'blue', 'blue' = 'water'), define a dictionary and translate exactly as stated, ignoring real-world meaning.
## Word-sentence coding

Given several coded sentences, find which code word recurs in the sentences that share an original word. Intersect the common words: the common code word is the common meaning. Sketch a small table with each sentence's words on separate lines.
## Mixed rules

Some codes alternate between two operations or apply a rule only to vowels (or consonants). Break the word into pieces to see the pattern. Check parity of positions (odd positions +2, even −1). If a rule works for the examples, apply it carefully, including wrapping around (Z + 1 = A).
## Speed
Memorise EJOTY (5, 10, 15, 20, 25) as anchors and 'A–M / N–Z' split for opposite letters. Write the alphabet with numbers once at the start of the section.

s: The alphabet has 26 letters. Counting from the front, a letter at position p is at position 27 − p when counted from the back (1st from front is 26th from back: 1 + 26 = 27). ∎

solved.q: If MOUSE is coded as NPVTF, how is HOUSE coded?

solved.q: If A = 1, B = 2, …, find the value of the word CAB.
In a code, 'ab cd ef' means 'sun is bright'; 'cd gh' means 'sun rises'; 'ef ij' means 'bright day'. What is the code for 'is'?
s: Common to the first two: cd = sun. Common to the first and third: ef = bright. So ab = is.

traps: Verify the rule on a second example.
Wrap around the alphabet (Z+1 = A).
Opposite letter is 27 − position, not 26 − position.

title: Number & Letter Series
analogy: Spotting the rhythm in a song. Once you hear the beat (the rule), you can predict the next note. Series puzzles ask you to find the rhythm in as few listens as possible.
explain: ## First look: differences and ratios

Write the differences between consecutive terms. If they are constant, it is an **arithmetic** pattern. If the differences themselves form a pattern (like 3, 5, 7, 9), take **second differences**: a constant second difference means the nth term is quadratic (n² + 1 gives 2, 5, 10, 17, 26). If successive ratios are constant it is **geometric**.
## Common families

Squares and cubes (n², n³, n² ± 1, n³ ± n); primes; Fibonacci-type (each term is the sum of the previous two); alternating series (two interleaved patterns — separate odd and even positions); series with operations that alternate (×2, +3, ×2, +3, …); and factorial-based (1, 2, 6, 24, 120). Learn squares to 25 and cubes to 10.
## Letter series

Convert letters to alphabet positions (A = 1 … Z = 26) and treat as a number series. For letter-cluster series (ABD, BCE, CDF…), analyse each position separately. Wrap around after Z. Look for skipped letters (+2, +3 steps) and alternating forward and backward moves.
## Missing and wrong terms

For a **missing** term, find the rule from the visible pattern and fill it in. For a **wrong** term, find the rule from the consistent majority of terms and see which term breaks it. Check the answer by verifying the rule on every term.
## Systematic approach

1) Check differences. 2) Check second differences. 3) Check ratios (×2, ×3, ×1.5). 4) Check whether terms are close to squares/cubes/primes. 5) Check odd and even positions separately. 6) Check combos (×2 + 1, ×3 − 2). Do not spend more than a minute per question: skip and come back.
## Sum and product patterns
Look for 'each term = sum of previous two' and 'each term = previous × position + something'. For twin sequences, the row below may be derived from the row above.
formulae: constant second difference d₂ ⇒ aₙ = (d₂/2)n² + bn + c

derivation.t: Why constant second differences mean a quadratic
s: If aₙ = An² + Bn + C then aₙ₊₁ − aₙ = A(2n + 1) + B — linear in n.
The second difference is then A(2(n+1)+1) − A(2n+1) = 2A, a constant. ∎ So the quadratic coefficient is d₂/2.

solved.q: Find the next term: 3, 6, 12, 24, ?
s: Ratio 2 each time → 48.

solved.q: Find the next term: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ?
s: Perfect squares → 36.

solved.q: Find the next term: 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ?
s: Each term is the sum of the previous two: 2 + 3 = 5, 3 + 5 = 8, 5 + 8 = 13.
So the next term is 8 + 13 = 21.

traps: Check second differences before giving up.
Interleaved series need separate analysis of odd/even positions.
Letter series wrap around after Z.

title: Number Operations
analogy: A new set of arithmetic rules invented for one puzzle: '5 ★ 3 = 28' might mean a² + b. You are the detective who deduces the rule from the examples and then plays the game.
explain: ## Symbol-defined operations

A problem defines a fake operator (★, #, @) with a rule like a ★ b = 2a + b², or replaces +, −, ×, ÷ with letters/symbols ('if + means ×, − means ÷…'). Do **exactly** what the definition says, ignoring normal arithmetic. Rewrite the expression by substituting the real operators first, then apply BODMAS.
## Substitution

When symbols swap meanings, rewrite the whole expression with the true operators before computing: '6 @ 3 # 2' with '@' = '+', '#' = '×' becomes 6 + 3 × 2 = 12. Be careful with BODMAS: multiplication/division before addition/subtraction; brackets first.
## Finding the rule from examples

Given 3 ♦ 2 = 11, 4 ♦ 3 = 19, find the rule. Try a² + b (3² + 2 = 11 ✓, 4² + 3 = 19 ✓). Test the guess on every example before using it. Candidates: sums/differences of squares, product ± sum, a × b + a, etc.
## Matrix and box puzzles
Rows or columns follow the same rule (e.g. the third number = first × second − 1). Find the rule from complete rows, then apply to the incomplete one. Check both row-wise and column-wise rules.
## Mathematical comparisons
Operators like >, <, = represented by symbols, with conclusions: translate to inequality chains. 'A @ B' meaning 'A > B' lets you chain: A @ B # C: A > B and B ≤ C → no relation between A and C.
## Workflow
Rewrite → substitute → compute with BODMAS → check units. Never reorder operations for convenience.
formulae: Brackets, Orders, Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction
× and ÷ have equal rank, left to right
replace the symbols with real operators FIRST

solved.q: If a ★ b = 2a + b², find 3 ★ 4.
If + means ×, − means ÷, × means − and ÷ means +, find 12 + 3 − 4 × 5 ÷ 2.
Given 2 ◆ 3 = 8 and 3 ◆ 4 = 15, find 4 ◆ 5.

traps: Substitute the real operators BEFORE applying BODMAS.
Test your rule on all examples.
× and ÷ are same rank: work left to right.

title: Data Sufficiency
analogy: A detective asking, 'is this evidence enough to name the culprit?' You don't need to catch the culprit (solve the problem); you only need to decide whether the clues you have are enough to do it uniquely.
explain: ## What you are asked

You are given a question and two statements. You must decide whether the question can be answered **with a definite (unique) answer** using: statement 1 alone, statement 2 alone, both together, or neither. You do NOT compute the final answer; you judge whether it is determined.
## Standard procedure

1) Understand the question: what is asked, and is it a yes/no or a value? 2) Evaluate statement 1 **alone** (ignore statement 2). 3) Evaluate statement 2 **alone** (ignore statement 1 — do not carry information across). 4) If neither alone works, combine. 5) If even together they are insufficient, the answer is 'neither'.
## Value vs yes/no questions

A **value** question needs one number. A **yes/no** question is sufficient if the statement gives a definite 'yes' *or* a definite 'no' every time; if the answer could be both yes and no, the statement is insufficient. Remember: a definite 'no' is sufficient.
## Counting equations and unknowns

For linear problems, you need as many independent equations as unknowns. Two unknowns with one equation → insufficient; but two equations might be dependent (a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂), so check independence. For inequalities or integer constraints, a unique answer might still exist (e.g. x is a positive integer and x < 2 ⇒ x = 1).
## Common traps

Using statement 1 information while judging statement 2; assuming extra facts (a quadrilateral being a square); forgetting restrictions (x is an integer, x > 0); treating 'maybe' as sufficient; computing the value when you only needed to decide if you could.
## Special LR forms
Many LR sufficiency questions ask about relations or ordering ('Who is taller, A or B?'). Build the partial order from each statement separately, then merge. Draw the diagram only as much as needed.
formulae: gives one definite value (or definite yes/no)
a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂ ⇒ really one equation
both 'always yes' and 'always no' are sufficient; 'sometimes' is not

solved.q: What is x? (1) x² = 9. (2) x > 0.
s: (1) alone: x = 3 or −3 — not unique. (2) alone: x > 0 only — not enough.
Together: x = 3. Both together are needed.

solved.q: Is Raj older than Sam? (1) Raj is older than Tina. (2) Tina is older than Sam.
s: (1) alone: nothing about Sam. (2) alone: nothing about Raj.
Together: Raj > Tina > Sam ⇒ yes. Both together are needed.
(1) alone: x + y = 5 — enough! (2) alone gives x − y only.
So statement (1) alone is sufficient.

traps: Judge each statement alone first.
A definite 'no' is sufficient for a yes/no question.
Don't add facts that aren't given.

title: Statement–Action & Cause
analogy: A manager's judgment call. Given a situation, which actions actually address it, which are overkill, and which are unrelated? You grade the options by directness, practicality and proportion.
explain: ## Courses of action

You are given a problem statement and two or more proposed actions. An action **follows** if it (1) directly addresses the problem, (2) is practical and within reach, and (3) is proportionate — neither too weak nor too extreme. Actions that blame, punish all, or wait for others without need usually do not follow; neither do actions that ignore the statement's facts.
## Assumptions

An **assumption** is an unstated premise that must be true for the statement to make sense. Test by negating it: if the statement collapses when the assumption is false, then it was assumed. 'Buy a ticket now, prices will rise soon' assumes prices might rise and that tickets are available. Words like 'only', 'all', 'best' make assumptions too strong to be valid.
## Inferences and conclusions

An **inference** must follow from the given facts without outside knowledge. Judge as 'definitely true', 'probably true', 'insufficient data', 'probably false', 'definitely false'. Do not use real-world knowledge unless the statement implies it. Extreme words (always, never, all) are usually too strong.
## Cause and effect

Given two statements, decide if one is the **immediate/principal cause**, a **remote cause**, a **consequence**, or **independent**. The cause usually precedes the effect and explains it. Both can be effects of a common cause. Ask: 'if A hadn't happened, would B still occur?'
## Strengthening and weakening arguments

An argument is strengthened by facts that support its premise or link to the conclusion; weakened by evidence that breaks the link or introduces a contradicting cause. The best strengthener closes a gap; the best weakener opens one.
## Process
Read the statement, underline the problem, evaluate each option against directness, practicality and proportion, then choose.
formulae: negate it; if the statement fails, it is an assumption
always, never, only, all ⇒ usually too extreme

diagrams.svg: <svg class="fig" viewBox="0 0 366 170" role="img" aria-label="statement and action" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><text class="t" x="54.8" y="44.9" text-anchor="start">Statement: Floods have hit the district.</text><text class="tm" x="54.8" y="68.5" text-anchor="start">Course of action ?</text><text class="t" x="54.8" y="85.0" text-anchor="start">✔ relief camps (addresses the problem directly)</text><text class="tm" x="54.8" y="101.5" text-anchor="start">✘ suspend all schools nationwide (disproportionate)</text></svg>
diagrams.cap: A good action addresses the actual problem proportionately; extreme or unrelated actions don't follow.

solved.q: Statement: Many commuters report long delays at a railway crossing. Actions: I. Build an overbridge. II. Ban all private vehicles. Which follow?
s: I: direct and practical → follows. II: extreme, disproportionate → does not follow.

solved.q: Statement: 'Use brand X toothpaste for stronger teeth.' Which is an assumption: (a) People care about strong teeth. (b) All toothpastes are the same.
s: (a) must hold for the advertisement to work → assumption. (b) contradicts the advertisement.

solved.q: Fuel prices rose sharply; bus fares were raised the next week. Which is cause and which is effect?
s: The fuel price rise increased operating costs, leading to higher fares. Cause: fuel price rise; effect: fare rise.

traps: Extreme actions (punish everyone, shut down) rarely follow.
Test assumptions by negation.
Don't import outside knowledge into inferences.

title: Vocabulary Building
analogy: Breaking a word into LEGO pieces. Most hard words are built from prefixes, roots and suffixes that you already half-know. Understand the pieces and you can read thousands of words you've never seen, plus guess meanings from context like a detective.
explain: ## Root, prefix, suffix

A **root** carries the core meaning (spect = look, bene = good, ject = throw), a **prefix** modifies it (in-, un-, mis-, anti-, pre-), a **suffix** changes the part of speech (-ous, -tion, -ize). 'Inspect' = in + spect (look into), 'benevolent' = bene + vol (wish well). Knowing 50 common roots opens up hundreds of words.
## Synonyms and shades of meaning

Synonyms are words with similar meanings but usually different **connotations** (positive/negative, formal/informal): thrifty (positive) vs miserly (negative), slender (positive) vs skinny. In synonym questions, pick the option that matches both the meaning and the tone of the word. The surrounding sentence usually resolves ambiguity between the senses of a word.
## Antonyms

An antonym is the opposite in meaning. Check the **part of speech** and the **degree**: the opposite of 'frugal' is 'extravagant' (not just 'rich'). Beware of options that are synonyms of the word (a frequent trap). Prefix clues: if the word has a negative prefix (in-, un-), the antonym often drops it.
## Words in context

When a word has several meanings ('bear', 'fine', 'plain'), the context chooses. Read the whole sentence, replace the word with each option, and pick the one that keeps the sentence logical. Look for **signal words**: 'but', 'however' (contrast) and 'because', 'therefore' (same direction).
## Learning and retaining

Use spaced repetition: learn a word with a sentence, an image, and a related word. Group by root and by theme. When you meet a new word in reading, guess before checking, which strengthens memory. In the exam, if you don't know a word, break it down, decide whether it feels positive or negative, and use elimination.
formulae: bene = good;  mal = bad;  spect = look;  ject = throw;  scrib/script = write;  voc = call;  chron = time;  anthrop = man
un-/in-/dis- = not;  re- = again;  pre- = before;  anti- = against;  sub- = under
positive / neutral / negative shade of the same denotation
but, although, however = contrast;  because, hence = cause

solved.q: Choose the synonym of 'frugal': (a) wasteful (b) thrifty (c) rich (d) generous
s: 'Frugal' means careful with money, so 'thrifty' is the synonym.

solved.q: Antonym of 'benevolent': (a) kind (b) malevolent (c) generous (d) gentle
s: bene (good) vs mal (bad): malevolent is the opposite.

solved.q: 'The critic's remarks were scathing.' The word 'scathing' most nearly means:
s: Critics' remarks that are 'scathing' are severely critical and harsh.

traps: Antonym questions often include a synonym as a trap.
Match connotation as well as denotation.
Always test the option in the sentence.

title: Idioms, Phrases & One-Word Substitution
analogy: Idioms are inside jokes the language tells itself: you can't decode 'kick the bucket' word-by-word, you have to know the story. One-word substitutes are the language's shorthand: instead of 'a person who loves books', we say 'bibliophile'.
explain: ## Idioms

An **idiom** is a phrase whose meaning is not the sum of its words: 'a piece of cake' (very easy), 'break the ice' (start a conversation), 'hit the sack' (go to bed). Learn them by meaning **and** by a vivid picture. Most exam idioms come in themes: effort ('burn the midnight oil'), failure ('go down the drain'), secrecy ('let the cat out of the bag'), money ('cost an arm and a leg'). In multiple-choice, eliminate literal readings.
## Phrases and proverbs

Proverbs compress experience: 'A stitch in time saves nine' (act early). Their meaning is often a lesson; understand the principle, not the words. Questions ask for the closest meaning, so find the principle (prevention, patience, caution).
## One-word substitution

Replace a long description with a single word: 'one who knows everything' → omniscient; 'a government by the people' → democracy; 'that cannot be avoided' → inevitable; 'a speech without preparation' → extempore. The best way to learn is by prefix-root groups: -cide = killing (suicide, homicide), -phobia = fear, -cracy = rule, -arch = leader, omni- = all, bi- = two.
## Verbal analogies

An analogy 'A : B :: C : D' says that A relates to B just as C relates to D. First state the **relationship** in a sentence ('B is the tool used for A', 'B is a part of A', 'B is the intense form of A'), then test each option with the same sentence. Common relations: synonym, antonym, part–whole, tool–user, cause–effect, degree (warm : hot), function, category–example.
## Strategy

If you don't know an idiom, think of the images and the context in which you've heard it. For analogies always make the sentence **specific** — vague relationships admit multiple options. Eliminate options that break the sentence.
formulae: -cide = killing;  -phobia = fear;  -cracy = rule;  -arch = ruler;  omni = all;  -vore = eater
polyglot (many languages), misanthrope (hates people), philanthropist (loves mankind), ambidextrous (both hands)
synonym · antonym · part–whole · tool–worker · cause–effect · degree · category

solved.q: One who can speak many languages:
s: poly (many) + glot (tongue) = polyglot.

solved.q: 'To beat around the bush' means:
s: It means avoiding the main point, speaking indirectly.

solved.q: Hot : Scalding :: Cold : ?  (a) Cool (b) Freezing (c) Warm (d) Mild
s: Relationship: second is the extreme degree of the first. Extreme of cold = freezing.

traps: Don't read idioms literally.
State the analogy relationship precisely before testing options.
Learn roots to decode one-word substitutes.

title: Grammar: Agreement & Tenses
analogy: A sentence is a machine with matching plugs: the subject and verb must fit each other in number, and the verb must fit the time of the story. Most grammar errors are plugs that don't match.
explain: ## Subject–verb agreement

A singular subject takes a singular verb ('The boy runs'), a plural subject a plural verb ('The boys run'). Find the **true subject**, ignoring words in between: 'The **list** of items **is** long' (list is the subject, not items). Phrases like 'along with', 'as well as', 'together with' do not make the subject plural: 'The captain, along with his players, **is** here.'
## Tricky subjects

Two subjects joined by **and** are plural ('Tom and Jerry are'), unless they form one idea ('Bread and butter is…'). With **or/nor/either…or/neither…nor** the verb agrees with the subject **nearer** to it. **Each, every, either, neither, everyone, somebody** are singular. Collective nouns (team, committee) are singular if acting as a unit, plural if members act individually. Words like **news, mathematics, physics, measles** are singular despite -s. 'A number of' takes a plural verb; 'the number of' a singular.
## Tenses

Simple present for habits and facts; present continuous for actions now; present perfect (has/have + V3) for past actions with present relevance ('I have lost my keys'); simple past for finished time ('I lost them yesterday'); past perfect (had + V3) for the earlier of two past actions; future with will/shall. **Do not mix** present perfect with a finished-time word like 'yesterday'.
## Sequence of tenses

If the main verb is in the past, the subordinate clause is normally in the past ('He said that he was tired') — except for universal truths ('He said that the earth **moves** round the sun'). In conditionals: If + present, will + base ('If it rains, I will stay'); If + past, would + base ('If I were rich, I would travel'); If + past perfect, would have + V3 (for unreal past).
## Common verb forms

Irregular verbs: go–went–gone, see–saw–seen, write–wrote–written. After modals (can, will, should), use the base form. Gerund (-ing) vs infinitive: enjoy + -ing, want + to + verb. Parallel structure: keep forms matched in a list ('She likes reading, writing and to swim' ✗ → 'swimming').
## Error-spotting method
Read the sentence, find the subject and its verb, check agreement, then check tense consistency and form of each verb.
formulae: each, every, either, neither, everyone, nobody, news, mathematics
or / nor / either…or / neither…nor → verb agrees with the nearer subject
along with, as well as, together with, in addition to
had V3 (earlier past) → V2 (past) → has/have V3 → V1/Ving → will V1
If+present, will+V1;  If+past, would+V1;  If+had V3, would have V3

solved.q: Choose the correct form: 'Neither the teacher nor the students (is/are) present.'
s: With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: 'students' → are.

solved.q: Correct the sentence: 'He has gone to Mumbai yesterday.'
s: 'Yesterday' is a finished-time word, so use the simple past: 'He went to Mumbai yesterday.'

solved.q: Identify the error: 'The committee have decided its policy.'
s: Collective noun acting as a unit takes a singular verb, and 'its' is singular: 'The committee has decided its policy.'

traps: Ignore interrupting phrases when finding the subject.
Finished-time words need simple past.
Collective nouns: unit = singular.

title: Grammar: Prepositions, Articles & Pronouns
analogy: Prepositions are the small hinges that hold sentences together: 'in', 'on', 'at' pick where an idea lives in time and space. The rules are pattern-based, so you learn them like chess openings: by seeing them often.
explain: ## Prepositions of time and place

**At** a point (at 5 pm, at the bus stop); **on** a surface or a day (on the table, on Monday, on 5 May); **in** an enclosed space or a longer period (in the room, in July, in 2020, in the morning). **By** a deadline ('by Friday'); **for** a duration ('for two hours'); **since** a starting point ('since 2010').
## Dependent prepositions and collocations

Many words are tied to particular prepositions: **afraid of**, **good at**, **interested in**, **depend on**, **different from**, **capable of**, **fond of**, **accuse of**, **prevent from**, **congratulate on**. Learn as chunks, not rules. Collocations are natural word pairs: 'make a decision' (not do), 'do homework' (not make), 'heavy rain', 'strong tea'.
## Articles

Use **a/an** for a singular countable noun mentioned first or in a general sense (a before consonant sounds, an before vowel sounds: **an hour**, **a university**); **the** for a specific, known noun, unique things (the sun), superlatives (the best), and rivers/oceans (the Ganga). No article with plural general nouns (Dogs are loyal), uncountable general nouns (Water is essential), and most proper nouns (India).
## Pronouns

Pronoun must agree with its antecedent in number, person and gender. Use subject forms for subjects (I, he, they) and object forms for objects (me, him, them): 'between you and me' (not I). **Who** for subjects, **whom** for objects. Reflexive pronouns (myself) are used when the subject and object are the same, not as a fancy 'me'. Avoid ambiguous reference ('He told his friend he was late' — who?).
## Determiners and quantifiers

**Few/many** with countable plurals; **little/much** with uncountables; 'a few' (some) is positive, 'few' (almost none) negative. **Fewer** for countable, **less** for uncountable. **Each other** for two, **one another** for more.
## Typical errors
'He is senior than me' → senior to me; 'discuss about' → discuss (no 'about'); 'return back' → return; 'one of the boy' → one of the boys.
formulae: at (clock time) · on (day/date) · in (month/year/season) · by (deadline) · since/for
good at · afraid of · interested in · depend on · different from · prevent from
a/an: general singular;  the: specific / unique / superlative

solved.q: Fill in: 'She is very good ___ mathematics.'
s: The standard collocation is 'good at'.

solved.q: Correct: 'He is the most intelligent of the two brothers.'
s: For comparing two, use the comparative: 'the more intelligent of the two'.

solved.q: 'Between you and ___' (I / me)?
s: After a preposition use the object form: 'between you and me'.

traps: Learn prepositions as chunks, not individual words.
Use the object pronoun after prepositions.
Count nouns take fewer; mass nouns take less.

title: Error Spotting, Confused Words & Sentence Usage
analogy: A proofreader's checklist. Rather than reading for meaning and getting lulled, you scan systematically for the usual suspects: agreement, tense, preposition, pronoun, article, parallelism, word choice.
explain: ## The checklist

Read the sentence once for sense, then run down the list: (1) **Subject–verb agreement** (find the real subject). (2) **Tense consistency** and correct verb form. (3) **Pronoun** agreement and case. (4) **Articles and prepositions**. (5) **Adjective/adverb** use (good vs well; comparatives for two, superlatives for three or more; no double comparatives like 'more better'). (6) **Parallelism** in lists and comparisons. (7) **Modifier placement** (dangling or misplaced phrases). (8) **Word choice** (confused pairs). If a part is underlined, check just that part against the list.
## Commonly confused words

accept (receive) / except (excluding); affect (verb: influence) / effect (noun: result); principal (head, main) / principle (rule); complement (completes) / compliment (praise); stationary (still) / stationery (paper); council (body) / counsel (advice); farther (distance) / further (additional); lie (recline) / lay (put down); lose / loose; its (possessive) / it's (it is); their / there / they're.
## Dangling and misplaced modifiers

A modifying phrase must sit next to what it describes. 'Walking down the road, the trees looked lovely' wrongly suggests the trees were walking. Correct: 'Walking down the road, I thought the trees looked lovely.' A phrase that begins with a participle ('Having finished…') must refer to the subject of the main clause.
## Sentence completion

Read the sentence, identify the **logical relationship** the blank requires: contrast ('Although he was ___, he finished'), cause ('Because it was ___, we left'), definition. Predict a word before looking at the options, then choose the one that fits meaning, tone and grammar. Check both blanks for two-blank sentences.
## Usage questions
Questions ask which sentence uses a word correctly (e.g. 'principal' vs 'principle'). Substitute the dictionary meaning of the word into each sentence; the incorrect one will not make sense.
## Time management
Don't dwell; if no error stands out, the sentence may indeed be correct ('No error' is an option in many exams). Prefer the option that fixes an obvious rule violation.
formulae: SV agreement · tense · pronoun · article · preposition · adjective/adverb · parallelism · modifier · word choice
comparative for 2, superlative for 3+;  never 'more better'

solved.q: Find the error: 'The effect of the new policy are visible everywhere.'
s: Subject 'effect' is singular, so the verb should be 'is'. Error: 'are'.

solved.q: Choose the correct word: 'The medicine had no ___ on him.' (affect / effect)
s: 'Effect' is the noun meaning result. 'had no effect on him'.

solved.q: Correct: 'Having finished the report, the movie started.'
s: The participial phrase must modify the person who finished: 'Having finished the report, I watched the movie' / 'After I had finished the report, the movie started.'

traps: Scan with the checklist, not by feel.
Participial phrases must modify the subject.
'No error' is a valid answer.

title: Para Jumbles & Odd Sentence
analogy: Reassembling a necklace from loose beads: each bead is a sentence, and the string is the thread of the argument. Find the beads that obviously start the string, look for the clasps that join pairs, and then thread the rest in order.
explain: ## Find the opening

A good opening sentence introduces the topic **without depending on anything before it**: no pronouns referring back ('this', 'they', 'it' without a clear noun), no 'however', 'therefore', 'also', 'moreover'. It usually states a general idea or defines a concept. Scan for the sentence that could stand on its own at the beginning of a paragraph.
## Find the mandatory pairs

Look for strong links: **pronoun → noun** (a sentence using 'he' follows the sentence naming him); **'this' + noun** refers to something just stated; **general → specific** (idea → example); **cause → effect**; **chronology** (dates, 'first…then…finally'); **connectors** like 'however' (contrast with the previous idea), 'for instance' (example of the previous idea), 'thus' (conclusion). Match these pairs first; they shrink the number of possible orders dramatically.
## Build the chain

Join pairs into chains, order the chains by the opening/closing clues, then check the whole paragraph for flow. If options are given, use them: eliminate options that violate a confirmed pair. Usually, once you fix the opener and one strong pair, only one option survives.
## Odd sentence out

Find the main theme of the paragraph (what most of the sentences are about). The odd sentence introduces a **different subject**, a different time, or a tone shift. Test by removing it: the remaining sentences should flow without a gap.
## Closing sentences
The last sentence often concludes ('Thus', 'Therefore', 'In short'), generalises, or points to the future. It should not introduce a new topic or leave a dangling reference.
## Practise reading for structure
Read editorials to notice how writers move from claim to evidence to implication. Time yourself: 1–2 minutes per jumble.

solved.q: Order: (A) However, the idea did not catch on. (B) In 1990, Tim proposed a new system. (C) It was meant to simplify filing. (D) Few officials understood it.
s: B introduces Tim and the system (no back-reference) → opener. C 'It' refers to the system → follows B. A 'However' contrasts with the intent → next. D explains why it did not catch on.
Order: B C A D.

solved.q: Which sentence is odd? 1. Cats are independent. 2. They sleep a lot. 3. Their senses are sharp. 4. Python is a popular programming language.
s: Sentences 1–3 are about cats. Sentence 4 changes the topic.

solved.q: Which is a better opener: 'This made them angry.' or 'The council raised taxes in March.'?
s: 'This' refers to something earlier, so cannot be the opener. The second sentence stands alone.
solved.a: The council raised taxes in March.

traps: Don't start with a sentence that has a dangling 'this/they'.
Use mandatory pairs to cut options.
The odd sentence changes the SUBJECT, not just the sentence style.

title: Reading Comprehension
analogy: Following a conversation at a table. You catch the main point, notice who disagrees with whom, and know the speaker's mood. A comprehension question then asks: what did she actually say, what did she imply, and what would she think about something new?
explain: ## Read for structure, not for every word

On a first pass get: the **topic**, the **author's tone** (critical, neutral, supportive), and the **role of each paragraph** (introduces the issue, presents a view, gives an example, concedes, concludes). Mark contrast words (**but, however, although, yet**) because the author's own view usually follows them, and emphasis words (**crucially, in fact, importantly**).
## Question types

**Main idea / title:** the most comprehensive statement, neither too narrow (one detail) nor too broad. **Detail (fact) questions:** go back to the exact lines; the answer is stated. **Inference:** the answer is strongly supported but not stated word for word; stay close to the text. **Vocabulary-in-context:** the word's meaning in this passage, not the dictionary first meaning. **Tone / attitude:** pick the shade carefully (critical vs sceptical vs scathing). **Purpose / function of a paragraph:** why did the author include this? **Application:** what would the author likely say about a new case?
## Elimination patterns

Wrong options typically are: **extreme** (always, never, only, completely), **out of scope** (true in the real world but not in the passage), **reversal** (opposite of the text), **partial truth** (right fact, wrong emphasis), or **distortion** (changes a key word). Pick the option that is supported by the text and uses its qualified language.
## Passage types

**Argumentative** (claim, evidence, counterclaim): track the author's position. **Descriptive/expository** (explains how something works): track the sequence. **Narrative/literary**: pay attention to tone and imagery. **Data/Science-based**: restate technical sentences in plain language.
## Time management

Spend about 2–3 minutes on the passage and ~1 minute per question. If a question requires too much searching, move on. Read the **question stem and options carefully** — one word like 'EXCEPT' or 'NOT' flips the answer.
## Improving

Read long-form pieces daily, summarise each paragraph in one line, and practise paraphrasing. Review wrong answers by finding the sentence that proves the correct option and the word that makes the wrong one wrong.
formulae: topic · tone · role of each paragraph
but, however, yet, although (contrast);  therefore, thus (conclusion);  for instance (example)
extreme · out of scope · reversal · partial truth · distortion
must be strongly supported by the text, not merely possible

solved.q: A passage criticises a policy for ignoring rural needs but acknowledges that it boosted urban growth. Which is the best description of the author's attitude?
s: The author concedes a benefit yet is critical overall. 'Critical but balanced' fits; 'hostile' is too extreme and 'neutral' ignores the criticism.

solved.q: 'The study found that stress increases risk, though the effect was small.' Which statement is supported? (a) Stress always causes illness. (b) Stress is linked to a slightly higher risk. (c) Stress is harmless.
s: (a) extreme ('always'), (c) contradicts, (b) matches 'increases risk … effect small'.

solved.q: In the sentence 'The minister's plan was a bold gamble', 'gamble' is used to suggest:
s: A gamble implies risk and uncertain outcome, not a guaranteed success.

traps: Extreme words (always, never, only) are red flags.
Inference ≠ guess: stay close to the text.
Check for NOT/EXCEPT in the question.
